Despite his popularity with the people of the Arab world, by mid-1957 his only regional ally was Syria.[160] In September, Turkish troops massed along the Syrian border, giving credence to rumors that the Baghdad Pact countries were attempting to topple Syria's leftist government.[160] Nasser sent a contingent force to Syria as a symbolic display of solidarity, further elevating his prestige in the Arab world, and particularly among Syrians.[160]

As political instability grew in Syria, delegations from the country were sent to Nasser demanding immediate unification with Egypt.[161] Nasser initially turned down the request, citing the two countries' incompatible political and economic systems, lack of contiguity, the Syrian military's record of intervention in politics, and the deep factionalism among Syria's political forces.[161] However, in January 1958, a second Syrian delegation managed to convince Nasser of an impending communist takeover and a consequent slide to civil strife.[162] Nasser subsequently opted for union, albeit on the condition that it would be a total political merger with him as its president, to which the delegates and Syrian president Shukri al-Quwatli agreed.[163] On 1 February, the United Arab Republic (UAR) was proclaimed and, according to Dawisha, the Arab world reacted in "stunned amazement, which quickly turned into uncontrolled euphoria."[164] Nasser ordered a crackdown against Syrian communists, dismissing many of them from their governmental posts.[165][166]

Nasser seated alongside Crown Prince Muhammad al-Badr of North Yemen (center) and Shukri al-Quwatli (right), February 1958. North Yemen joined the UAR to form the United Arab States, a loose confederation.

On a surprise visit to Damascus to celebrate the union on 24 February, Nasser was welcomed by crowds in the hundreds of thousands.[167] Crown Prince Imam Badr of North Yemen was dispatched to Damascus with proposals to include his country in the new republic. Nasser agreed to establish a loose federal union with Yemen—the United Arab States—in place of total integration.[168] While Nasser was in Syria, King Saud planned to have him assassinated on his return flight to Cairo.[169] On 4 March, Nasser addressed the masses in Damascus and waved before them the Saudi check given to Syrian security chief and, unbeknownst to the Saudis, ardent Nasser supporter Abdel Hamid Sarraj to shoot down Nasser's plane.[170] As a consequence of Saud's plot, he was forced by senior members of the Saudi royal family to informally cede most of his powers to his brother, King Faisal, a major Nasser opponent who advocated pan-Islamic unity over pan-Arabism.[171]

A day after announcing the attempt on his life, Nasser established a new provisional constitution proclaiming a 600-member National Assembly (400 from Egypt and 200 from Syria) and the dissolution of all political parties.[171] Nasser gave each of the provinces two vice-presidents: Boghdadi and Amer in Egypt, and Sabri al-Asali and Akram al-Hawrani in Syria.[171] Nasser then left for Moscow to meet with Nikita Khrushchev. At the meeting, Khrushchev pressed Nasser to lift the ban on the Communist Party, but Nasser refused, stating it was an internal matter which was not a subject of discussion with outside powers. Khrushchev was reportedly taken aback and denied he had meant to interfere in the UAR's affairs. The matter was settled as both leaders sought to prevent a rift between their two countries.[172]

With the establishment of the United Arab Republic, the United States under President Eisenhower attempted to build better relations and initiate a rapprochement between the two countries, contrasting with the previously cautious stance of the American government towards Nasser.[173] In particular, Nasser sought American assistance in his ideological cold war with Abdel Karim Qasim in Iraq and his ideology of Qasimism, which conflicted with Nasser's pan-Arab nationalism.[174] However, due to major ideological differences, no significant long-term working relationship developed between Nasser and Eisenhower.[173]

Influence on the Arab world

The holy march on which the Arab nation insists, will carry us forward from one victory to another ... the flag of freedom which flies over Baghdad today will fly over Amman and Riyadh. Yes, the flag of freedom which flies over Cairo, Damascus, and Baghdad today will fly over the rest of the Middle East ...

— Gamal Abdel Nasser, 19 July in Damascus[175]

In Lebanon, clashes between pro-Nasser factions and supporters of staunch Nasser opponent, then-President Camille Chamoun, culminated in civil strife by May.[176] The former sought to unite with the UAR, while the latter sought Lebanon's continued independence.[176] Nasser delegated oversight of the issue to Sarraj, who provided limited aid to Nasser's Lebanese supporters through money, light arms, and officer training[177]—short of the large-scale support that Chamoun alleged.[178][179] Nasser did not covet Lebanon, seeing it as a "special case", but sought to prevent Chamoun from a second presidential term.[180] In Oman, the Jebel Akhdar War between the rebels in the interior of Oman against the British-backed Sultanate of Oman prompted Nasser to support the rebels in what was considered a war against colonialism between 1954 and 1959.[181][182]

Nasser (right) and Lebanese president Fuad Chehab (to Nasser's right) at the Syrian–Lebanese border during talks to end the crisis in Lebanon. Akram al-Hawrani stands third to Nasser's left, and Abdel Hamid Sarraj stands to Chehab's right, March 1959.

On 14 July 1958, Iraqi army officers Abdel Karim Qasim and Abdel Salam Aref overthrew the Iraqi monarchy and, the next day, Iraqi prime minister and Nasser's chief Arab antagonist, Nuri al-Said, was killed.[183] The entire Iraqi royal family was killed, and Al-Said's and Iraqi crown prince 'Abd al-Ilah's bodies were mutilated and dragged across Baghdad.[184] Nasser recognized the new government and stated that "any attack on Iraq was tantamount to an attack on the UAR".[185] On 15 July, US marines landed in Lebanon, and British special forces in Jordan, upon the request of those countries' governments to prevent them from falling to pro-Nasser forces. Nasser felt that the revolution in Iraq left the road for pan-Arab unity unblocked.[185] On 19 July, for the first time, he declared that he was opting for full Arab union, although he had no plan to merge Iraq with the UAR.[175] While most members of the Iraqi Revolutionary Command Council (RCC) favored Iraqi-UAR unity,[186] Qasim sought to keep Iraq independent and resented Nasser's large popular base in the country.[183]

In the fall of 1958, Nasser formed a tripartite committee consisting of Zakaria Mohieddin, al-Hawrani, and Salah Bitar to oversee developments in Syria.[187] By moving the latter two, who were Ba'athists, to Cairo, he neutralized important political figures who had their own ideas about how Syria should be run.[187] He put Syria under Sarraj, who effectively reduced the province to a police state by imprisoning and exiling landholders who objected to the introduction of Egyptian agricultural reform in Syria, as well as communists.[187] Following the Lebanese election of Fuad Chehab in September 1958, relations between Lebanon and the UAR improved considerably.[188] On 25 March 1959, Chehab and Nasser met at the Lebanese–Syrian border and compromised on an end to the Lebanese crisis.[188]

Nasser waving to crowds in Damascus, Syria, October 1960

Relations between Nasser and Qasim grew increasingly bitter on 9 March,[189] after Qasim's forces suppressed a rebellion in Mosul, launched a day earlier by a pro-Nasser Iraqi RCC officer backed by UAR authorities.[190] Nasser had considered dispatching troops to aid his Iraqi sympathizers, but decided against it.[191] He clamped down on Egyptian communist activity due to the key backing Iraqi communists provided Qasim. Several influential communists were arrested, including Nasser's old comrade Khaled Mohieddin, who had been allowed to re-enter Egypt in 1956.[189]

By December, the political situation in Syria was faltering and Nasser responded by appointing Amer as governor-general alongside Sarraj. Syria's leaders opposed the appointment and many resigned from their government posts. Nasser later met with the opposition leaders and in a heated moment, exclaimed that he was the elected president of the UAR and those who did not accept his authority could "walk away".[187]

Collapse of the union and aftermath

Opposition to the union mounted among some of Syria's key elements,[192] namely the socioeconomic, political, and military elites.[193] In response to Syria's worsening economy, which Nasser attributed to its control by the bourgeoisie, in July 1961, Nasser decreed socialist measures that nationalized wide-ranging sectors of the Syrian economy.[194] He also dismissed Sarraj in September to curb the growing political crisis. Aburish states that Nasser was not fully capable of addressing Syrian problems because they were "foreign to him".[195] In Egypt, the economic situation was more positive, with a GNP growth of 4.5 percent and a rapid growth of industry.[195] In 1960, Nasser nationalized the Egyptian press, which had already been cooperating with his government, in order to steer coverage towards the country's socioeconomic issues and galvanize public support for his socialist measures.[91]

On 28 September 1961, secessionist army units launched a coup in Damascus, declaring Syria's secession from the UAR.[196] In response, pro-union army units in northern Syria revolted and pro-Nasser protests occurred in major Syrian cities.[193] Nasser sent Egyptian Special Forces to Latakia to bolster his allies, but withdrew them two days later, citing a refusal to allow inter-Arab fighting.[197] Addressing the UAR's breakup on 5 October,[198] Nasser accepted personal responsibility[197] and declared that Egypt would recognize an elected Syrian government.[198] He privately blamed interference by hostile Arab governments.[197] According to Heikal, Nasser suffered something resembling a nervous breakdown after the dissolution of the union; he began to smoke more heavily and his health began to deteriorate.[197]

Revival on regional stage
See also: North Yemen Civil War
Nasser (center) receiving Algerian president Ahmed Ben Bella (right) and Iraqi president Abdel Salam Aref (left) for the Arab League summit in Alexandria, September 1964. Ben Bella and Aref were close allies of Nasser.

Nasser's regional position changed unexpectedly when Yemeni officers led by Nasser supporter Abdullah al-Sallal overthrew Imam Badr of North Yemen on 27 September 1962.[199] Al-Badr and his tribal partisans began receiving increasing support from Saudi Arabia to help reinstate the kingdom, while Nasser subsequently accepted a request by Sallal to militarily aid the new government on 30 September.[200] Consequently, Egypt became increasingly embroiled in the drawn-out civil war, with 60,000 Egyptian soldiers deployed in North Yemen in March 1966. In August 1967, in order to make up for Egyptian losses during the Six-Day War, Nasser recalled 15,000 troops from North Yemen. As part of the Khartoum Resolution at the 1967 Arab League summit in the same month, Egypt announced that it was ready to withdraw all its soldiers from North Yemen and it did so by the end of 1967.[200] 26,000 Egyptian soldiers were killed during the intervention.[201] Most of Nasser's old colleagues had questioned the wisdom of continuing the war, but Amer reassured Nasser of their coming victory.[202] Nasser later remarked in 1968 that intervention in Yemen was a "miscalculation".[200]

In July 1962, Algeria became independent of France.[202] As a staunch political and financial supporter of the Algerian independence movement, Nasser considered the country's independence to be a personal victory.[202] Amid these developments, a pro-Nasser clique in the Saudi royal family led by Prince Talal defected to Egypt, along with the Jordanian chief of staff, in early 1963.[203]

On 8 February 1963, a military coup in Iraq led by a Ba'athist–Nasserist alliance toppled Qasim, who was subsequently shot dead. Abdel Salam Aref, a Nasserist, was chosen to be the new president.[202] A similar alliance toppled the Syrian government on 8 March.[204] On 14 March, the new Iraqi and Syrian governments sent Nasser delegations to push for a new Arab union.[205] At the meeting, Nasser lambasted the Ba'athists for "facilitating" Syria's split from the UAR,[206] and asserted that he was the "leader of the Arabs".[205] A transitional unity agreement stipulating a federal system[205] was signed by the parties on 17 April and the new union was set to be established in May 1965.[207] However, the agreement fell apart weeks later when Syria's Ba'athists purged Nasser's supporters from the officers corps. A failed counter-coup by a Nasserist colonel followed, after which Nasser condemned the Ba'athists as "fascists".[208]

Nasser before Yemeni crowds on his arrival to Sanaa, April 1964. In front of Nasser and giving a salute is Yemeni President Abdullah al-Sallal

In January 1964, Nasser called for an Arab League summit in Cairo to establish a unified Arab response against Israel's plans to divert the Jordan River's waters for economic purposes, which Syria and Jordan deemed an act of war.[209] Nasser blamed Arab divisions for what he deemed "the disastrous situation".[210] He discouraged Syria and Palestinian guerrillas from provoking the Israelis, conceding that he had no plans for war with Israel.[210] During the summit, Nasser developed cordial relations with King Hussein, and ties were mended with the rulers of Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Morocco.[209] In May, Nasser moved to formally share his leadership position over the Palestine issue[210] by initiating the creation of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO).[210][211] In practice, Nasser used the PLO to wield control over the Palestinian fedayeen.[211] Its head was to be Ahmad Shukeiri, Nasser's personal nominee.[210]

After years of foreign policy coordination and developing ties, Nasser, President Sukarno of Indonesia, President Tito of Yugoslavia, and Prime Minister Nehru of India founded the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) in 1961.[212] Its declared purpose was to solidify international non-alignment and promote world peace amid the Cold War, end colonization, and increase economic cooperation among developing countries.[213] In 1964, Nasser was made president of the NAM and held the second conference of the organization in Cairo.[214]

Nasser played a significant part in the strengthening of African solidarity in the late 1950s and early 1960s, although his continental leadership role had increasingly passed to Algeria since 1962.[215] During this period, Nasser made Egypt a refuge for anti-colonial leaders from several African countries and allowed the broadcast of anti-colonial propaganda from Cairo.[215] Beginning in 1958, Nasser had a key role in the discussions among African leaders that led to the establishment of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) in 1963.[215]

Modernization efforts and internal dissent
Government officials attending Friday prayers at al-Azhar Mosque, 1959. From left to right; Interior Minister Zakaria Mohieddin, Nasser, Social Affairs Minister Hussein el-Shafei and National Union Secretary Anwar Sadat
Al-Azhar

In 1961, Nasser sought to firmly establish Egypt as the leader of the Arab world and to promote a second revolution in Egypt with the purpose of merging Islamic and socialist thinking.[216] To achieve this, he initiated several reforms to modernize al-Azhar, which serves as the de facto leading authority in Sunni Islam, and to ensure its prominence over the Muslim Brotherhood and the more conservative Wahhabism promoted by Saudi Arabia.[216] Nasser had used al-Azhar's most willing ulema (scholars) as a counterweight to the Brotherhood's Islamic influence, starting in 1953.[71]

Nasser instructed al-Azhar to create changes in its syllabus that trickled to the lower levels of Egyptian education, consequently allowing the establishment of coeducational schools and the introduction of evolution into school curriculum. The reforms also included the merger of religious and civil courts.[216] Moreover, Nasser forced al-Azhar to issue a fatwā admitting Shia Muslims, Alawites, and Druze into mainstream Islam; for centuries prior, al-Azhar deemed them to be "heretics".[216]

Rivalry with Amer

Following Syria's secession, Nasser grew concerned with Amer's inability to train and modernize the army, and with the state within a state Amer had created in the military command and intelligence apparatus.[217][218] In late 1961, Nasser established the Presidential Council and decreed it the authority to approve all senior military appointments, instead of leaving this responsibility solely to Amer.[219][220] Moreover, he instructed that the primary criterion for promotion should be merit and not personal loyalties.[219] Nasser retracted the initiative after Amer's allies in the officers corps threatened to mobilize against him.[220]

In early 1962 Nasser again attempted to wrest control of the military command from Amer.[220] Amer responded by directly confronting Nasser for the first time and secretly rallying his loyalist officers.[219][221] Nasser ultimately backed down, wary of a possible violent confrontation between the military and his civilian government.[222] According to Boghdadi, the stress caused by the UAR's collapse and Amer's increasing autonomy forced Nasser, who already had diabetes, to practically live on painkillers from then on.[223]

National Charter and second term
Nasser being sworn in for a second term as Egypt's president, 25 March 1965

In October 1961, Nasser embarked on a major nationalization program for Egypt, believing the total adoption of socialism was the answer to his country's problems and would have prevented Syria's secession.[224] In order to organize and solidify his popular base with Egypt's citizens and counter the army's influence, Nasser introduced the National Charter in 1962 and a new constitution.[217] The charter called for universal health care, affordable housing, vocational schools, greater women's rights and a family planning program, as well as widening the Suez Canal.[217]

Nasser also attempted to maintain oversight of the country's civil service to prevent it from inflating and consequently becoming a burden to the state.[217] New laws provided workers with a minimum wage, profit shares, free education, free health care, reduced working hours, and encouragement to participate in management. Land reforms guaranteed the security of tenant farmers,[225] promoted agricultural growth, and reduced rural poverty.[226] As a result of the 1962 measures, government ownership of Egyptian business reached 51 percent,[227] and the National Union was renamed the Arab Socialist Union (ASU).[224] With these measures came more domestic repression, as thousands of Islamists were imprisoned, including dozens of military officers.[224] Nasser's tilt toward a Soviet-style system led his aides Boghdadi and Hussein el-Shafei to submit their resignations in protest.[199]

During the presidential referendum in Egypt, Nasser was re-elected to a second term as UAR president and took his oath on 25 March 1965. He was the only candidate for the position, with virtually all of his political opponents forbidden by law from running for office, and his fellow party members reduced to mere followers. That same year, Nasser had the Muslim Brotherhood chief ideologue Sayyed Qutb imprisoned.[228] Qutb was charged and found guilty by the court of plotting to assassinate Nasser, and was executed in 1966.[228] Beginning in 1966, as Egypt's economy slowed and government debt became increasingly burdensome, Nasser began to ease state control over the private sector, encouraging state-owned bank loans to private business and introducing incentives to increase exports.[229] During the '60s, the Egyptian economy went from sluggishness to the verge of collapse, the society became less free, and Nasser's appeal waned considerably.[230]

Six-Day War
Main article: Six-Day War
Nasser (center), King Hussein of Jordan (left) and Egyptian Army Chief of Staff Abdel Hakim Amer (right) at the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces headquarters in Cairo before signing a mutual defense pact, 30 May 1967

In mid May 1967, the Soviet Union issued warnings to Nasser of an impending Israeli attack on Syria, although Chief of Staff Mohamed Fawzi considered the warnings to be "baseless".[231][232] According to Kandil, without Nasser's authorization, Amer used the Soviet warnings as a pretext to dispatch troops to Sinai on 14 May, and Nasser subsequently demanded UNEF's withdrawal.[232][233] Earlier that day, Nasser received a warning from King Hussein of Israeli-American collusion to drag Egypt into war.[234] The message had been originally received by Amer on 2 May, but was withheld from Nasser until the Sinai deployment on 14 May.[234][235] Although in the preceding months, Hussein and Nasser had been accusing each other of avoiding a fight with Israel,[236] Hussein was nonetheless wary that an Egyptian–Israeli war would risk the West Bank's occupation by Israel.[234] Nasser still felt that the US would restrain Israel from attacking due to assurances that he received from the US and Soviet Union.[237] In turn, he also reassured both powers that Egypt would only act defensively.[237]

On 21 May, Amer asked Nasser to order the Straits of Tiran blockaded, a move Nasser believed Israel would use as a casus belli.[234] Amer reassured him that the army was prepared for confrontation,[238][239] but Nasser doubted Amer's assessment of the military's readiness.[238] According to Nasser's vice president Zakaria Mohieddin, although "Amer had absolute authority over the armed forces, Nasser had his ways of knowing what was really going on".[240] Moreover, Amer anticipated an impending Israeli attack and advocated a preemptive strike.[241][242] Nasser refused the call[242][243] upon determination that the air force lacked pilots and Amer's handpicked officers were incompetent.[243] Still, Nasser concluded that if Israel attacked, Egypt's quantitative advantage in manpower and arms could stave off Israeli forces for at least two weeks, allowing for diplomacy towards a ceasefire.[244] Israel repeated declarations it had made in 1957 that any closure of the Straits would be considered an act of war, or justification for war, but Nasser closed the Straits to Israeli shipping on 22–23 May. Towards the end of May, Nasser increasingly exchanged his positions of deterrence for deference to the inevitability of war,[244][245] under increased pressure to act by both the general Arab populace and various Arab governments.[231][246] On 26 May Nasser declared, "our basic objective will be to destroy Israel".[247] On 30 May, King Hussein committed Jordan in an alliance with Egypt and Syria.[248]

Some of the attending heads of state at the Arab League Summit in Khartoum following the Six-Day War. From left to right: Faisal of Saudi Arabia, Nasser, Abdullah al-Sallal of Yemen, Sabah Al-Salim Al-Sabah of Kuwait and Abd al-Rahman Arif of Iraq, 2 September 1967

On the morning of 5 June, the Israeli Air Force struck Egyptian air fields, destroying much of the Egyptian Air Force. Before the day ended, Israeli armored units had cut through Egyptian defense lines and captured the town of el-Arish.[249] The next day, Amer ordered the immediate withdrawal of Egyptian troops from Sinai—causing the majority of Egyptian casualties during the war.[250] Israel quickly captured Sinai and the Gaza Strip from Egypt, the West Bank from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria.

According to Sadat, it was only when the Israelis cut off the Egyptian garrison at Sharm el-Sheikh that Nasser became aware of the situation's gravity.[249] After hearing of the attack, he rushed to army headquarters to inquire about the military situation.[251] The simmering conflict between Nasser and Amer subsequently came to the fore, and officers present reported the pair burst into "a nonstop shouting match".[251] The Supreme Executive Committee, set up by Nasser to oversee the conduct of the war, attributed the repeated Egyptian defeats to the Nasser–Amer rivalry and Amer's overall incompetence.[249] According to Egyptian diplomat Ismail Fahmi, who became foreign minister during Sadat's presidency, the Israeli invasion and Egypt's consequent defeat was a result of Nasser's dismissal of all rational analysis of the situation and his undertaking of a series of irrational decisions.[252]

Resignation and aftermath

I have taken a decision with which I need your help. I have decided to withdraw totally and for good from any official post or political role, and to return to the ranks of the masses, performing my duty in their midst, like any other citizen. This is a time for action, not grief. ... My whole heart is with you, and let your hearts be with me. May God be with us—hope, light, and guidance in our hearts.

— Nasser's 9 June resignation speech, which was retracted the next day[253]
Egyptian demonstrators protesting Nasser's resignation, 1967

During the first four days of the war, the general population of the Arab world believed Arab radio station fabrications of imminent Arab victory.[253] On 9 June, Nasser appeared on television to inform Egypt's citizens of their country's defeat.[253][254] He announced his resignation on television later that day, and ceded all presidential powers to his then-Vice President Zakaria Mohieddin, who had no prior information of this decision and refused to accept the post.[254] It was in this resignation speech that the Six Day War was first called the "setback". The second sentence of his speech ran: "We cannot hide from ourselves the fact that we have met with a grave setback [naksa] in the last few days"—the "naksa" or "setback" for Egypt being the destruction of its armed forces, the loss of the entire Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza region, and the national humiliation and disgrace of losing a war to the vastly smaller Israeli Army.

Hundreds of thousands of sympathizers poured into the streets in mass demonstrations throughout Egypt and across the Arab world rejecting his resignation,[255] chanting, "We are your soldiers, Gamal!"[256] Nasser retracted his decision the next day.[256]

On 11 July, Nasser replaced Amer with Mohamed Fawzi as general commander,[257][258] over the protestations of Amer's loyalists in the military, 600 of whom marched on army headquarters and demanded Amer's reinstatement.[259] After Nasser sacked thirty of the loyalists in response,[259] Amer and his allies devised a plan to topple him on 27 August.[260] Nasser was tipped off about their activities and, after several invitations, he convinced Amer to meet him at his home on 24 August.[260] Nasser confronted Amer about the coup plot, which he denied before being arrested by Mohieddin. Amer allegedly committed suicide (others claims state he was poisoned) on 14 September.[261] Despite his souring relationship with Amer, Nasser spoke of losing "the person closest to [him]".[262] Thereafter, Nasser began a process of depoliticizing the armed forces, arresting dozens of leading military and intelligence figures loyal to Amer.[261]

At the 29 August Arab League summit in Khartoum, Nasser's usual commanding position had receded as the attending heads of state expected Saudi King Faisal to lead. A ceasefire in the Yemen War was declared and the summit concluded with the Khartoum Resolution,[263] which, according to Abd al Azim Ramadan, left only one option—a war with Israel.[264]

The Soviet Union soon resupplied the Egyptian military with about half of its former arsenals and broke diplomatic relations with Israel. Nasser cut relations with the US following the war, and, according to Aburish, his policy of "playing the superpowers against each other" ended.[265] In November, Nasser accepted UN Resolution 242, which called for Israel's withdrawal from territories acquired in the war. His supporters claimed Nasser's move was meant to buy time to prepare for another confrontation with Israel, while his detractors believed his acceptance of the resolution signaled a waning interest in Palestinian independence.[266]

Final years of presidency
Domestic reforms and governmental changes
Nasser delivering his final speech to the nation on 23 July 1970

Nasser appointed himself the additional roles of prime minister and supreme commander of the armed forces on 19 June 1967.[267] From 3–4 August 1967, the Arab Socialist Union (ASU)'s executive committee held a debate wherein Nasser bitterly attacked the current single-party system and proposed the creation of a second party.[268] This 'real opposition' would be led by Free Officers Abdel Latif Boghdadi and Kamal el-Din Hussein,[269] who were both former government members who had resigned following differences with Nasser's policies. It would also have been granted access to the same resources enjoyed by the ASU, including its own newspaper. Parliament would be dissolved to make way for elections in December.[269] However, this proposal was met with resistance from his inner circle, including Zakaria Mohieddin and Sadat, who raised concerns about potential economic instability caused by a two-party system and argued that the timing of the move was unsuitable given the current crisis.[270] Nasser's proposal was not implemented.

Angry at the military court's perceived leniency with air force officers charged with negligence during the 1967 war, workers and students launched protests calling for major political reforms in late February 1968.[271][272] Nasser responded to the demonstrations, the most significant public challenge to his rule since workers' protests in March 1954, by removing most military figures from his cabinet and appointing eight civilians in place of several high-ranking members of the ASU.[273][274] By 3 March, Nasser directed Egypt's intelligence apparatus to focus on external rather than domestic espionage, and declared the "fall of the mukhabarat state".[274]

On 30 March, Nasser proclaimed a manifesto stipulating the restoration of civil liberties, greater parliamentary independence from the executive,[272] major structural changes to the ASU, and a campaign to rid the government of corrupt elements.[273] A public referendum approved the proposed measures in May, and held subsequent elections for the Supreme Executive Committee, the ASU's highest decision-making body.[272] Observers noted that the declaration signaled an important shift from political repression to liberalization, although its promises would largely go unfulfilled.[273]

Nasser appointed Sadat and Hussein el-Shafei as his vice presidents in December 1969. By then, relations with his other original military comrades, namely Khaled and Zakaria Mohieddin and former vice president Sabri, had become strained.[275] By mid-1970, Nasser pondered replacing Sadat with Boghdadi after reconciling with the latter.[276]

War of Attrition and regional diplomatic initiatives
Nasser observing the Suez front with Egyptian officers during the War of Attrition. General Commander Mohamed Fawzi is directly behind Nasser, and to their left is Chief of Staff Abdel Moneim Riad, November 1968
Nasser brokering a ceasefire between Yasser Arafat of the PLO (left) and King Hussein of Jordan (right) at the emergency Arab League summit in Cairo on 27 September 1970, one day before Nasser's death

Meanwhile, in January 1968, Nasser commenced the War of Attrition to reclaim territory captured by Israel, ordering attacks against Israeli positions east of the then-blockaded Suez Canal.[277] In March, Nasser offered Yasser Arafat's Fatah movement arms and funds after their performance against Israeli forces in the Battle of Karameh that month.[278] He also advised Arafat to think of peace with Israel and the establishment of a Palestinian state comprising the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.[278] Nasser effectively ceded his leadership of the "Palestine issue" to Arafat.[266]

Israel retaliated against Egyptian shelling with commando raids, artillery shelling and air strikes. This resulted in an exodus of civilians from Egyptian cities along the Suez Canal's western bank.[279][280][281] Nasser ceased all military activities and began a program to build a network of internal defenses, while receiving the financial backing of various Arab states.[281] The war resumed in March 1969.[281] In November, Nasser brokered an agreement between the PLO and the Lebanese military that granted Palestinian guerrillas the right to use Lebanese territory to attack Israel.[282]

In June 1970, Nasser accepted the US-sponsored Rogers Plan, which called for an end to hostilities and an Israeli withdrawal from Egyptian territory, but it was rejected by Israel, the PLO, and most Arab states except Jordan.[276] Nasser had initially rejected the plan, but conceded under pressure from the Soviet Union, which feared that escalating regional conflict could drag it into a war with the US.[283][284] He also determined that a ceasefire could serve as a tactical step toward the strategic goal of recapturing the Suez Canal.[285] Nasser forestalled any movement toward direct negotiations with Israel. In dozens of speeches and statements, Nasser posited the equation that any direct peace talks with Israel were tantamount to surrender.[286] Following Nasser's acceptance, Israel agreed to a ceasefire and Nasser used the lull in fighting to move surface-to-air missiles towards the canal zone.[283][284]

Meanwhile, tensions in Jordan between an increasingly autonomous PLO and King Hussein's government had been simmering;[287] following the Dawson's Field hijackings, a military campaign was launched to rout out PLO forces. The offensive elevated risks of a regional war and prompted Nasser to hold an emergency Arab League summit on 27 September in Cairo,[288] where he forged a ceasefire.[289]

Death and funeral
Main article: Death and state funeral of Gamal Abdel Nasser
Nasser's funeral procession attended by five million mourners in Cairo, 1 October 1970

As the Arab League summit closed on 28 September 1970, hours after escorting the last Arab leader to leave, Nasser suffered a heart attack. He was immediately transported to his house, where his physicians tended to him. Nasser died several hours later, around 6 p.m. at age 52.[290] Heikal, Sadat, and Nasser's wife Tahia were at his deathbed.[291] According to his doctor, al-Sawi Habibi, Nasser's likely cause of death was arteriosclerosis, varicose veins, and complications from long-standing diabetes. Nasser was also a heavy smoker with a family history of heart disease—two of his brothers died in their fifties from the same condition.[292] The state of Nasser's health was not known to the public prior to his death.[292][293] He had suffered heart attacks before, in 1966 and September 1969.[citation needed]

Following the announcement of Nasser's death, most Arabs were in a state of shock.[291] Nasser's funeral procession through Cairo on 1 October was attended by at least five million mourners.[294][295][296] The 10-kilometer (6.2 mi) procession to his burial site began at the old RCC headquarters with a flyover by MiG-21 jets. His flag-draped coffin was attached to a gun carriage pulled by six horses and led by a column of cavalrymen.[296] All Arab heads of state attended, with the exception of Saudi King Faisal.[297] King Hussein and Arafat cried openly, and Muammar Gaddafi of Libya fainted from emotional distress twice.[295] A few major non-Arab dignitaries were present, including Soviet Premier Alexei Kosygin and French Prime Minister Jacques Chaban-Delmas.[295]

Gamal Abdel Nasser Mosque in Cairo, the site of his burial

Almost immediately after the procession began, mourners engulfed Nasser's coffin chanting, "There is no God but Allah, and Nasser is God's beloved... Each of us is Nasser."[296] Police unsuccessfully attempted to quell the crowds and, as a result, most of the foreign dignitaries were evacuated.[296] The final destination was the Nasr Mosque, which was afterwards renamed Abdel Nasser Mosque, where Nasser was buried.[296]

Because of his ability to motivate nationalistic passions, "men, women, and children wept and wailed in the streets" after hearing of his death, according to Nutting.[290] The general Arab reaction was of mourning, with thousands of people pouring onto the streets of major cities throughout the Arab world.[296] Over a dozen people were killed in Beirut as a result of the chaos, and in Jerusalem, roughly 75,000 Arabs marched through the Old City chanting, "Nasser will never die."[296] As a testament to his unchallenged leadership of the Arab people, following his death, the headline of the Lebanese Le Jour read, "One hundred million human beings—the Arabs—are orphans."[298] Sherif Hetata, a former political prisoner[299] and later member of Nasser's ASU,[300] said that "Nasser's greatest achievement was his funeral. The world will never again see five million people crying together."[295]

Legacy
Nasser presenting prominent and blind writer Taha Hussein (standing in front of Nasser) with a national honors prize for literature, 1959

Nasser made Egypt fully independent of British influence,[301][302] and the country became a major power in the developing world under his leadership.[301] One of Nasser's main domestic efforts was to establish social justice, which he deemed a prerequisite to liberal democracy.[303] During his presidency, ordinary citizens enjoyed unprecedented access to housing, education, jobs, health services and nourishment, as well as other forms of social welfare, while feudalistic influence waned.[301][304]

However, these advances came at the expense of civil liberties. In Nasser's Egypt, the media were tightly controlled, mail was opened, and telephones were wiretapped.[305] He was elected in 1956, 1958 and 1965 in plebiscites in which he was the sole candidate, each time claiming unanimous or near-unanimous support. With few exceptions, the legislature did little more than approve Nasser's policies. As the legislature was made up almost entirely of government supporters, Nasser effectively held all governing power in the nation.

By the end of his presidency, employment and working conditions improved considerably, although poverty was still high in the country and substantial resources allocated for social welfare had been diverted to the war effort.[303]

The national economy grew significantly through agrarian reform, major modernization projects such as the Helwan steel works and the Aswan Dam, and nationalization schemes such as that of the Suez Canal.[301][304] However, the marked economic growth of the early 1960s took a downturn for the remainder of the decade, only recovering in 1970.[306] Egypt experienced a "golden age" of culture during Nasser's presidency, according to historian Joel Gordon, particularly in film, television, theater, radio, literature, fine arts, comedy, poetry, and music.[307] Egypt under Nasser dominated the Arab world in these fields,[304][307] producing cultural icons.[304]

During Mubarak's presidency, Nasserist political parties began to emerge in Egypt, the first being the Arab Democratic Nasserist Party (ADNP).[308][309] The party carried minor political influence,[310] and splits between its members beginning in 1995 resulted in the gradual establishment of splinter parties,[311] including Hamdeen Sabahi's 1997 founding of Al-Karama.[312] Sabahi came in third place during the 2012 presidential election.[313] Nasserist activists were among the founders of Kefaya, a major opposition force during Mubarak's rule.[312] On 19 September 2012, four Nasserist parties (the ADNP, Karama, the National Conciliation Party, and the Popular Nasserist Congress Party) merged to form the United Nasserist Party.[314]

Public image
Nasser speaking to a homeless Egyptian man and offering him a job, after the man was found sleeping below the stage where Nasser was seated, 1959

Nasser was known for his accessibility and direct relationship with ordinary Egyptians.[315][316] His availability to the public, despite assassination attempts against him, was unparalleled among his successors.[317] A skilled orator,[318] Nasser gave 1,359 speeches between 1953 and 1970, a record for any Egyptian head of state.[319] Historian Elie Podeh wrote that a constant theme of Nasser's image was "his ability to represent Egyptian authenticity, in triumph or defeat".[315] The national press also helped to foster his popularity and profile—more so after the nationalization of state media.[317] Historian Tarek Osman wrote:

The interplay in the Nasser 'phenomenon' between genuine expression of popular feeling and state-sponsored propaganda may sometimes be hard to disentangle. But behind it lies a vital historical fact: that Gamal Abdel Nasser signifies the only truly Egyptian developmental project in the country's history since the fall of the Pharaonic state. There had been other projects ... But this was different—in origin, meaning and impact. For Nasser was a man of the Egyptian soil who had overthrown the Middle East's most established and sophisticated monarchy in a swift and bloodless move—to the acclaim of millions of poor, oppressed Egyptians—and ushered in a programme of 'social justice', 'progress and development', and 'dignity'.[320]

Nasser waving to crowds in Mansoura, 1960

While Nasser was increasingly criticized by Egyptian intellectuals following the Six-Day War and his death in 1970, the general public was persistently sympathetic both during and after Nasser's life.[315] According to political scientist Mahmoud Hamad, writing in 2008, "nostalgia for Nasser is easily sensed in Egypt and all Arab countries today".[321] General malaise in Egyptian society, particularly during the Mubarak era, augmented nostalgia for Nasser's presidency, which increasingly became associated with the ideals of national purpose, hope, social cohesion, and vibrant culture.[307]

Until the present day, Nasser serves as an iconic figure throughout the Arab world,[301][322] a symbol of Arab unity and dignity,[323][324][325] and a towering figure in modern Middle Eastern history.[38] He is also considered a champion of social justice in Egypt.[326][327] Time writes that despite his mistakes and shortcomings, Nasser "imparted a sense of personal worth and national pride that [Egypt and the Arabs] had not known for 400 years. This alone may have been enough to balance his flaws and failures."[296]

Historian Steven A. Cook wrote in July 2013, "Nasser's heyday still represents, for many, the last time that Egypt felt united under leaders whose espoused principles met the needs of ordinary Egyptians."[328] During the Arab Spring, which resulted in a revolution in Egypt, photographs of Nasser were raised in Cairo and Arab capitals during anti-government demonstrations.[329][330] According to journalist Lamis Andoni, Nasser had become a "symbol of Arab dignity" during the mass demonstrations.[329]

Criticism
Anwar Sadat (left) and Nasser in the National Assembly, 1964. Sadat succeeded Nasser as president in 1970 and significantly departed from Nasser's policies throughout his rule.

Sadat declared his intention to "continue the path of Nasser" in his 7 October 1970 presidential inauguration speech,[331] but began to depart from Nasserist policies as his domestic position improved following the 1973 October War.[310][331] President Sadat's Infitah policy sought to open Egypt's economy for private investment.[332] According to Heikal, ensuing anti-Nasser developments until the present day led to an Egypt "[half] at war with Abdel-Nasser, half [at war] with Anwar El-Sadat".[304]

Nasser's Egyptian detractors considered him a dictator who thwarted democratic progress, imprisoned thousands of dissidents, and led a repressive administration responsible for numerous human rights violations.[304] Islamists in Egypt, particularly members of the politically persecuted Brotherhood, viewed Nasser as oppressive, tyrannical, and demonic.[333] Samer S. Shehata, who wrote an article on "The Politics of Laughter: Nasser, Sadat, and Mubarek in Egyptian Political Jokes" noted that "with the new regime came the end of parliamentary politics and political freedoms, including the right to organize political parties, and freedoms of speech and the press".[334] Liberal writer Tawfiq al-Hakim described Nasser as a "confused Sultan" who employed stirring rhetoric, but had no actual plan to achieve his stated goals.[332]

Some of Nasser's liberal and Islamist critics in Egypt, including the founding members of the New Wafd Party and writer Jamal Badawi, dismissed Nasser's popular appeal with the Egyptian masses during his presidency as being the product of successful manipulation and demagoguery.[335] Egyptian political scientist Alaa al-Din Desouki blamed the 1952 revolution's shortcomings on Nasser's concentration of power, and Egypt's lack of democracy on Nasser's political style and his government's limitations on freedom of expression and political participation.[336] American political scientist Mark Cooper asserted that Nasser's charisma and his direct relationship with the Egyptian people "rendered intermediaries (organizations and individuals) unnecessary".[337] He opined that Nasser's legacy was a "guarantee of instability" due to Nasser's reliance on personal power and the absence of strong political institutions under his rule.[337] Historian Abd al-Azim Ramadan wrote that Nasser was an irrational and irresponsible leader, blaming his inclination to solitary decision-making for Egypt's losses during the Suez War, among other events.[338] Miles Copeland, Jr., a Central Intelligence Agency officer known for his close personal relationship with Nasser,[339] said that the barriers between Nasser and the outside world have grown so thick that all but the information that attest to his infallibility, indispensability, and immortality has been filtered out.[340]

Zakaria Mohieddin, who was Nasser's vice president, said that Nasser gradually changed during his reign. He ceased consulting his colleagues and made more and more of the decisions himself. Although Nasser repeatedly said that a war with Israel will start at a time of his, or Arab, choosing, in 1967 he started a bluffing game "but a successful bluff means your opponent must not know which cards you are holding. In this case Nasser's opponent could see his hand in the mirror and knew he was only holding a pair of deuces" and Nasser knew that his army is not prepared yet. "All of this was out of character...His tendencies in this regard may have been accentuated by diabetes... That was the only rational explanation for his actions in 1967".[240]

Antisemitism allegations

During an interview with Gerhard Frey in the German neo-Nazi newspaper National-Zeitung on May 1, 1964, Nasser said that "no person, not even the most simple one, takes seriously the lie of the six million Jews that were murdered [in the Holocaust]."[341][342][343] However, he is not known to have ever again publicly called the figure of six million into question, perhaps because his advisors and East German contacts had advised him on the subject.[344] Nasser, convinced of its authenticity, also encouraged the distribution of the antisemitic fabrication The Protocols of the Elders of Zion. He believed that the Jews greatly influenced the global financial market and that they ultimately strove for world domination. Nasser also hired former Nazi officials like Johann von Leers to distribute antisemitic propaganda. He is, however, thought to have been more moderate in that regard than contemporary political powers like Young Egypt or the Muslim Brotherhood.[345][346]

Regional leadership
Jaafar Nimeiry of Sudan (left), Nasser, and Muammar Gaddafi of Libya (right) at the Tripoli Airport, 1969. Nimeiry and Gaddafi were influenced by Nasser's pan-Arabist ideas and the latter sought to succeed him as "leader of the Arabs".

Through his actions and speeches, and because he was able to symbolize the popular Arab will, Nasser inspired several nationalist revolutions in the Arab world.[320] He defined the politics of his generation and communicated directly with the public masses of the Arab world, bypassing the various heads of states of those countries—an accomplishment not repeated by other Arab leaders.[335] The extent of Nasser's centrality in the region made it a priority for incoming Arab nationalist heads of state to seek good relations with Egypt, in order to gain popular legitimacy from their own citizens.[347]

To varying degrees,[38] Nasser's statist system of government was continued in Egypt and emulated by virtually all Arab republics,[348] namely Algeria, Syria, Iraq, Tunisia, Yemen, Sudan, and Libya.[38][348] Ahmed Ben Bella, Algeria's first president, was a staunch Nasserist.[349] Abdullah al-Sallal drove out the king of North Yemen in the name of Nasser's pan-Arabism.[199] Other coups influenced by Nasser included those that occurred in Iraq in July 1958 and Syria in 1963.[350] Muammar Gaddafi, who overthrew the Libyan monarchy in 1969, considered Nasser his hero and sought to succeed him as "leader of the Arabs".[351] Also in 1969, Colonel Gaafar Nimeiry, a supporter of Nasser, took power in Sudan.[352] The Arab Nationalist Movement (ANM) helped spread Nasser's pan-Arabist ideas throughout the Arab world, particularly among the Palestinians, Syrians, and Lebanese,[353][354] and in South Yemen, the Persian Gulf, and Iraq.[354] While many regional heads of state tried to emulate Nasser, Podeh opined that the "parochialism" of successive Arab leaders "transformed imitation [of Nasser] into parody".[348]

Portrayal in film

In 1963, Egyptian director Youssef Chahine produced the film El Nasser Salah El Dine ("Saladin The Victorious"), which intentionally drew parallels between Saladin, considered a hero in the Arab world, and Nasser and his pan-Arabist policies.[355] Nasser is played by Ahmed Zaki in Mohamed Fadel's 1996 Nasser 56. The film set the Egyptian box office record at the time, and focused on Nasser during the Suez Crisis.[356][357] It is also considered a milestone in Egyptian and Arab cinema as the first film to dramatize the role of a modern-day Arab leader.[358] Together with the 1999 Syrian biopic Gamal Abdel Nasser, the films marked the first biographical movies about contemporary public figures produced in the Arab world.[359] He is portrayed by Amir Boutrous in the Netflix television series The Crown. Nasser is also portrayed by Amr Saad in the 2025 Egyptian film El Sett, a biopic about the iconic Egyptian singer and actress Umm Kulthum.[360][361]

Personal life
Nasser and his family in Manshiyat al-Bakri, 1963. From left to right, his daughter Mona, his wife Tahia Kazem, daughter Hoda, son Abdel Hakim, son Khaled, son Abdel Hamid, and Nasser.

In 1944, Nasser married Tahia Kazem (1920–1992), the daughter of a wealthy Iranian father and an Egyptian mother, both of whom had died when she was young. She had been introduced to Nasser through her brother, Abdel Hamid Kazim, a merchant friend of Nasser's, in 1943.[362] After their wedding, the couple moved into a house in Manshiyat al-Bakri, a suburb of Cairo, where they lived for the rest of their lives. Nasser's entry into the officer corps in 1937 secured him relatively well-paid employment in a society where most people lived in poverty.[29] Nasser and Tahia would sometimes discuss politics at home, but for the most part Nasser kept his career separate from his family life. He preferred to spend most of his free time with his children.[363]

Nasser and Tahia had two daughters and three sons:[364]

Hoda, b. 1945.
Mona, b. 1947.
Khalid, 1949–2011. The most active politically. Said to have co-founded (with Egyptian diplomat Mahmoud Noureddin [ar]) a secret leftist organization, Egypt's Revolution [ar] (Thawrat Miṣr), which was accused of assassinating Israeli members of the Shin Bet stationed in Egypt in the late 1980s. Khalid took refuge in Yugoslavia and was eventually pardoned by President Hosni Mubarak.
Abd al-Hamid, b. 1951.
Abd al-Hakim, b. 1955. Appears regularly in Egyptian and regional media, heads the museum dedicated to the life of his father.

Although he was a proponent of secular politics, Nasser was an observant Muslim who made the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca in 1954 and 1965.[365][366] He was known to be personally incorruptible,[367][368][369][370] a characteristic which further enhanced his reputation among the citizens of Egypt and the Arab world.[369] Nasser's personal hobbies included playing chess, photography, watching American films, reading Arabic, English, and French magazines, and listening to classical music.[371][372]

Nasser practices photography at his home in Cairo, 1969

Nasser was a chain smoker.[292][368][373] He maintained 18-hour workdays and rarely took time off for vacations. The combination of smoking and working long hours contributed to his poor health. He was diagnosed with diabetes in the early 1960s and by the time of his death in 1970, he also had arteriosclerosis, heart disease, and high blood pressure. He suffered two major heart attacks (in 1966 and 1969), and was on bed rest for six weeks after the second episode. State media reported that Nasser's absence from the public view at that time was a result of influenza.[292]

# Abstract 

In the mid-twentieth century, Gamal Abdel Nasser emerged as a powerful figure in Egypt and the rest of the Arab world, seeking to uplift the region in the era of decolonization. While contemporary scholars have analyzed Nasserism as a contradiction of itself, an ideology that originated as liberation but resulted in autocratic rule, less attention has been paid to instead break down what made Nasserism so appealing to his audience. I draw upon Max Weber’s theory of charismatic authority and Maurice Charland’s concept of constitutive rhetoric in interpreting Nasserism in three phases: as a political theory, as a ruling ideology, and as a legacy. I read The Philosophy of the Revolution , examine a selection of Nasser's speeches at moments of political crisis and victory, and then the works and addresses of subsequent leaders. Gamal Abdel Nasser’s power cannot be understood through conventional measures like the military success of Egypt during his rule, but through his application of rhetoric. This study shows the importance and method of accounting for rhetorical and charismatic effects in an understanding of populist leaders. 

Keywords: Nasser, constitutive rhetoric, charismatic authority, Pan-Arabism, 5

# Introduction 

For nearly two decades, Gamal Nasser stood as the symbolic voice of the Arab world. He emerged as a leading figure during the era of decolonization in the Global South amidst the backdrop of the Cold War, positioning himself not just as Egypt’s president, but a representative of a broader anti-imperialist movement in the Arab world, where he served as symbol of unity, resistance and a shared vision of greatness that transcended national borders. 

Nasser’s rise to power cannot be understood without factoring in the conditions that plagued Egypt during the mid-twentieth century. Before taking over, the United Kingdom held a large influence over the country, despite being granted independence in 1922, and the monarchy of King Farouk was ripe with corruption and political dissatisfaction. With this environment, the Free Officers, a group of nationalist military figures that included Nasser, orchestrated the 1952 Egyptian Revolution, ushering in a new political era for the nation. 

Nasser was nothing like the political elites that governed Egypt before the revolution. His military background created an image of a leader rooted in discipline and service to the nation. Nasser also presented himself as a leader capable of restoring the dignity of a nation that had been lost due to years of exploitation from colonial powers and corrupt elites. After his consolidation of power in 1954, the publication of his post-revolution memoirs, The Philosophy of the Revolution , outlined a political vision for the country that extended beyond national borders. 

This vision would come to define Nasser; he dreamed of turning a fragmented Arab world into a unified community bound by a shared culture, history, and destiny. The nationalization of the Suez Canal in 1956 marked the beginning of his effort, where it served as not only a direct challenge to European control and Egypt fully reclaiming its sovereignty, but 6

also a symbolic victory for Arabs across the entire region. His promotion of Pan-Arabism and founding of the United Arab Republic was an ambitious attempt to legitimize his vision by establishing a state built upon his ideals. His involvement in the Non-Aligned Movement positioned him as a leader unwilling to bend a knee to the Cold War superpowers. His adoption of Arab socialism further reinforced his image as a leader committed to the social justice of the Egyptian people and economic shift of the nation. 

Despite these achievements, Nasser’s leadership was not without setbacks. Syria’s secession from the United Arab Republic exposed the fact that national interests trumped the broader Pan-Arab vision. Egypt’s unintended long-term involvement in the North Yemen Civil War strained its military, economy, and relations amongst regional powers. Nasser’s most significant defeat came in the Six-Day War, which dealt a severe blow to his military, his credibility as a leader, and the true strength of Arab unity. 

These defeats raise an important question: how was Nasser able to maintain his political legitimacy despite these setbacks? Egypt’s military strength and geopolitical strategy fail to fully account for Nasser’s influence. His power has to be understood through his ability to shape narrative and construct identity. 

To examine Nasser through a rhetorical lens gives the answer to the stated question. To understand what gave him power requires one to look beyond standard measures of success to consider how one can gain power through identity and narrative. Nasser’s appeal was not fully derived from his control over Egypt or ability to achieve victory, but from how he shaped events to his own interpretation and gave it to the audience. His choice to frame defeats as minor setbacks to the Pan-Arab project and victories as collective achievements of the Arab world gave 7

a sense of unity and purpose to his audience, where the immediate outcomes did not matter, for it was all part of the bigger picture of full liberation in the region. 

Nasser’s case also gives insight into how political legitimacy can be constructed and maintained through the power of rhetoric. Through rhetoric, leaders can redefine an existing identity and influence one's perception of success and failure. 

Nasser’s leadership was fundamentally rooted in his use of charismatic authority and constitutive rhetoric. Through the latter, he redefined what it meant to be Egyptian and Arab, binding these two identities together through a shared destiny that transcended national borders. Through charismatic authority, he presented himself as the leader of the Arab struggle. Constitutive rhetoric was Nasser’s most powerful tool, for it’s what truly allowed him to export his appeal outside of Egypt by resonating with an audience that spanned the entire Arab world. Charismatic authority still served a role, where it allowed Nasser to serve as the embodiment of the Arab identity he created, thus becoming the leader of the Pan-Arab movement. But these mechanisms that allowed for his rise to power also had their limitations revealed once confronted with moments of crisis, particularly during setbacks and after Nasser’s death. By first analyzing how Nasser constructed his authority and rhetoric, analyzing how it functioned in moments of victory and defeat, and finally exploring how his legitimacy was adapted and reinterpreted by other leaders, this paper demonstrates that Nasserism was not just a political movement, but a rhetorical project whose strength ultimately depended on the very things that also limited it. 8

# Nasserism as a Theory 

Definition of Nasserism and its Employment in Other Works 

Nasserism is the political ideology of Gamal Nasser, one of the core leaders behind the 1952 Revolution. It dominated Egyptian politics for nearly twenty years from the 1950s up until 1970 after Nasser’s death. This ideology combines Pan-Arabism, Arab socialism, progressive social justice, and a state-capitalist form of economic development. Nasserism called for nationalization of a nation’s key economic industries, land reform to uplift the lower economic classes, and anti-Western intervention in the Middle East. Beginning in Egypt, it gained widespread support across the Arab world after the Suez Crisis of 1956 and served as a source of inspiration for similar movements across the world during the mid-20th century. 

Scholars present Nasser’s legacy in Egypt as a complex issue. Nasser is seen as the nation’s liberator that uplifted those overlooked by leaders before him, but he failed to grant the Egyptian people their political agency. 1 He brought about an era of left-wing dominance in Egyptian politics during his rule, yet he forced other groups of leftists to conform to his ideology under threats of imprisonment. His treatment angered them, but his other actions gained their admiration. This relationship spanned generations. A descendant of a man imprisoned under Nasser’s regime recounts: “He was a strange man! Even though he had imprisoned my father, I was incapable of hating him, for he was able to enroll me, thanks to him, in the faculty of medicine, like the children of the elite. Even when they were being tortured they chanted his name. They believed that what was happening to them was a kind of bitter misunderstanding.” 2

As the leader of Egypt, Nasser employed a unique blend of rhetoric and charisma throughout The Philosophy of the Revolution to legitimize his rule over the nation and role as leader of his Pan-Arab movement in the Arab world. Through the use of constitutive rhetoric–where a speaker constructs a collective identity into existence–Nasser not only redefines what it means to be an Egyptian, but also an Arab. Charismatic authority, legitimacy derived from personal appeal and extraordinary qualities, allowed Nasser to present his own proper leadership credentials to justify why he should be the leader of not just Egypt, but of the entire Arab world’s liberation movement. Constitutive rhetoric, however, cannot function on its own. It needs a leadership situation that makes it possible for success, and charismatic authority legitimizes one’s own success. 

The Philosophy of the Revolution 

The Philosophy of the Revolution is Nasser’s reflection on the 1952 Revolution. It expresses an ideological foundation for the revolution and his vision for Egypt’s future and the new role it can play in the Arab world and Global South. Originally distributed into three separate articles between 1953 and 1954, The Philosophy of the Revolution was officially published as a book available for worldwide distribution in 1955. 6 While the book does not explicitly discuss what happened the day of the revolution, it serves to justify the revolution’s actions and to be used as a blueprint for the future. In it, we see his firsthand employment of his rhetorical blend. The Philosophy of the Revolution was published during the consolidation of Nasser’s new regime, where he faced intense domestic instability and international pressure.

Constitutive Rhetoric: The Creation of a New Identity 

> C

onstitutive rhetoric was first articulated in Maurice Charland’s article, "Constitutive Rhetoric: the Case of the Peuple Québecéois. ” There he argues that rather than persuading individuals in groups that already exist, rhetoric can create a collective identity that individuals 16 

come to inhabit. Charland challenges the traditional understanding of rhetoric’s use to influence audiences that already exist. Instead, rhetoric calls a group of people into existence by addressing them as if they already exist. When individuals recognize themselves in an address, they become subjects of that rhetoric. 15 Over time, they are no longer French speaking Canadians, but become participants of a historical and politically active group. 

Rhetoric has the power to construct a unified identity by framing a group around a shared past, struggle, or destiny. Charland examines how political rhetoric created the identity of the “peuple québécois ” (Québécois people) as a distinct national identity. Québécois people were given a shared past through the oppression faced under British rule, a shared struggle through ongoing oppression under Canadian rule, and assigned a collective destiny with national sovereignty as the end goal. 16 By addressing individuals as members of a unified national group, they recognize themselves within that identity. They are no longer French-speaking Canadians, but become participants of a historical and politically active group. Nationalist rhetoric presents the new collective identity as having a shared history of oppression, current struggle, and future destiny. Past oppression now becomes a foundational trauma that began the uniting of the people within the identity together. The ongoing rule under Canada now becomes a continuation of the historical injustices under British rule, just now under a different subjugator. Painting it this way makes the provincial government seem like the bread and circus of the Québécois people, keeping them content enough so they remain unaware of the control the Canadian government still has. Sovereignty now becomes not just a single option among many, but now a necessity for the destiny of this group.

Constitutive rhetoric creates three ideological effects that change how individuals understand themselves, their history, and their freedom. The first is identity transcending “the limitations of the individual body and will.” 17 Shared identity transcends the limitations of the individual, where they no longer become singular actors fighting for a common goal, but are now members of the collective identity. The second is a connection between the living Québécois and the dead by providing a link between the French Canadian settlers and those today, legitimizing their territorial claims. 18 By connecting the Québécois people to French settlers, the rhetoric establishes a link that stretches across generations, it legitimizes the present territorial claims of Quebec. The people no longer become simple inhabitants of the land, but the inheritors of the land of their people. The final effect is the illusion of freedom. 19 The Québécois people are presented as freely striving for their independence, yet that is not the case. They are compelled by the rhetoric of a shared destiny to support independence not by choice, but from a narrative that demands it as the only outcome. 

Charland offers a framework to understand how Nasser constructed the identities of the Egyptian and Arab people, which he used to carry him forward in achieving his goals for Egypt and the Arab world. Throughout Nasser’s rhetoric, he utilizes constitutive rhetoric he redefines what it means to belong to these two identities, transforming them from cultural labels into a unified community. Like Charland’s analysis of the Québécois, Nasser places his audience within a historical struggle, where imperialism is framed as a shared past and present that binds the Arab world together.

# Application of Constitutive Rhetoric in TPotR 

Formation of the Egyptian Identity 

In TPotR, Nasser elevates the Egyptian people’s identity into historical agents, where they go from victims of the corrupt monarchy and colonialism into active participants of the nation’s new revolutionary destiny. He describes the July 23rd revolution as a “realisation of hope”. 20 Phrasing the revolution as a “realisation of hope” blends Egypt’s past, present, and future together. The past now becomes a period of dormant desire for change amongst the people, the present is that fulfillment of change, and the future is the continuation of Egypt’s destiny. The Egyptian people are no longer citizens witnessing a change in government, but inheritors of the nation’s new destiny and participants in how it gets to unfold. # Application of Charismatic Authority in TPotR 

Charismatic Authority: The Qualities of a Leader 

The concept of charismatic authority is best interpreted in Politics as a Vocation , an essay written by sociologist Max Weber. It explains the nature of politics, how political legitimacy is granted, and the kind of person for politics. 

Weber articulates three ways a leader can justify their own power. Traditional authority is granted through long standing customs, legal authority derives from the law, and charismatic authority is based upon “the absolutely personal devotion and personal confidence in revelation, heroism, or other qualities of individual leadership.” 30 Through charismatic authority, people obey not because of tradition nor because the law says so, but because they believe the leader has either unique qualities or is called upon to take upon the leadership role for a special reason. 31 

Charismatic authority is strong, yet incredibly fragile at the same time. While traditional authority relies on custom and legal authority relies on institutionalized laws, charismatic authority relies only on the belief that the leader has exceptional qualities. Legitimacy is only kept so long the people believe their leader continues to have these qualities. However, the power    

> 31 Ibid, 4.
> 30 Max Weber, Politics as a Vocation , (New York:Oxford University Press, 1946), 4.

23 

in charismatic authority comes from the ability to bypass institutions and traditions because it is not rooted in either. 

An individual with charismatic authority cannot solely rely on emotional appeal. They must have true dedication to the cause. Weber highlights two types of people in politics: one who “lives for” it and one who “lives off” it. A leader that strives for the former makes politics their life. They either enjoy the power from it or have meaning from it because he is fulfilling some sort of cause. The latter is someone that does politics simply to make an income. 32 Charismatic authority relies on the leader living for politics. The people must believe that their leader is genuinely committed to a moral cause, and that they are motivated not by self-interest. 

The biggest drawback of charismatic authority is its instability. No matter how long the legitimacy of a leader may last, it must undergo routinization to ensure its survivability. The leaders of a revolution cannot live forever, so to ensure their ideas do not die with them, they must institutionalize it within their state’s political structure, ensuring the survivability of the regime. This allows for a proper bureaucratic system to form, allowing the leadership to shift from one of charismatic authority to legal authority. 33 The regime moves from one built off a revolution and moral cause to a rules-based authority detached from having the people’s best interests at heart. In exchange for longevity, the passion common in charismatic authority is now dwindled. This presents a paradox: in order for the revolution to survive long after the leader, it must no longer carry aspects of the revolution. Revolution may bring about change, but only routinization can preserve the regime long after the death of the revolutionary. 

Weber’s analysis of charismatic authority offers a framework on how Nasser justified his leadership. He argues that charismatic authority relies on the people believing that the leader has

# Nasserism as a Theory in Practice 

How are Victories and Defeats Applied? 

In this section, I examine Nasser’s military and political victories and defeats through a rhetorical lens to reveal how his legitimacy depended on the ability to frame victories as proof of Arab unity, but it unraveled during defeats, which revealed the gap between theory and reality. The particular victories and defeats examined in this analysis serve a purpose of representing key moments when Nasser’s rhetoric was either reinforced or challenged in the Arab world. He grounded his leadership in charismatic authority, which presented him as not just Egypt’s president, but also the embodiment of a broader Arab struggle against imperialism. He formed a personal connection with audiences across the Arab world. But charismatic authority, while legitimizing his rule in Egypt, could only take him so far outside of the nation. It proved why he was a proper leader for his country, but why should other Arab nations see him as their liberator? His use of constitutive rhetoric to define not just what it meant to be Egyptian, but also Arab transformed two separate cultural or national identities into a community with a shared destiny. 

By linking these two identities together, the victories of the Egyptian people became the victories of the entire Arab world, further strengthening not just his legitimacy as a regional leader, but also the appeal of the Nasserist project. Yet while the victories of Nasserism strengthened his rhetoric, each defeat revealed the tensions and contradictions of Nasser’s grand vision. These events were moments the Nasserist project was put to the test. Victories such as the Suez Crisis showed how Nasser could transform an action that benefited Egypt into a symbolic victory for the Arab world, strengthening the appeal of him as a leader and of Pan-Arabism. Yet setbacks such as Syria’s secession from the United Arab Republic and the Six-Day War exposed 31 

the flaws of his vision. The specific cases reveal how Nasser’s authority was tied to how he could frame events rhetorically. Victories were easy to frame as evidence as to why his vision is right for the region, showing the strength of Arab unity and reinforcing his legitimacy across the region. But when they contradicted his narrative, the limitations of Nasserism’s real-world application became apparent. Yet when other leaders might have fallen, Nasser’s rhetoric framed these defeats as a setback that could be overcome. Though this could only go so far, and after the humiliation of the Six-Day War, Nasser was forced to take accountability for his failures.

The Suez Canal stood as a sore spot for Egyptian nationalists like Nasser. Their former colonizer still retained control over “the security of imperial communications, defense, the protection of foreign interests and minorities, and the Sudan.” 43 The “protection of foreign interests” referred directly to the continued control of the canal through the Suez Company, a company jointly controlled by French and British interests. The Suez Canal served as a vital artery of both global trade and power, allowing maritime commerce to travel directly from Europe to Asia from the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, which leads directly to the Indian Ocean, saving vital travel time, and it connected France and Britain to their colonies in Asia. What is the Third Persona? 

Along with charismatic authority and constitutive rhetoric, certain events allowed Nasser to use rhetoric in order to construct a “third persona,” or an “other”. This excluded group served as an opposition to Nasser’s vision, whether it was imperial powers or religious and national groups. Traditional rhetorical analysis only focuses on two groups in rhetoric–the speaker (first persona) and the intended audience (second persona)–while ignoring the possibility of a third group: those that the speaker intentionally excludes from who they see as their audience (third persona). 50 

The third persona is not just left out of the conversation, but they are invisible–the first persona does not even see them as worthy of being addressed. According to Philip Wander, the author who coined the term, it does not mean the excluded groups are not to be identified by “‘you’ and ‘I’...who are not to become part of ‘our’ audience or even be allowed to respond to what ‘we’ say”, it is a form of erasure where excluded groups become “non-subjects.” 51 This erasure is significant because it severs any ties the third persona has to the identity of the audience constructed by the speaker’s rhetoric. This goes beyond marginalization, where marginalized groups still have a voice in society (albeit smaller than non-marginalized groups). If a group is not the audience, but the “non-subject”, they have no voice or ability to challenge the speaker or attempt to claim membership in the new identity. The power of rhetoric lies not only in the ability to convince the audience to adapt their new identity, but its ability to set boundaries in who can be a part of this new group and who becomes excluded from recognition.

Nasser’s Victory Over the United States and Soviet Union 

A victory of Nasser was his ability to successfully balance relations with both the United States and the Soviet Union, where he gained economic and military support from both superpowers without bending the knee to either. 

Nasser did what he could to ensure Egypt did not become too reliant on either the United States or Soviet Union. He presented himself as a figure capable of defending his nation’s sovereignty. Nasser’s recognition of China was not an alignment with the Soviet Bloc, but an alignment of an alternative outside of superpower influence. However, his interaction with the United States was an outright refusal of alignment to one of the superpowers. His refusal to align with the United States despite financial coercion reinforced the image of an individual that cannot be corrupted and who prioritized his commitment to Egypt’s autonomy in a polarized world.
