# Nasserism as a Legacy 

The Death of Nasser 

With Nasser’s death, it marked not just the death of a leader, but the unraveling of a political system built around that leader. After eighteen years in power, he left behind a nation that was deeply shaped by his vision now uncertain on how to move forward without him. For the broader Arab world, the wandering role, originally held by Nasser, was now left vacant. His death revealed the collapse of his charismatic authority, which partly served as the foundation of his government’s legitimacy after the Egyptian Revolution, and the appeal of the Nasserist project across the Arab world. Unlike traditional or legal authority, his unique authority was difficult to replicate because there was only one Gamal Nasser, for his legitimacy was built upon his unique fusion of rhetoric that no successor could replicate. 

The death of Gamal Nasser left a power vacuum in Egypt and the rest of the Arab world, for the collapse of his charismatic authority and constitutive rhetoric after his death exposed the fragility of Nasserism being built around the individual that created it. However, it did not die with him. Instead, its core components were either adapted or reinterpreted by leaders in an attempt to form their legitimacy without the figure who once defined it. 

# Nasser’s Successors in Egypt 

Due to the fact that Nasser’s legitimacy was built around his unique qualities and rhetorical ability, his death Nasser meant that future Egyptian leaders were unable to replicate and carry on his legitimacy to support their own rule. Instead, post-Nasser leaders reconstructed 49 

his legitimacy through unique rhetorical strategies of their own. Anwar Sadat’s speeches to the People’s Assembly in Egypt and Israel’s Knesset indicate a shift from Nasser’s Pan-Arab rhetoric to a framework grounded in peace, the national interests of Egypt, and moral responsibility. Hosni Mubarak’s speech during the 2011 Egyptian revolution reveals his attempt to maintain his authority through nationalist rhetoric and casting himself as a necessary paternal figure for the country, even though the protests exposed the limitations of his legitimacy he built off stability and control. Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s “Democracy in the Middle East” 72 and resignation speech emphasizes gradual political change, security, and the legitimacy of those in power over the mass mobilization of the people desired by Nasser. Nasser’s charismatic leadership model did not die with him, but became reshaped to fit his successors in a far more state-centered government. This reflects the downside of charismatic authority–routinization–where in order for the regime to survive, the revolutionary characteristics needed to be abandoned in favor of a more stable and bureaucratic government. Seeing as Sadat was the first to take on the Egyptian presidency after Nasser’s death, he will serve as the first example.

# The Defining Legacy 

Nasser’s rise and mass appeal cannot be understood through just the conventional measures of political success. While his leadership was marked by significant achievements and failures, his ability to maintain legitimacy across the Arab world reveals a power rooted in rhetoric. Through constitutive rhetoric, Nasser redefined what it meant to be Arab, transforming the identity from that of just shared culture or language into one with a shared political destiny. His charismatic authority allowed him to serve as the embodiment of this identity, positioning himself as not just the president of Egypt, but also the leader of the broader Arab struggle. These working together are what allowed Nasser to escape from the confines of Egypt and extend his influence across the entire Arab world. 

The examination of Nasser’s victories and defeats reveal the strengths and limitations of the Nasserist project. During the nationalization of the Suez Canal, he reframed the outcome as a victory not just for Egypt, but the entire Arab world. His rhetoric reinforced a shared sense of pride and collective achievement. However, the collapse of the United Arab Republic exposed the tension between Arab unity and national interests, while Egypt’s role in the North Yemen Civil War weakened its image as a regional power. The most significant defeat was the Six-Day War, where it rattled Nasser’s credibility as a leader and the image of Arab unity. While rhetoric is powerful, it still cannot override political and military limitations. 

Despite these setbacks, Nasser’s influence did not collapse. Despite stepping down from the presidency after the devastating defeat in 1967, mass public support kept him in power. His choice to accept responsibility helped reinforce the people’s love for him and preserved legitimacy that otherwise might’ve been lost. Political legitimacy, when rooted in rhetoric, can 64 

endure conventional measures of political success, but it’s also heavily dependent on the outcome of reality. 

The fragility of charismatic authority became apparent after Nasser’s death in 1970. Successive leaders in Egypt were forced to reconstruct his legitimacy for their own political survival, but also departing from key aspects of Nasserism. Anwar Sadat shifted from Pan-Arabism and the collective Arab struggle in favor of prioritizing national interests and pursuing peace. Hosni Mubarak’s legitimacy was built off of the stale stability he offered, but it came crumbling down during the 2011 Egyptian Revolution. Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has drawn on some aspects of Nasser’s image through moral obligation, but differs from how political change should be brought about. 

Across the Arab world, leaders like Saddam Hussein, Muammar Gaddafi, and Hafez al-Assad fragmented Nasser’s rhetoric. While these leaders employ themes of the former Egyptian president, they lack the ability to resonate outside their own borders. There is great difficulty in reproducing legitimacy so closely tied to a specific individual.

His ability to construct a new Arab identity and position himself as its figurehead allowed him to achieve appeal that extended far beyond Egypt. But the setbacks during his time in power and the reinterpretation and fragmentation of his legitimacy after his death reveals the instability of a regime built on a charismatic figure and a constructed identity. # Abstract 

In the mid-twentieth century, Gamal Abdel Nasser emerged as a powerful figure in Egypt and the rest of the Arab world, seeking to uplift the region in the era of decolonization. While contemporary scholars have analyzed Nasserism as a contradiction of itself, an ideology that originated as liberation but resulted in autocratic rule, less attention has been paid to instead break down what made Nasserism so appealing to his audience. I draw upon Max Weber’s theory of charismatic authority and Maurice Charland’s concept of constitutive rhetoric in interpreting Nasserism in three phases: as a political theory, as a ruling ideology, and as a legacy. I read The Philosophy of the Revolution , examine a selection of Nasser's speeches at moments of political crisis and victory, and then the works and addresses of subsequent leaders. Gamal Abdel Nasser’s power cannot be understood through conventional measures like the military success of Egypt during his rule, but through his application of rhetoric. This study shows the importance and method of accounting for rhetorical and charismatic effects in an understanding of populist leaders. 

Keywords: Nasser, constitutive rhetoric, charismatic authority, Pan-Arabism, 5

# Introduction 

For nearly two decades, Gamal Nasser stood as the symbolic voice of the Arab world. He emerged as a leading figure during the era of decolonization in the Global South amidst the backdrop of the Cold War, positioning himself not just as Egypt’s president, but a representative of a broader anti-imperialist movement in the Arab world, where he served as symbol of unity, resistance and a shared vision of greatness that transcended national borders. 

Nasser’s rise to power cannot be understood without factoring in the conditions that plagued Egypt during the mid-twentieth century. Before taking over, the United Kingdom held a large influence over the country, despite being granted independence in 1922, and the monarchy of King Farouk was ripe with corruption and political dissatisfaction. With this environment, the Free Officers, a group of nationalist military figures that included Nasser, orchestrated the 1952 Egyptian Revolution, ushering in a new political era for the nation. 

Nasser was nothing like the political elites that governed Egypt before the revolution. His military background created an image of a leader rooted in discipline and service to the nation. Nasser also presented himself as a leader capable of restoring the dignity of a nation that had been lost due to years of exploitation from colonial powers and corrupt elites. After his consolidation of power in 1954, the publication of his post-revolution memoirs, The Philosophy of the Revolution , outlined a political vision for the country that extended beyond national borders. 

This vision would come to define Nasser; he dreamed of turning a fragmented Arab world into a unified community bound by a shared culture, history, and destiny. The nationalization of the Suez Canal in 1956 marked the beginning of his effort, where it served as not only a direct challenge to European control and Egypt fully reclaiming its sovereignty, but 6

also a symbolic victory for Arabs across the entire region. His promotion of Pan-Arabism and founding of the United Arab Republic was an ambitious attempt to legitimize his vision by establishing a state built upon his ideals. His involvement in the Non-Aligned Movement positioned him as a leader unwilling to bend a knee to the Cold War superpowers. His adoption of Arab socialism further reinforced his image as a leader committed to the social justice of the Egyptian people and economic shift of the nation. 

Despite these achievements, Nasser’s leadership was not without setbacks. Syria’s secession from the United Arab Republic exposed the fact that national interests trumped the broader Pan-Arab vision. Egypt’s unintended long-term involvement in the North Yemen Civil War strained its military, economy, and relations amongst regional powers. Nasser’s most significant defeat came in the Six-Day War, which dealt a severe blow to his military, his credibility as a leader, and the true strength of Arab unity. 

These defeats raise an important question: how was Nasser able to maintain his political legitimacy despite these setbacks? Egypt’s military strength and geopolitical strategy fail to fully account for Nasser’s influence. His power has to be understood through his ability to shape narrative and construct identity. 

To examine Nasser through a rhetorical lens gives the answer to the stated question. To understand what gave him power requires one to look beyond standard measures of success to consider how one can gain power through identity and narrative. Nasser’s appeal was not fully derived from his control over Egypt or ability to achieve victory, but from how he shaped events to his own interpretation and gave it to the audience. His choice to frame defeats as minor setbacks to the Pan-Arab project and victories as collective achievements of the Arab world gave 7

a sense of unity and purpose to his audience, where the immediate outcomes did not matter, for it was all part of the bigger picture of full liberation in the region. 

Nasser’s case also gives insight into how political legitimacy can be constructed and maintained through the power of rhetoric. Through rhetoric, leaders can redefine an existing identity and influence one's perception of success and failure. 

Nasser’s leadership was fundamentally rooted in his use of charismatic authority and constitutive rhetoric. Through the latter, he redefined what it meant to be Egyptian and Arab, binding these two identities together through a shared destiny that transcended national borders. Through charismatic authority, he presented himself as the leader of the Arab struggle. Constitutive rhetoric was Nasser’s most powerful tool, for it’s what truly allowed him to export his appeal outside of Egypt by resonating with an audience that spanned the entire Arab world. Charismatic authority still served a role, where it allowed Nasser to serve as the embodiment of the Arab identity he created, thus becoming the leader of the Pan-Arab movement. But these mechanisms that allowed for his rise to power also had their limitations revealed once confronted with moments of crisis, particularly during setbacks and after Nasser’s death. By first analyzing how Nasser constructed his authority and rhetoric, analyzing how it functioned in moments of victory and defeat, and finally exploring how his legitimacy was adapted and reinterpreted by other leaders, this paper demonstrates that Nasserism was not just a political movement, but a rhetorical project whose strength ultimately depended on the very things that also limited it. 8

# Nasserism as a Theory 

Definition of Nasserism and its Employment in Other Works 

Nasserism is the political ideology of Gamal Nasser, one of the core leaders behind the 1952 Revolution. It dominated Egyptian politics for nearly twenty years from the 1950s up until 1970 after Nasser’s death. This ideology combines Pan-Arabism, Arab socialism, progressive social justice, and a state-capitalist form of economic development. Nasserism called for nationalization of a nation’s key economic industries, land reform to uplift the lower economic classes, and anti-Western intervention in the Middle East. Beginning in Egypt, it gained widespread support across the Arab world after the Suez Crisis of 1956 and served as a source of inspiration for similar movements across the world during the mid-20th century. 

Scholars present Nasser’s legacy in Egypt as a complex issue. Nasser is seen as the nation’s liberator that uplifted those overlooked by leaders before him, but he failed to grant the Egyptian people their political agency. 1 He brought about an era of left-wing dominance in Egyptian politics during his rule, yet he forced other groups of leftists to conform to his ideology under threats of imprisonment. His treatment angered them, but his other actions gained their admiration. This relationship spanned generations. A descendant of a man imprisoned under Nasser’s regime recounts: “He was a strange man! Even though he had imprisoned my father, I was incapable of hating him, for he was able to enroll me, thanks to him, in the faculty of medicine, like the children of the elite. Even when they were being tortured they chanted his name. They believed that what was happening to them was a kind of bitter misunderstanding.” 2

As the leader of Egypt, Nasser employed a unique blend of rhetoric and charisma throughout The Philosophy of the Revolution to legitimize his rule over the nation and role as leader of his Pan-Arab movement in the Arab world. Constitutive rhetoric, however, cannot function on its own. It needs a leadership situation that makes it possible for success, and charismatic authority legitimizes one’s own success.

The Philosophy of the Revolution was published during the consolidation of Nasser’s new regime, where he faced intense domestic instability and international pressure.

Constitutive Rhetoric: The Creation of a New Identity 

> C

onstitutive rhetoric was first articulated in Maurice Charland’s article, "Constitutive Rhetoric: the Case of the Peuple Québecéois. ” There he argues that rather than persuading individuals in groups that already exist, rhetoric can create a collective identity that individuals 16 

come to inhabit. Charland challenges the traditional understanding of rhetoric’s use to influence audiences that already exist. Instead, rhetoric calls a group of people into existence by addressing them as if they already exist. When individuals recognize themselves in an address, they become subjects of that rhetoric. 15 Over time, they are no longer French speaking Canadians, but become participants of a historical and politically active group. 

Rhetoric has the power to construct a unified identity by framing a group around a shared past, struggle, or destiny. Charland examines how political rhetoric created the identity of the “peuple québécois ” (Québécois people) as a distinct national identity. Québécois people were given a shared past through the oppression faced under British rule, a shared struggle through ongoing oppression under Canadian rule, and assigned a collective destiny with national sovereignty as the end goal. 16 By addressing individuals as members of a unified national group, they recognize themselves within that identity. They are no longer French-speaking Canadians, but become participants of a historical and politically active group. Nationalist rhetoric presents the new collective identity as having a shared history of oppression, current struggle, and future destiny. Past oppression now becomes a foundational trauma that began the uniting of the people within the identity together. The ongoing rule under Canada now becomes a continuation of the historical injustices under British rule, just now under a different subjugator. Painting it this way makes the provincial government seem like the bread and circus of the Québécois people, keeping them content enough so they remain unaware of the control the Canadian government still has. Sovereignty now becomes not just a single option among many, but now a necessity for the destiny of this group.

Constitutive rhetoric creates three ideological effects that change how individuals understand themselves, their history, and their freedom. The first is identity transcending “the limitations of the individual body and will.” 17 Shared identity transcends the limitations of the individual, where they no longer become singular actors fighting for a common goal, but are now members of the collective identity. The people no longer become simple inhabitants of the land, but the inheritors of the land of their people. The final effect is the illusion of freedom. 19 The Québécois people are presented as freely striving for their independence, yet that is not the case. They are compelled by the rhetoric of a shared destiny to support independence not by choice, but from a narrative that demands it as the only outcome. 

Charland offers a framework to understand how Nasser constructed the identities of the Egyptian and Arab people, which he used to carry him forward in achieving his goals for Egypt and the Arab world. # Application of Constitutive Rhetoric in TPotR 

Formation of the Egyptian Identity 

In TPotR, Nasser elevates the Egyptian people’s identity into historical agents, where they go from victims of the corrupt monarchy and colonialism into active participants of the nation’s new revolutionary destiny. He describes the July 23rd revolution as a “realisation of hope”. 20 Phrasing the revolution as a “realisation of hope” blends Egypt’s past, present, and future together. The past now becomes a period of dormant desire for change amongst the people, the present is that fulfillment of change, and the future is the continuation of Egypt’s destiny. The Egyptian people are no longer citizens witnessing a change in government, but inheritors of the nation’s new destiny and participants in how it gets to unfold. This rhetorical move also presents the illusion of freedom mentioned by Charland. The people seem to have freedom of choice by being historical agents, but to accept Nasser’s identity as a historical agent is to accept that the path of the revolution is the only way to go. 

Emphasizing the need for a social revolution, Nasser portrays the goals of the revolution as something ongoing. His Egyptian audience now becomes positioned as co-authors of their nation’s history, with their identity bound to the continued success of his revolutionary project. To Nasser, the social revolution was one in which “the classes of society would struggle against each other until justice for all countrymen has been gained and conditions have become stable”. 21 

Nasser presents a collective identity whose destiny plays out over time. The struggle Nasser describes does not necessarily mean instability, but a necessary stepping stone in completing the revolution. But Nasser’s rhetoric does not stop at redefining what it means to be Egyptian. He

# Application of Charismatic Authority in TPotR 

Charismatic Authority: The Qualities of a Leader 

The concept of charismatic authority is best interpreted in Politics as a Vocation , an essay written by sociologist Max Weber. It explains the nature of politics, how political legitimacy is granted, and the kind of person for politics. 

Weber articulates three ways a leader can justify their own power. Traditional authority is granted through long standing customs, legal authority derives from the law, and charismatic authority is based upon “the absolutely personal devotion and personal confidence in revelation, heroism, or other qualities of individual leadership.” 30 Through charismatic authority, people obey not because of tradition nor because the law says so, but because they believe the leader has either unique qualities or is called upon to take upon the leadership role for a special reason. 31 

Charismatic authority is strong, yet incredibly fragile at the same time. While traditional authority relies on custom and legal authority relies on institutionalized laws, charismatic authority relies only on the belief that the leader has exceptional qualities. Legitimacy is only kept so long the people believe their leader continues to have these qualities. However, the power    

> 31 Ibid, 4.
> 30 Max Weber, Politics as a Vocation , (New York:Oxford University Press, 1946), 4.

23 

in charismatic authority comes from the ability to bypass institutions and traditions because it is not rooted in either. 

An individual with charismatic authority cannot solely rely on emotional appeal. They must have true dedication to the cause. Weber highlights two types of people in politics: one who “lives for” it and one who “lives off” it. A leader that strives for the former makes politics their life. They either enjoy the power from it or have meaning from it because he is fulfilling some sort of cause. The latter is someone that does politics simply to make an income. 32 Charismatic authority relies on the leader living for politics. The people must believe that their leader is genuinely committed to a moral cause, and that they are motivated not by self-interest. 

The biggest drawback of charismatic authority is its instability. No matter how long the legitimacy of a leader may last, it must undergo routinization to ensure its survivability. The leaders of a revolution cannot live forever, so to ensure their ideas do not die with them, they must institutionalize it within their state’s political structure, ensuring the survivability of the regime. This allows for a proper bureaucratic system to form, allowing the leadership to shift from one of charismatic authority to legal authority. 33 The regime moves from one built off a revolution and moral cause to a rules-based authority detached from having the people’s best interests at heart. In exchange for longevity, the passion common in charismatic authority is now dwindled. This presents a paradox: in order for the revolution to survive long after the leader, it must no longer carry aspects of the revolution. Revolution may bring about change, but only routinization can preserve the regime long after the death of the revolutionary. 

Weber’s analysis of charismatic authority offers a framework on how Nasser justified his leadership. He argues that charismatic authority relies on the people believing that the leader has

# Nasserism as a Theory in Practice 

How are Victories and Defeats Applied? 

In this section, I examine Nasser’s military and political victories and defeats through a rhetorical lens to reveal how his legitimacy depended on the ability to frame victories as proof of Arab unity, but it unraveled during defeats, which revealed the gap between theory and reality. The particular victories and defeats examined in this analysis serve a purpose of representing key moments when Nasser’s rhetoric was either reinforced or challenged in the Arab world. He grounded his leadership in charismatic authority, which presented him as not just Egypt’s president, but also the embodiment of a broader Arab struggle against imperialism. He formed a personal connection with audiences across the Arab world. But charismatic authority, while legitimizing his rule in Egypt, could only take him so far outside of the nation. It proved why he was a proper leader for his country, but why should other Arab nations see him as their liberator? His use of constitutive rhetoric to define not just what it meant to be Egyptian, but also Arab transformed two separate cultural or national identities into a community with a shared destiny. 

By linking these two identities together, the victories of the Egyptian people became the victories of the entire Arab world, further strengthening not just his legitimacy as a regional leader, but also the appeal of the Nasserist project. Yet while the victories of Nasserism strengthened his rhetoric, each defeat revealed the tensions and contradictions of Nasser’s grand vision. These events were moments the Nasserist project was put to the test. Victories such as the Suez Crisis showed how Nasser could transform an action that benefited Egypt into a symbolic victory for the Arab world, strengthening the appeal of him as a leader and of Pan-Arabism. Yet setbacks such as Syria’s secession from the United Arab Republic and the Six-Day War exposed 31 

the flaws of his vision. The specific cases reveal how Nasser’s authority was tied to how he could frame events rhetorically. Victories were easy to frame as evidence as to why his vision is right for the region, showing the strength of Arab unity and reinforcing his legitimacy across the region. But when they contradicted his narrative, the limitations of Nasserism’s real-world application became apparent. Yet when other leaders might have fallen, Nasser’s rhetoric framed these defeats as a setback that could be overcome. Though this could only go so far, and after the humiliation of the Six-Day War, Nasser was forced to take accountability for his failures. 

# The Victories of Nasserism 

Victory of the Suez Crisis 

The Suez Canal stood as a sore spot for Egyptian nationalists like Nasser. Even though Egypt gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1922, their independent status was not even worth the paper it was written on. Their former colonizer still retained control over “the security of imperial communications, defense, the protection of foreign interests and minorities, and the Sudan.” 43 The “protection of foreign interests” referred directly to the continued control of the canal through the Suez Company, a company jointly controlled by French and British interests. The Suez Canal served as a vital artery of both global trade and power, allowing maritime commerce to travel directly from Europe to Asia from the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, which leads directly to the Indian Ocean, saving vital travel time, and it connected France and Britain to their colonies in Asia. Those in control of the canal not only had a say in

What is the Third Persona? 

Along with charismatic authority and constitutive rhetoric, certain events allowed Nasser to use rhetoric in order to construct a “third persona,” or an “other”. This excluded group served as an opposition to Nasser’s vision, whether it was imperial powers or religious and national groups. Traditional rhetorical analysis only focuses on two groups in rhetoric–the speaker (first persona) and the intended audience (second persona)–while ignoring the possibility of a third group: those that the speaker intentionally excludes from who they see as their audience (third persona). 50 

The third persona is not just left out of the conversation, but they are invisible–the first persona does not even see them as worthy of being addressed. According to Philip Wander, the author who coined the term, it does not mean the excluded groups are not to be identified by “‘you’ and ‘I’...who are not to become part of ‘our’ audience or even be allowed to respond to what ‘we’ say”, it is a form of erasure where excluded groups become “non-subjects.” 51 This erasure is significant because it severs any ties the third persona has to the identity of the audience constructed by the speaker’s rhetoric. This goes beyond marginalization, where marginalized groups still have a voice in society (albeit smaller than non-marginalized groups). If a group is not the audience, but the “non-subject”, they have no voice or ability to challenge the speaker or attempt to claim membership in the new identity. The power of rhetoric lies not only in the ability to convince the audience to adapt their new identity, but its ability to set boundaries in who can be a part of this new group and who becomes excluded from recognition.

# Nasserism as a Legacy 

The Death of Nasser 

With Nasser’s death, it marked not just the death of a leader, but the unraveling of a political system built around that leader. After eighteen years in power, he left behind a nation that was deeply shaped by his vision now uncertain on how to move forward without him. For the broader Arab world, the wandering role, originally held by Nasser, was now left vacant. His death revealed the collapse of his charismatic authority, which partly served as the foundation of his government’s legitimacy after the Egyptian Revolution, and the appeal of the Nasserist project across the Arab world. Unlike traditional or legal authority, his unique authority was difficult to replicate because there was only one Gamal Nasser, for his legitimacy was built upon his unique fusion of rhetoric that no successor could replicate. 

The death of Gamal Nasser left a power vacuum in Egypt and the rest of the Arab world, for the collapse of his charismatic authority and constitutive rhetoric after his death exposed the fragility of Nasserism being built around the individual that created it. However, it did not die with him. Instead, its core components were either adapted or reinterpreted by leaders in an attempt to form their legitimacy without the figure who once defined it. 

# Nasser’s Successors in Egypt 

Due to the fact that Nasser’s legitimacy was built around his unique qualities and rhetorical ability, his death Nasser meant that future Egyptian leaders were unable to replicate and carry on his legitimacy to support their own rule. Instead, post-Nasser leaders reconstructed 49 

his legitimacy through unique rhetorical strategies of their own. Anwar Sadat’s speeches to the People’s Assembly in Egypt and Israel’s Knesset indicate a shift from Nasser’s Pan-Arab rhetoric to a framework grounded in peace, the national interests of Egypt, and moral responsibility. Hosni Mubarak’s speech during the 2011 Egyptian revolution reveals his attempt to maintain his authority through nationalist rhetoric and casting himself as a necessary paternal figure for the country, even though the protests exposed the limitations of his legitimacy he built off stability and control. Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s “Democracy in the Middle East” 72 and resignation speech emphasizes gradual political change, security, and the legitimacy of those in power over the mass mobilization of the people desired by Nasser. Nasser’s charismatic leadership model did not die with him, but became reshaped to fit his successors in a far more state-centered government. This reflects the downside of charismatic authority–routinization–where in order for the regime to survive, the revolutionary characteristics needed to be abandoned in favor of a more stable and bureaucratic government. Seeing as Sadat was the first to take on the Egyptian presidency after Nasser’s death, he will serve as the first example.

His model of leadership is evident in his thesis paper during his time at the United States Army War College, “Democracy in the Middle East”, where he outlines his vision for gradual political development, and in his resignation speech, where he frames his candidacy as a continuation of national duty rather than a personal pursuit of power. While el-Sisi’s “Democracy in the Middle East” is not trying to be the next Philosophy of the Revolution , his thesis provides viable context to how he views the necessary speed of political change in contrast to Nasser. 

In “Democracy in the Middle East”, el-Sisi's vision of political development contrasts sharply from Nasser’s vision of political change through mobilization of the masses. 87 Rather than advocating for revolutionary change, el-Sisi argues that democracy in the region must emerge in a “logical, steady, and controlled manner” shaped by the specific conditions of Middle Eastern societies. 88 This shift towards gradual reform reflects a belief that rapid political change can risk instability and social unrest, particularly in nations with strong religious and religious foundations. In el-Sisi’s model, the state, rather than the people, determine the speed and direction of political development.

# Successors of Nasser in the Arab World 

Nasser’s legacy extended far beyond Egypt’s borders, shaping the leadership styles of figures across the Arab world. Leaders such as Saddam Hussein, Muammar Gaddafi, and Hafez al-Assad adopted elements of the Nasserist model, invoking themes of anti-imperialism and Arab unity in an attempt to position themselves as leaders of the broader Arab struggle. But unlike Nasser, these figures were unable to replicate his rhetorical success and appeal across the region. Instead of mobilizing the Arab people, their rhetoric was tied to the interests and survival of their individual regimes. As seen during the 1979 Ba’ath Party Purge, Saddam’s rule relied heavily on coercion and public spectacles, constructing legitimacy through fear. Gaddafi’s The Green Book

# The Defining Legacy 

Nasser’s rise and mass appeal cannot be understood through just the conventional measures of political success. While his leadership was marked by significant achievements and failures, his ability to maintain legitimacy across the Arab world reveals a power rooted in rhetoric. Through constitutive rhetoric, Nasser redefined what it meant to be Arab, transforming the identity from that of just shared culture or language into one with a shared political destiny. His charismatic authority allowed him to serve as the embodiment of this identity, positioning himself as not just the president of Egypt, but also the leader of the broader Arab struggle. These working together are what allowed Nasser to escape from the confines of Egypt and extend his influence across the entire Arab world. 

The examination of Nasser’s victories and defeats reveal the strengths and limitations of the Nasserist project. During the nationalization of the Suez Canal, he reframed the outcome as a victory not just for Egypt, but the entire Arab world. His rhetoric reinforced a shared sense of pride and collective achievement. However, the collapse of the United Arab Republic exposed the tension between Arab unity and national interests, while Egypt’s role in the North Yemen Civil War weakened its image as a regional power. The most significant defeat was the Six-Day War, where it rattled Nasser’s credibility as a leader and the image of Arab unity. While rhetoric is powerful, it still cannot override political and military limitations. 

Despite these setbacks, Nasser’s influence did not collapse. Despite stepping down from the presidency after the devastating defeat in 1967, mass public support kept him in power. His choice to accept responsibility helped reinforce the people’s love for him and preserved legitimacy that otherwise might’ve been lost. Political legitimacy, when rooted in rhetoric, can 64 

endure conventional measures of political success, but it’s also heavily dependent on the outcome of reality. 

The fragility of charismatic authority became apparent after Nasser’s death in 1970. Successive leaders in Egypt were forced to reconstruct his legitimacy for their own political survival, but also departing from key aspects of Nasserism. Anwar Sadat shifted from Pan-Arabism and the collective Arab struggle in favor of prioritizing national interests and pursuing peace. Hosni Mubarak’s legitimacy was built off of the stale stability he offered, but it came crumbling down during the 2011 Egyptian Revolution. Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has drawn on some aspects of Nasser’s image through moral obligation, but differs from how political change should be brought about. 

Across the Arab world, leaders like Saddam Hussein, Muammar Gaddafi, and Hafez al-Assad fragmented Nasser’s rhetoric. While these leaders employ themes of the former Egyptian president, they lack the ability to resonate outside their own borders. There is great difficulty in reproducing legitimacy so closely tied to a specific individual.

His ability to construct a new Arab identity and position himself as its figurehead allowed him to achieve appeal that extended far beyond Egypt. But the setbacks during his time in power and the reinterpretation and fragmentation of his legitimacy after his death reveals the instability of a regime built on a charismatic figure and a constructed identity. Rhetoric can unify and mobilize the masses, but it cannot ignore the importance of institutional strength and tensions that emerge once it’s put into practice.

**Jennifer Finney Boylan** is the inaugural Anna Quindlen Writer in Residence at Barnard College of Columbia University.Her column appears on the op-ed page of the _New York Times_ on alternate Wednesdays. Author of sixteen books, her 2003 memoir _She’s Not There_ was the first bestselling work by a transgender American. She serves on the Board of Trustees of PEN America, the nonprofit advocating for authors, readers, and freedom of expression. From 2011 to 2018 she served on the Board of Directors of GLAAD, acting as co-chair from 2013-17.

![Image 3: Jane Brox](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/Brox_Jane.jpg?fv=B6uX15DM&itok=P2KNPZ1B)

**Jane Brox**‘s fifth book,_Silence_, was published in January 2019, and was selected as an Editors’ Choice by the _New York Times Book Review._ Her previous book, _Brilliant: The Evolution of Artificial Light_, was named one of the top ten nonfiction books of 2010 by _Time_ magazine. She is also the author of _Clearing Land: Legacies of the American Farm_, _Five Thousand Days Like This One_, and _Here and Nowhere Else_. Brox’s essays have appeared in many journals and magazines, including the _Georgia Review_ and _NewYorker.com_, and they’ve been anthologized in _Best American Essays_, _The Norton Book of Nature Writing_, and the _Pushcart Prize Anthology_. She has been awarded grants from the Guggenheim Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Massachusetts Cultural Council. She is on the faculty of Lesley University’s low-residency MFA Program and lives in Maine.

![Image 4: Reyna Grande](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2021-02/grande_reyna_high%20rest__cropped.jpg?fv=vZk30jcL&itok=dT05wlD3)

**Reyna Grande** is the author of the bestselling memoir, _The Distance Between Us_, where she writes about her life before and after coming from Mexico to the United States as an undocumented immigrant. The much-anticipated sequel, _A Dream Called Home_, was released in October 2018. Her other works include the novels, _Across a Hundred Mountains_ and _Dancing with Butterflies_, which were published to critical acclaim. Her books have been adopted as the common read selection by schools, colleges and cities across the country. Reyna has received an American Book Award, the El Premio Aztlán Literary Award, and the International Latino Book Award. In 2012, she was a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Awards, and in 2015 she was honored with a Luis Leal Award for Distinction in Chicano/Latino Literature. The young reader’s version of _The Distance Between Us_ received a 2017 Honor Book Award for the Américas Award for Children’s and Young Adult Literature, a 2016 Eureka! Honor Awards from the California Reading Association, and an International Literacy Association Children’s Book Award 2017. Currently, she teaches creative writing, travels across the country and abroad to give presentations about her books, and is at work on her next book.

## The Hybrid Poem

_A workshop designed to discuss multimodal ways of writing and reading the poem that uses images or combines with prose in interesting ways, or which uses videos or visual narratives._

![Image 15: Paisley Rekdal](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2021-02/rekdal_paisley__cropped.jpg?fv=Eb6KuUF3&itok=y43TF6LE)

**Paisley Rekdal**is the author of _Appropriate: A Provocation_, which examines cultural appropriation; a book-length essay, _The Broken Country: On Trauma, a Crime, and the Continuing Legacy of Vietnam,_ which won the 2016 AWP Nonfiction Prize; _The Night My Mother Met Bruce Lee_ _;_ the hybrid photo-text memoir _Intimate;_ and six books of poetry: _Nightingale_, which re-writes many of the myths in Ovid’s _The Metamorphoses_ _; \_A Crash of Rhinos;\__ _Six Girls Without Pants;_ _The Invention of the Kaleidoscope;_ _Animal Eye_, a finalist for the 2013 Kingsley Tufts Prize and winner of the UNT Rilke Prize; and _Imaginary Vessels_, finalist for the 2018 Kingsley Tufts Prize and the Washington State Book Award. ## Writing for the Screen

**Dean Bakopoulos**’ first novel, _Please Don’t Come Back from the Moon_, was a _New York Times_ Notable Book; A WGA screenwriter, Dean co-wrote the critically-acclaimed film adaptation. His most recent novel is the bestselling _Summerlong_, now in development as a television series. The winner of a Guggenheim and two NEA fellowships, Bakopoulos is writer-in-residence at Grinnell College and teaches in the Warren Wilson MFA Program. He also teaches an MFA-level workshop in TV writing each fall at the University of Iowa. Bakopoulos is an executive producer of the HBO Max series, _Made for Love_, based on the novel by Alissa Nutting.

## Nonfiction

![Image 2: Jennifer Finney Boylan](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/Boylan_Jennifer%20Finney%20289.jpg?fv=6gNmzpyr&itok=BW1AqcL0)

**Jennifer Finney Boylan** is the inaugural Anna Quindlen Writer in Residence at Barnard College of Columbia University.Her column appears on the op-ed page of the _New York Times_ on alternate Wednesdays. Author of sixteen books, her 2003 memoir _She’s Not There_ was the first bestselling work by a transgender American. She serves on the Board of Trustees of PEN America, the nonprofit advocating for authors, readers, and freedom of expression. From 2011 to 2018 she served on the Board of Directors of GLAAD, acting as co-chair from 2013-17.

![Image 3: Jane Brox](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/Brox_Jane.jpg?fv=B6uX15DM&itok=P2KNPZ1B)

**Jane Brox**‘s fifth book,_Silence_, was published in January 2019, and was selected as an Editors’ Choice by the _New York Times Book Review._ Her previous book, _Brilliant: The Evolution of Artificial Light_, was named one of the top ten nonfiction books of 2010 by _Time_ magazine. She is also the author of _Clearing Land: Legacies of the American Farm_, _Five Thousand Days Like This One_, and _Here and Nowhere Else_. Brox’s essays have appeared in many journals and magazines, including the _Georgia Review_ and _NewYorker.com_, and they’ve been anthologized in _Best American Essays_, _The Norton Book of Nature Writing_, and the _Pushcart Prize Anthology_. She has been awarded grants from the Guggenheim Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Massachusetts Cultural Council. She is on the faculty of Lesley University’s low-residency MFA Program and lives in Maine.

![Image 4: Reyna Grande](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2021-02/grande_reyna_high%20rest__cropped.jpg?fv=vZk30jcL&itok=dT05wlD3)

**Reyna Grande** is the author of the bestselling memoir, _The Distance Between Us_, where she writes about her life before and after coming from Mexico to the United States as an undocumented immigrant. The much-anticipated sequel, _A Dream Called Home_, was released in October 2018. Her other works include the novels, _Across a Hundred Mountains_ and _Dancing with Butterflies_, which were published to critical acclaim. Her books have been adopted as the common read selection by schools, colleges and cities across the country. Reyna has received an American Book Award, the El Premio Aztlán Literary Award, and the International Latino Book Award. In 2012, she was a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Awards, and in 2015 she was honored with a Luis Leal Award for Distinction in Chicano/Latino Literature. The young reader’s version of _The Distance Between Us_ received a 2017 Honor Book Award for the Américas Award for Children’s and Young Adult Literature, a 2016 Eureka! Honor Awards from the California Reading Association, and an International Literacy Association Children’s Book Award 2017. Currently, she teaches creative writing, travels across the country and abroad to give presentations about her books, and is at work on her next book.

## Poetry

![Image 5: Reginald Dwayne Betts](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/Betts_Reginald%20Dwayne.jpg?fv=z9HfB7xg&itok=y8vj9QME)

**Reginald Dwayne Betts** transformed himself from a sixteen-year old kid sentenced to nine-years in prison to a critically acclaimed writer and graduate of the Yale Law School. He has written three collections of poetry, B _astards of the Reagan Era_,_Shahid Reads His Own Palm_, and, most recently, _Felon_. His memoir,_A Question of Freedom: A Memoir of Learning, Survival, and Coming of Age in Prison_ won the 2010 NAACP Image Award. Named a 2018 Guggenheim Foundation Fellow and a 2018 National Endowment for the Arts Fellow, Betts’s writing has generated national attention and earned him a Soros Justice Fellowship, a Radcliffe Fellowship, a Ruth Lily Fellowship, and a New America Fellowship. Betts has been featured in the _New York Times_,_New Yorker_, and the _Washington Post_. He has also been interviewed on National Public Radio’s _Fresh Air_, The Travis Smiley Show and others. He holds a B.A. from the University of Maryland; an MFA from Warren Wilson College, where he was a Holden Fellow; and, a J.D. from Yale Law School, where he was awarded the Israel H. Perez Prize for best student note or comment appearing in the Yale Law Journal. He is a PhD in Law candidate at Yale University and as a Liman Fellow, he spent a year representing clients in the New Haven Public Defender’s Office.

![Image 6: Gabrielle Calvocoressi](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/Calvocoressi_Gabrielle.jpg?fv=wzbnR_Al&itok=pDJ11U6w)

**Gabrielle Calvocoressi**is the author of _The Last Time I Saw Amelia Earhart;_ _Apocalyptic Swing,_ a finalist for the LA Times Book Prize; and _Rocket Fantastic_, winner of the Audre Lorde Award for Lesbian Poetry. Calvocoressi is the recipient of numerous awards and fellowships including a Stegner Fellowship and Jones Lectureship from Stanford University, a Rona Jaffe Woman Writer’s Award,a Lannan Foundation residency in Marfa, Texas,the Bernard F. Conners Prize from the _Paris Review,_ and a residency from the Civitella di Ranieri Foundation, among others. Calvocoressi’s poems have been published or are forthcoming in numerous magazines and journals including _The Baffler, New York Times_,_Poetry_,_Boston Review_,_Kenyon Review_,_Tin House,_ and the _New Yorker_. Calvocoressi is an Editor-at-Large at _Los Angeles Review of Books_, and Poetry Editor at _Southern Cultures._ Works in progress include a non-fiction book entitled,_The Year I Didn’t Kill Myself_ and a novel,_The Alderman of the Graveyard_. Calvocoressi teaches at UNC Chapel Hill and lives in Carrboro, North Carolina,where joy, compassion, and social justice are at the center of their personal and poetic practice.

![Image 7: Victoria Chang](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/Chang_Victoria.jpg?fv=OC1fLTPH&itok=0GLzYPI7)

**Victoria Chang**’s latest book of poems is _OBIT_, her middle grade verse novel, _Love, Love_, and a book of essays, are all forthcoming.Her other poetry books are _Barbie Chang,_ _Salvinia Molesta,_ and _Circle_. Her children’s picture book, _Is Mommy?_, was named a _New York Times_ Notable Book.She has also published a middle grade novel, _Love, Love_. She has received a Guggenheim Fellowship, a Lannan Residency Fellowship, a Sustainable Arts Foundation Fellowship, the Poetry Society of America’s Alice Fay Di Castagnola Award, a Pushcart Prize, and a MacDowell Fellowship.She serves as the program chair for Antioch’s low-residency MFA program in creative writing.She lives in Los Angeles with her family.

![Image 8: Vievee Francis](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2021-02/Francis_Vievee__cropped.jpg?fv=BZo9OK69&itok=iXhKKOXn)

**Vievee Francis**is the author of three books of poetry:_Blue-Tail Fly_;_Horse in the Dark_(winner of the Cave Canem Northwestern University Poetry Prize for a second collection); and _Forest Primeval_(winner of the Hurston/Wright Legacy Award and the 2017 Kingsley-Tufts Poetry Award). Her work has appeared in numerous print and online journals, textbooks, and anthologies, including _Poetry_,_Best American Poetry 2010_,_2014_,_2017_, and _Angles of Ascent: A Norton Anthology of Contemporary African American Poetry_. She has been a participant in the Cave Canem Workshops, a Poet-in-Residence for the Alice Lloyd Scholars Program at the University of Michigan, and teaches poetry writing in the Callaloo Creative Writing Workshop (USA, UK, and Barbados). In 2009 she received a Rona Jaffe Writer’s Award, and in 2010, a Kresge Fellowship. She serves as an associate editor of _Callaloo_ and an Associate Professor of English and Creative Writing at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire.

![Image 9: Jennifer Grotz](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2021-02/Jennifer%20Grotz__high%20res__please%20credit%20Marion%20Ettlinger__cropped.jpg?fv=FeMA4zPw&itok=qDg61H_6)

**Jennifer Grotz**, Director of the Bread Loaf Writers’ Conferences, is the author of three books of poetry:_Cusp_, _The Needle_, and most recently, _Window Left Open_. Also a translator, her _Psalms of All My Days_, translations from the French poet Patrice de La Tour du Pin, appeared in 2014. _Rochester Knockings_, by the Tunisian novelist Hubert Haddad, appeared in 2015. With the poet and translator Piotr Sommer, she has recently co-translated from the Polish _Everything I Don’t Know_, the selected poems of Jerzy Ficowski, forthcoming this spring from World Poetry Books. A recipient of fellowships from the National Endowment of the Arts, the Guggenheim Foundation, the Camargo Foundation, and the Rona Jaffe Foundation, she teaches poetry and translation at the University of Rochester.

![Image 10: A. Van Jordan](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2021-02/Jordan_A%20Van__cropped.jpg?fv=BEUfEA1_&itok=g3DifjKf)

**A. Van Jordan** is the author of four collections: _Rise_, which won the PEN/Oakland Josephine Miles Award (2001);_M-A-C-N-O-L-I-A_, (2005), which was listed as one the Best Books of 2005 by the _London Times_; _Quantum Lyrics_, (2007); and _The Cineaste_, (2013). Jordan has been awarded a Whiting Writers Award, an Anisfield-Wolf Book Award, and a Pushcart Prize. He is also a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship (2007), a United States Artists Fellowship (2009)**,**and aLannan Literary Award in Poetry (2015). He has taught at a number of institutions including, Prince George’s Community College, The University of North Carolina at Greensboro, The University of Texas at Austin, where he was tenured as an Associate Professor, Rutgers University-Newark where he served as the Henry Rutgers Presidential Professor, and at the University of Michigan, where he currently serves as the Robert Hayden Collegiate Professor.

![Image 11: Matthew Olzmann](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2021-02/olzmann_matt__cropped.jpg?fv=eNqk4qlj&itok=TQZdwwbf)

**Matthew Olzmann** is the author of two collections of poems,_Mezzanines_, which was selected for the Kundiman Prize; and _Contradictions in the Design,_ both from Alice James Books. He’s been awarded fellowships from Kundiman, the Kresge Arts Foundation, and the MacDowell Colony. His writing has appeared in _Best American Poetry, Kenyon Review, New England Review, Brevity_ and elsewhere. Currently, he teaches at Dartmouth College and in the MFA Program for Writers at Warren Wilson College.

![Image 12: Carl Phillips](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-10/Carl%20Phillips_cropped.jpg?fv=ky73fE_o&itok=zKlYX0PV)

Other honors include the Aiken Taylor Award for Modern American Poetry, the Kingsley Tufts Award, a Lambda Literary Award, the PEN/USA Award for Poetry, and fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Library of Congress, the Academy of American Poets, and the American Academy of Arts and Letters. She received a 2018 Literature Award from the American Academy of Arts and Letters and a 2013 Guggenheim Foundation Fellowship.Her poems have appeared in _Best American Poetry, The Nation, New Yorker, Paris Review, Poetry_, and elsewhere.She is Associate Professor of English and Creative Writing at Rutgers University-Newark and lives in Verona, New Jersey.

![Image 23: Dinaw Mengestu](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/Mengestu_Dinaw.jpg?fv=du3WUlbu&itok=11_xniIY)

Mengestu was chosen for the 5 under 35 Award by the National Book Foundation in 2007 and was named on the _New Yorker_’s “20 under 40” list in 2010. He is also the recipient of a Lannan Fiction Fellowship, _The Guardian_ First Book Award, the _Los Angeles Times_ Book Prize, among other awards. He is the author of three novels: _The Beautiful Things That Heaven Bears_ (2008), _How to Read the Air_ (2010), and _All Our Names_. His work has been translated into more than fifteen languages.

![Image 24: Elizabeth Nunez](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/Nunez_Elizabeth.jpg?fv=jv6OkvVQ&itok=b6MkNJbO)

**Elizabeth Nunez** immigrated to the U.S. from Trinidad after completing high school. She is the award-winning author of a memoir and nine novels, four of them selected as _New York Times_ Editors’ Choice. Her two most recent books are _Not for Everyday Use,_ a memoir, and _Even in Paradise_, a novel._Not for Everyday Use_ won the 2015 Hurston Wright Legacy Award for nonfiction and is an Oprah online book club selection. _Even in Paradise_, was an O, the Oprah Magazine and Essence Magazine selection. Nunez’s other novels are: _Boundaries_, nominated for the 2012 NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Literary Fiction; _Anna In-Between_ which won the PEN Oakland Award for Literary Excellence and was long-listed for an IMPAC Dublin International Literary Award; _Prospero’s Daughter_ which was 2006 Novel of the Year for _Black Issues Book Review_ and for _Mosaic Magazine._ Her novel, _Bruised Hibiscus_, won an American Book Award, and _Beyond `the Limbo Silence_ won the Independent Publishers Book Award. Her other novels include _Grace; Discretion,_ short-listed for the Hurston/Wright Legacy Award; and _When Rocks Dance_. She is co-editor of the anthology _Blue Latitudes: Caribbean Women Writers at Home and Abroad_. Nunez is the co-founder of the National Black Writers Conference and was director for fourteen years. She is executive producer of the New York Emmy-nominated CUNY-TV series _Black Writers in America_ and has served on the jury for national and international literary prizes/awards, including the international Dublin IMPAC Literary prize, the Ernest Gaines Literary prize, and the Fulbright Award for Creative Writing. Nunez received her PhD in English Literature from New York University and is currently a Distinguished Professor at Hunter College, the City University of New York.

**Jess Row** is the author of the novel _Your Face in Mine,_ a book of essays, _White Flights: Race, Fiction, and the American Imagination_, and two collections of short stories, _The Train to Lo Wu_ and _Nobody Ever Gets Lost_.His work has appeared in the _New Yorker, The Atlantic, Tin House,_ and _Granta,_ and he has received a Guggenheim Fellowship, a National Endowment for the Arts Fellowship, and a Whiting Writers Award. He teaches writing at the College of New Jersey, serves on the curatorial board of the Racial Imaginary Institute, and is a senior dharma teacher in the Kwan Um School of Zen.

![Image 26: Marisa Silver](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/Silver_Marisa.jpg?fv=5DzTk8sn&itok=CnauU0Q9)

**Marisa Silver**’smost recent novel, _The Mysteries_, was published in May. She is the author of six other works of fiction, including the novels _Mary Coin_, a _New York Times_ Bestseller, and _Little Nothing_, a _New York Times_ Editors’ Choice. Her short fiction has appeared in the _New Yorker_ and _The Atlantic.com,_ as well as other publications and has been included in _Best American Short Stories_, and _O. Henry Prize Stories_. Silver has received fellowships from the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation and the New York Public Library’s Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers. She teaches at the MFA Program for Writers at Warren Wilson College.

![Image 27: Laura van den Berg](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2020-09/van%20den%20Berg_Laura.jpg?fv=qjCcW3SI&itok=LwqAD8sZ)

**Laura van den Berg** is the author of the story collections _What the World Will Look Like When All the Water Leaves Us_ and _The Isle of Youth_, and the novels _Find Me_ and _The Third Hotel_, a finalist for the New York Public Library Young Lions Fiction Award. She is the recipient of a Rosenthal Family Foundation Award from the American Academy of Arts and Letters, the Bard Fiction Prize, a PEN/O. Henry Prize, MacDowell Colony and Civitella Ranieri fellowships, and is a two-time finalist for the Frank O’Connor International Short Story Award. Her most recent collection, _I Hold a Wolf by the Ears,_ was published by FSG in 2020 and named a “best summer read” by the _New York Times, Time Magazine, Esquire, Harper’s Bazaar_, and _Entertainment Weekly_, among others. Born and raised in Florida, Laura splits her time between Central Florida and the Boston area, where she is a faculty member of the creative writing program at Harvard.

![Image 28: Tiphanie Yanique](https://www.middlebury.edu/writers-conferences/sites/default/files/styles/300x400/public/2021-02/Yanique_Photo__cropped_0.jpg?fv=mCYXph3M&itok=AhQwZeQ9)

**Tiphanie Yanique** is the author of the short story collection, _How to Escape from a Leper Colony_, the picture book _I Am the Virgin Islands_, the novel _Land of Love and Drowning, and a collection of poems, Wife_. _BookPage_ listed her as one of the Fourteen Women to watch out for in 2014. ## Prof. Hassan Nofal, Professor of Rhetoric and Modern Literary Criticism at the Faculty of Girls

 2026-06-10 

![Image 6](https://www.asu.edu.eg/141090/_mediacenter/2026/png/89e6526172c813af54031ef22b109d48.png)

• A great character with contributions to the field of literature that cannot be ignored or overlooked. He lived an academic and professional career during which he gave much and much to science, literature, and to students. He is Prof. Hassan Nofal, full-time professor of rhetoric and modern literary criticism at the Faculty of Girls, Ain Shams University.

• Prof. Youssef Hassan Nofal was born in early October 1938. Thanks to his efforts, he was able to assume the position of former Vice Dean of the Faculty of Girls for Postgraduate Studies and Research.

• He is also a member of the Egyptian Scientific Academy, and the founding dean of the Faculty of Education in Port Said. He supervised and discussed 360 master’s and doctoral theses at the universities of Egypt, Libya, Gaza, Saudi Arabia, and Sudan.

• He wrote books that are considered important references in modern literary criticism, which reached 40 books on poetry, narrative, and play criticism, in addition to 200 research papers.

#### **His writings**

• Prof. Youssef Hassan Nofal authored the Encyclopedia of Collections of Modern Poetry in the Arab World, which includes more than 9,000 poets, and revealed unknown poets. He also authored the Encyclopedia of Arab and Islamic Heritage Relics in more than 1,500 pages.

• He is also a poet who has five collections published in Complete Works by Dar al-Kutub, a storyteller, and has a collection (The Lost) by the General Book Authority, in addition to various books and studies.

• He also participated in writing encyclopedias: preparing several entries in the encyclopedia of “Notable Arab and Muslim Scholars,” the Arab League Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, September 2003, and preparing some entries in an encyclopedia on literary figures in the same organization. Preparing several entries in the Encyclopedia of Notable Figures commissioned by The Royal Aal al-Bayt Foundation in Jordan. Review Bibliography of the Arabic Novel, American University, supervised by Dr. Hamdi Al-Sukot, and my name was mentioned in the introduction. Preparation of some entries in a bibliography on contemporary Arab poets, American University, supervised by Hamdi Al-Sukot.

#### **His journalistic interests**

• He also worked as editor-in-chief of the Scientific Yearbook of the Faculty of Girls, Ain Shams University, during the period from 1976-1979, then its deputy editor-in-chief from 1995-1998, and its developer during the agency, then its editorial advisor until now.

• He also served as a member of the editorial board of the Emirates Facultyof Arts magazine during his loan, and a member of the editorial board of Al-Wasatiya magazine, on behalf of the Al-Wasatiya group. He published in most Egyptian and Arab literary magazines, such as Faculty of Girls, Kuwait University Magazine, the Emirates Facultyof Arts magazine, Dar Al-Ulum newspaper, and Al-Bayan Kuwaiti newspaper. The magazine of the Arabic Language Academy, the New Story and Culture, Criticism Literature, Al-Faisal, Al-Helal, and conference books of the Supreme Council of Culture.

#### **Writings about him**

• Because of his career and professionalism, many wrote about him, including: Ahmed Kamal Zaki, about the book by Muhammad Abdul Halim Abdullah, published by King Saud University, in Al-Faisal Magazine, Riyadh, October 1983. The critic Dr. Mohamed Abd El-Muttalib wrote in his book (The Authority of Poetry), issued by the Culture Palaces Authority in Egypt, entitled (The Poetic Dictionary in the Collection of Youssef Nofel, “As Birds Migrate”), based on his close experience with the poet fifty-five years ago. The critic had analyzed his poem The Black Stone on the Cultural Program Radio in Egypt, and published the book (A Poem and a Poet), which bore the name of the program. He also analyzed the poem “Gertie” on Channel 2 of Egyptian Television.

• As written by Dr. Hassan opened the door on the waterfalls of light in New Culture magazine, April 1998, and Muhammad Hassan Abdullah, and Abdel Moneim Awad Youssef, on the authority of Ahmed, and Dr. El-sayed Fadl, Dr. Abdul Rahim Al-Kurdi, Dr. Abu Al-Qasim Rashwan, Dr. Abdel Moneim Abu Zeid, Dr. Ahmed Al-Saghir, in a book issued by the Culture Palaces Authority, Greater Cairo and North Upper Egypt, entitled “Youssef Nofal: Studies and Testimonies at a Conference held in May 2009.” Likewise, Muhammad Abd al-Muttalib, Azza Abu al-Najah, Khaled Fahmy, Nada al-Husseini, Basma Bayoumi, and others wrote in a book issued by the Arabic Language Department at the Faculty of Girls, which includes research at the forum (Youssef Nofal, Navigating Memory) in February 2016.

#### **Master's theses about Dr. Nofel**

• Master's theses were also approved, covering his works and his scientific and literary career, including:

• The theory of poetry among the free verse poets in Egypt from the generation of pioneers to the generation of the sixties, by researcher Abdel Nasser Issawi, Dar Al Uloom, Cairo 2003, under the supervision of Ahmed Heikal and Abdel Latif Abdel Halim.

• Vision and artistic formation in the poetry of Youssef Nofal, Faculty of Education, Ain Shams University, 2015, supervised by Dr. Abdul Mardi Zakaria.

• The verbal sentence in the poetry of Youssef Nofal, a synthetic and analytical study, Faculty of Arts, Port Said University 2016, under the supervision of Dr. Nada Al-Hini.

• Poetry of Youssef Nofal, artistic study, Faculty of Arts, Sohag University, July 2018, under the supervision of Dr. Siham Rashid.

• Youssef Nofal as a critic, a study in the cultural approach, Faculty of Arts, Suez Canal University, Ismailia 2018, under the supervision of Dr. Saleh Attia Matar.

• Youssef Nofal’s poetry between theory and achievement, Faculty of Girls, Ain Shams University, 2019, supervised by Dr. Azza Abu Al-Najah, Dr. Basma Bayoumi, the membership of Muhammad Al-Tawoosi, and Dr. Ahmed Fouad.

• Youssef Nofal’s critical efforts between theory and practice, Tanta University, Faculty of Arts, by researcher Mahmoud, supervised by Dr. Hassan Abbas, Dr. Muhammad Al-Desouki.

• Trends of contemporary critics in the study of children’s literature in Egypt, 2021, Tanta University, by researcher Samah Abdel Aziz Adab Tanta, supervised by Dr. Fawzi Issa and Jamal Mahmoud, and membership by Dr. Salem.

• The Lost Collection by Youssef Nofal, a synthetic and analytical study, Faculty of Arts, Port Said, supervised by Dr. Nada Al-Husseini Nada (When discussing grammatical methods in the poetry of Youssef Nofal, Faculty of Arts, Port Said, supervised by Dr. Nada Al-Husseini.

#### **Membership of literary committees**

• Secretary of the Permanent Scientific Committee for the Promotion of Professors in Egyptian Universities (specializing in the Arabic language) by election from the beginning of October 2001 for a period of three years until the end of the eighth session in October 2004, then a member of the Permanent Committee for the Promotion of Assistant Professors from the beginning of the ninth session in October 2004 until October 2008, then Member of the Committee of Nine formed in October 2008 for promotion at the Supreme Council of Universities.

• Rapporteur of the tripartite committee for accrediting the Arabic language subjects for bachelor’s degrees in the colleges of education sector in Egyptian universities for seven years, then a member of it, and a member of the committees of the Supreme Council of Culture, the development committees of the Ministry of Education, and committees at Ain Shams University. He participated in the cultural, literary, and linguistic life of reading, audio, and viewing in Egypt and the Arab world in conferences, seminars and literary journalism.

• Member of the Organizing Committee of the Nineteenth World Papyrus Conference (September 1990), and a member of the Papyrus Center at Ain Shams University in the same period. Member of the Board of Directors of the Mubarak Public Library in Port Said from March 2005 until the end of February 2006, then a member of the Board of Trustees from March 2006 until now by decision of Mr. The city governor is a member of the Writers Union.

• Member of the Story Club, member of the Scientific Committee for Preparation for the International Poetry Conference at the Supreme Council of Culture, Head of the Arabic Language and Culture Division at the Center for Public Service and Community Development at Ain Shams University, and supervised and participated in the program for teaching Arabic to non-native speakers from University of Ghana students sent to the Center, and a member of the Center’s Board of Directors. Since 1993 for a few years, he has been a member of the board of directors and editor of (On) magazine, and a member of the scientific committee for preparing for the International Poetry Conference at the Supreme Council of Culture. Head of the Arabic language departments at the Faculty of Girls and faculties at Suez Canal University, the Faculty of Education in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and the Facultyof Arts, UAE University.

#### **Arbitration**

• Dr. Youssef Nofal also had a role in judging Egyptian and Arab competitions, promotion committees, and publishing in scientific journals. He was a member of the evaluation committee for Al Ain Private College in the Emirates in 1993, a member of the evaluation committee for the bachelor’s and master’s programs at the University of Sharjah (2-7 November 2001), and a member of the college evaluation committee. Islamic and Arabic Studies in Dubai, March 2002, and a member of the Committee for Developing Arabic Language Curricula in Faculties of Education in Egypt 2004, and a Member of the Committee for Developing Curricula in Faculties of Education in Egypt 2005, and a participant in developing the proposed study plans.

#### **Awards and honors**

• Prof. Youssef Nofal received dozens of appreciation and praise awards inside and outside Egypt, which are:

• State Appreciation Award from the Supreme Council of Culture in the field of literature in 2022.

• Cavafys International Prize Egypt and Greece 2019 in Literary and Critical Studies by selection, not submission.

• Egyptian Writers Union Excellence Award 2013

• Ain Shams University Appreciation Award in Arts 2011 and the Prize Medal.

• Poet of Mecca Muhammad Hassan Faki Award for Creativity in Poetry Criticism, awarded by the Zaki Yamani Cultural Foundation, alone.

• The Cairo and North Upper Egypt Writers Conference honored the “Honored Personality” and the authority issued a book about me that includes research and testimonials from specialists: 2009

1/14/2009 Honoring the El Sawy Culturewheel in the “Year of Dignity” on the occasion of receiving the “Wasatia” Group Award

• Story Club Award in Cairo, and obtaining the Club Shield on 4/30/2008

• First Prize in the Competition of Cultural Awareness and its Role in Reviving Values by Researching Culture and Values at the Supreme Council of Culture in Egypt 8/14/1988.

• Ideal Teacher Award, from the Teachers Syndicate, and I was chosen as one of the pioneers of education in Port Said Governorate, 1988.

• Award for research (The role of aids in teaching the Arabic language) from the Ministry of Education in Kuwait - January 1971.

• The second incentive award for research from the Ministry of Education in Kuwait, through a letter from the Undersecretary of the Ministry, 1/13/1971.

• Award for the research paper (School and Society in the Battle of Destiny) in the Second Education Week in Kuwait - December 1969.

• Prizes for writing and creativity in the branches: short stories, poetry, essays, and research from the Supreme Council of Arts and Letters in Egypt (Youth Competition and Arab Youth), more than once for consecutive years between the years 1962 and 1967, including: the first prize in the research entitled (The National Interpretation of the Struggle). Arab), and the first prize in the essay entitled (The Humanity and Creativity of Arab Civilization), and in the Youth Essay Competition for the year 1964/1965.

• Awards of the Local Authority for Arts, Literature and Social Sciences in Alexandria 1962 - 1963 in the short story on March 19, 1962, and obtaining the gold medal.

• Awards for writing research in the summer competition for university students from the Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs in Egypt between 1963 and 1965, both written and oral, including: the first prize for the research (The Civilization of Islam in Andalusia) - 1963 in the second summer competition, and the first for the research (The Civilization of the Arabs in Sicily) - 1964 in the third competition, and the Council printed it in a book (1965), and the first was about research (How did colonialism conspire against Palestine, and how do we recover it?) - 1965 in the fourth competition.

• Gold Medal in the Short Story Competition, Universities Youth Week, Assiut, 1964

• Obtaining the research award in the Fourth University Youth Week competition held in February 1960 with my research (The Role of Arab Nationalism in Building Arab Society)

• Prof. Hassan Nofal continues to offer a lot to science and literature in various forums, and he also has many fans and followers of his various works, writings, and publications.

• He received the Supreme Council for Islamic Sciences Award while still a student.

• In 1960, he won five different awards in the fields of short stories, poetry, critical essay, and one-act playwriting.

• Hassan Noufel contributed 37 books to the Arabic library, in addition to more than 200 research papers and articles, alongside compiling an encyclopedia of modern and contemporary Arabic poetry that included more than 7,500 poets.

• Among his most prominent works are “The Aesthetics of the Qur’anic Story,” “Dialogue in Arabic Drama,” and “The Short Story and the Novel Between the Generations of Taha Hussein and Naguib Mahfouz.”
