On 11 July, Nasser replaced Amer with Mohamed Fawzi as general commander,[257][258] over the protestations of Amer's loyalists in the military, 600 of whom marched on army headquarters and demanded Amer's reinstatement.[259] After Nasser sacked thirty of the loyalists in response,[259] Amer and his allies devised a plan to topple him on 27 August.[260] Nasser was tipped off about their activities and, after several invitations, he convinced Amer to meet him at his home on 24 August.[260] Nasser confronted Amer about the coup plot, which he denied before being arrested by Mohieddin. Amer allegedly committed suicide (others claims state he was poisoned) on 14 September.[261] Despite his souring relationship with Amer, Nasser spoke of losing "the person closest to [him]".[262] Thereafter, Nasser began a process of depoliticizing the armed forces, arresting dozens of leading military and intelligence figures loyal to Amer.[261]

At the 29 August Arab League summit in Khartoum, Nasser's usual commanding position had receded as the attending heads of state expected Saudi King Faisal to lead. A ceasefire in the Yemen War was declared and the summit concluded with the Khartoum Resolution,[263] which, according to Abd al Azim Ramadan, left only one option—a war with Israel.[264]

The Soviet Union soon resupplied the Egyptian military with about half of its former arsenals and broke diplomatic relations with Israel. Nasser cut relations with the US following the war, and, according to Aburish, his policy of "playing the superpowers against each other" ended.[265] In November, Nasser accepted UN Resolution 242, which called for Israel's withdrawal from territories acquired in the war. His supporters claimed Nasser's move was meant to buy time to prepare for another confrontation with Israel, while his detractors believed his acceptance of the resolution signaled a waning interest in Palestinian independence.[266]

Final years of presidency
Domestic reforms and governmental changes
Nasser delivering his final speech to the nation on 23 July 1970

Nasser appointed himself the additional roles of prime minister and supreme commander of the armed forces on 19 June 1967.[267] From 3–4 August 1967, the Arab Socialist Union (ASU)'s executive committee held a debate wherein Nasser bitterly attacked the current single-party system and proposed the creation of a second party.[268] This 'real opposition' would be led by Free Officers Abdel Latif Boghdadi and Kamal el-Din Hussein,[269] who were both former government members who had resigned following differences with Nasser's policies. It would also have been granted access to the same resources enjoyed by the ASU, including its own newspaper. Parliament would be dissolved to make way for elections in December.[269] However, this proposal was met with resistance from his inner circle, including Zakaria Mohieddin and Sadat, who raised concerns about potential economic instability caused by a two-party system and argued that the timing of the move was unsuitable given the current crisis.[270] Nasser's proposal was not implemented.

Angry at the military court's perceived leniency with air force officers charged with negligence during the 1967 war, workers and students launched protests calling for major political reforms in late February 1968.[271][272] Nasser responded to the demonstrations, the most significant public challenge to his rule since workers' protests in March 1954, by removing most military figures from his cabinet and appointing eight civilians in place of several high-ranking members of the ASU.[273][274] By 3 March, Nasser directed Egypt's intelligence apparatus to focus on external rather than domestic espionage, and declared the "fall of the mukhabarat state".[274]

On 30 March, Nasser proclaimed a manifesto stipulating the restoration of civil liberties, greater parliamentary independence from the executive,[272] major structural changes to the ASU, and a campaign to rid the government of corrupt elements.[273] A public referendum approved the proposed measures in May, and held subsequent elections for the Supreme Executive Committee, the ASU's highest decision-making body.[272] Observers noted that the declaration signaled an important shift from political repression to liberalization, although its promises would largely go unfulfilled.[273]

Nasser appointed Sadat and Hussein el-Shafei as his vice presidents in December 1969. By then, relations with his other original military comrades, namely Khaled and Zakaria Mohieddin and former vice president Sabri, had become strained.[275] By mid-1970, Nasser pondered replacing Sadat with Boghdadi after reconciling with the latter.[276]

War of Attrition and regional diplomatic initiatives
Nasser observing the Suez front with Egyptian officers during the War of Attrition. General Commander Mohamed Fawzi is directly behind Nasser, and to their left is Chief of Staff Abdel Moneim Riad, November 1968
Nasser brokering a ceasefire between Yasser Arafat of the PLO (left) and King Hussein of Jordan (right) at the emergency Arab League summit in Cairo on 27 September 1970, one day before Nasser's death

Meanwhile, in January 1968, Nasser commenced the War of Attrition to reclaim territory captured by Israel, ordering attacks against Israeli positions east of the then-blockaded Suez Canal.[277] In March, Nasser offered Yasser Arafat's Fatah movement arms and funds after their performance against Israeli forces in the Battle of Karameh that month.[278] He also advised Arafat to think of peace with Israel and the establishment of a Palestinian state comprising the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.[278] Nasser effectively ceded his leadership of the "Palestine issue" to Arafat.[266]

Israel retaliated against Egyptian shelling with commando raids, artillery shelling and air strikes. This resulted in an exodus of civilians from Egyptian cities along the Suez Canal's western bank.[279][280][281] Nasser ceased all military activities and began a program to build a network of internal defenses, while receiving the financial backing of various Arab states.[281] The war resumed in March 1969.[281] In November, Nasser brokered an agreement between the PLO and the Lebanese military that granted Palestinian guerrillas the right to use Lebanese territory to attack Israel.[282]

In June 1970, Nasser accepted the US-sponsored Rogers Plan, which called for an end to hostilities and an Israeli withdrawal from Egyptian territory, but it was rejected by Israel, the PLO, and most Arab states except Jordan.[276] Nasser had initially rejected the plan, but conceded under pressure from the Soviet Union, which feared that escalating regional conflict could drag it into a war with the US.[283][284] He also determined that a ceasefire could serve as a tactical step toward the strategic goal of recapturing the Suez Canal.[285] Nasser forestalled any movement toward direct negotiations with Israel. In dozens of speeches and statements, Nasser posited the equation that any direct peace talks with Israel were tantamount to surrender.[286] Following Nasser's acceptance, Israel agreed to a ceasefire and Nasser used the lull in fighting to move surface-to-air missiles towards the canal zone.[283][284]

Meanwhile, tensions in Jordan between an increasingly autonomous PLO and King Hussein's government had been simmering;[287] following the Dawson's Field hijackings, a military campaign was launched to rout out PLO forces. The offensive elevated risks of a regional war and prompted Nasser to hold an emergency Arab League summit on 27 September in Cairo,[288] where he forged a ceasefire.[289]

Death and funeral
Main article: Death and state funeral of Gamal Abdel Nasser
Nasser's funeral procession attended by five million mourners in Cairo, 1 October 1970

As the Arab League summit closed on 28 September 1970, hours after escorting the last Arab leader to leave, Nasser suffered a heart attack. He was immediately transported to his house, where his physicians tended to him. Nasser died several hours later, around 6 p.m. at age 52.[290] Heikal, Sadat, and Nasser's wife Tahia were at his deathbed.[291] According to his doctor, al-Sawi Habibi, Nasser's likely cause of death was arteriosclerosis, varicose veins, and complications from long-standing diabetes. Nasser was also a heavy smoker with a family history of heart disease—two of his brothers died in their fifties from the same condition.[292] The state of Nasser's health was not known to the public prior to his death.[292][293] He had suffered heart attacks before, in 1966 and September 1969.[citation needed]

Following the announcement of Nasser's death, most Arabs were in a state of shock.[291] Nasser's funeral procession through Cairo on 1 October was attended by at least five million mourners.[294][295][296] The 10-kilometer (6.2 mi) procession to his burial site began at the old RCC headquarters with a flyover by MiG-21 jets. His flag-draped coffin was attached to a gun carriage pulled by six horses and led by a column of cavalrymen.[296] All Arab heads of state attended, with the exception of Saudi King Faisal.[297] King Hussein and Arafat cried openly, and Muammar Gaddafi of Libya fainted from emotional distress twice.[295] A few major non-Arab dignitaries were present, including Soviet Premier Alexei Kosygin and French Prime Minister Jacques Chaban-Delmas.[295]

Gamal Abdel Nasser Mosque in Cairo, the site of his burial

Almost immediately after the procession began, mourners engulfed Nasser's coffin chanting, "There is no God but Allah, and Nasser is God's beloved... Each of us is Nasser."[296] Police unsuccessfully attempted to quell the crowds and, as a result, most of the foreign dignitaries were evacuated.[296] The final destination was the Nasr Mosque, which was afterwards renamed Abdel Nasser Mosque, where Nasser was buried.[296]

Because of his ability to motivate nationalistic passions, "men, women, and children wept and wailed in the streets" after hearing of his death, according to Nutting.[290] The general Arab reaction was of mourning, with thousands of people pouring onto the streets of major cities throughout the Arab world.[296] Over a dozen people were killed in Beirut as a result of the chaos, and in Jerusalem, roughly 75,000 Arabs marched through the Old City chanting, "Nasser will never die."[296] As a testament to his unchallenged leadership of the Arab people, following his death, the headline of the Lebanese Le Jour read, "One hundred million human beings—the Arabs—are orphans."[298] Sherif Hetata, a former political prisoner[299] and later member of Nasser's ASU,[300] said that "Nasser's greatest achievement was his funeral. The world will never again see five million people crying together."[295]

Legacy
Nasser presenting prominent and blind writer Taha Hussein (standing in front of Nasser) with a national honors prize for literature, 1959

Nasser made Egypt fully independent of British influence,[301][302] and the country became a major power in the developing world under his leadership.[301] One of Nasser's main domestic efforts was to establish social justice, which he deemed a prerequisite to liberal democracy.[303] During his presidency, ordinary citizens enjoyed unprecedented access to housing, education, jobs, health services and nourishment, as well as other forms of social welfare, while feudalistic influence waned.[301][304]

However, these advances came at the expense of civil liberties. In Nasser's Egypt, the media were tightly controlled, mail was opened, and telephones were wiretapped.[305] He was elected in 1956, 1958 and 1965 in plebiscites in which he was the sole candidate, each time claiming unanimous or near-unanimous support. With few exceptions, the legislature did little more than approve Nasser's policies. As the legislature was made up almost entirely of government supporters, Nasser effectively held all governing power in the nation.

By the end of his presidency, employment and working conditions improved considerably, although poverty was still high in the country and substantial resources allocated for social welfare had been diverted to the war effort.[303]

The national economy grew significantly through agrarian reform, major modernization projects such as the Helwan steel works and the Aswan Dam, and nationalization schemes such as that of the Suez Canal.[301][304] However, the marked economic growth of the early 1960s took a downturn for the remainder of the decade, only recovering in 1970.[306] Egypt experienced a "golden age" of culture during Nasser's presidency, according to historian Joel Gordon, particularly in film, television, theater, radio, literature, fine arts, comedy, poetry, and music.[307] Egypt under Nasser dominated the Arab world in these fields,[304][307] producing cultural icons.[304]

During Mubarak's presidency, Nasserist political parties began to emerge in Egypt, the first being the Arab Democratic Nasserist Party (ADNP).[308][309] The party carried minor political influence,[310] and splits between its members beginning in 1995 resulted in the gradual establishment of splinter parties,[311] including Hamdeen Sabahi's 1997 founding of Al-Karama.[312] Sabahi came in third place during the 2012 presidential election.[313] Nasserist activists were among the founders of Kefaya, a major opposition force during Mubarak's rule.[312] On 19 September 2012, four Nasserist parties (the ADNP, Karama, the National Conciliation Party, and the Popular Nasserist Congress Party) merged to form the United Nasserist Party.[314]

Public image
Nasser speaking to a homeless Egyptian man and offering him a job, after the man was found sleeping below the stage where Nasser was seated, 1959

Nasser was known for his accessibility and direct relationship with ordinary Egyptians.[315][316] His availability to the public, despite assassination attempts against him, was unparalleled among his successors.[317] A skilled orator,[318] Nasser gave 1,359 speeches between 1953 and 1970, a record for any Egyptian head of state.[319] Historian Elie Podeh wrote that a constant theme of Nasser's image was "his ability to represent Egyptian authenticity, in triumph or defeat".[315] The national press also helped to foster his popularity and profile—more so after the nationalization of state media.[317] Historian Tarek Osman wrote:

The interplay in the Nasser 'phenomenon' between genuine expression of popular feeling and state-sponsored propaganda may sometimes be hard to disentangle. But behind it lies a vital historical fact: that Gamal Abdel Nasser signifies the only truly Egyptian developmental project in the country's history since the fall of the Pharaonic state. There had been other projects ... But this was different—in origin, meaning and impact. For Nasser was a man of the Egyptian soil who had overthrown the Middle East's most established and sophisticated monarchy in a swift and bloodless move—to the acclaim of millions of poor, oppressed Egyptians—and ushered in a programme of 'social justice', 'progress and development', and 'dignity'.[320]

Nasser waving to crowds in Mansoura, 1960

While Nasser was increasingly criticized by Egyptian intellectuals following the Six-Day War and his death in 1970, the general public was persistently sympathetic both during and after Nasser's life.[315] According to political scientist Mahmoud Hamad, writing in 2008, "nostalgia for Nasser is easily sensed in Egypt and all Arab countries today".[321] General malaise in Egyptian society, particularly during the Mubarak era, augmented nostalgia for Nasser's presidency, which increasingly became associated with the ideals of national purpose, hope, social cohesion, and vibrant culture.[307]

Until the present day, Nasser serves as an iconic figure throughout the Arab world,[301][322] a symbol of Arab unity and dignity,[323][324][325] and a towering figure in modern Middle Eastern history.[38] He is also considered a champion of social justice in Egypt.[326][327] Time writes that despite his mistakes and shortcomings, Nasser "imparted a sense of personal worth and national pride that [Egypt and the Arabs] had not known for 400 years. This alone may have been enough to balance his flaws and failures."[296]

Historian Steven A. Cook wrote in July 2013, "Nasser's heyday still represents, for many, the last time that Egypt felt united under leaders whose espoused principles met the needs of ordinary Egyptians."[328] During the Arab Spring, which resulted in a revolution in Egypt, photographs of Nasser were raised in Cairo and Arab capitals during anti-government demonstrations.[329][330] According to journalist Lamis Andoni, Nasser had become a "symbol of Arab dignity" during the mass demonstrations.[329]

Criticism
Anwar Sadat (left) and Nasser in the National Assembly, 1964. Sadat succeeded Nasser as president in 1970 and significantly departed from Nasser's policies throughout his rule.

Sadat declared his intention to "continue the path of Nasser" in his 7 October 1970 presidential inauguration speech,[331] but began to depart from Nasserist policies as his domestic position improved following the 1973 October War.[310][331] President Sadat's Infitah policy sought to open Egypt's economy for private investment.[332] According to Heikal, ensuing anti-Nasser developments until the present day led to an Egypt "[half] at war with Abdel-Nasser, half [at war] with Anwar El-Sadat".[304]

Nasser's Egyptian detractors considered him a dictator who thwarted democratic progress, imprisoned thousands of dissidents, and led a repressive administration responsible for numerous human rights violations.[304] Islamists in Egypt, particularly members of the politically persecuted Brotherhood, viewed Nasser as oppressive, tyrannical, and demonic.[333] Samer S. Shehata, who wrote an article on "The Politics of Laughter: Nasser, Sadat, and Mubarek in Egyptian Political Jokes" noted that "with the new regime came the end of parliamentary politics and political freedoms, including the right to organize political parties, and freedoms of speech and the press".[334] Liberal writer Tawfiq al-Hakim described Nasser as a "confused Sultan" who employed stirring rhetoric, but had no actual plan to achieve his stated goals.[332]

Some of Nasser's liberal and Islamist critics in Egypt, including the founding members of the New Wafd Party and writer Jamal Badawi, dismissed Nasser's popular appeal with the Egyptian masses during his presidency as being the product of successful manipulation and demagoguery.[335] Egyptian political scientist Alaa al-Din Desouki blamed the 1952 revolution's shortcomings on Nasser's concentration of power, and Egypt's lack of democracy on Nasser's political style and his government's limitations on freedom of expression and political participation.[336] American political scientist Mark Cooper asserted that Nasser's charisma and his direct relationship with the Egyptian people "rendered intermediaries (organizations and individuals) unnecessary".[337] He opined that Nasser's legacy was a "guarantee of instability" due to Nasser's reliance on personal power and the absence of strong political institutions under his rule.[337] Historian Abd al-Azim Ramadan wrote that Nasser was an irrational and irresponsible leader, blaming his inclination to solitary decision-making for Egypt's losses during the Suez War, among other events.[338] Miles Copeland, Jr., a Central Intelligence Agency officer known for his close personal relationship with Nasser,[339] said that the barriers between Nasser and the outside world have grown so thick that all but the information that attest to his infallibility, indispensability, and immortality has been filtered out.[340]

Zakaria Mohieddin, who was Nasser's vice president, said that Nasser gradually changed during his reign. He ceased consulting his colleagues and made more and more of the decisions himself. Although Nasser repeatedly said that a war with Israel will start at a time of his, or Arab, choosing, in 1967 he started a bluffing game "but a successful bluff means your opponent must not know which cards you are holding. In this case Nasser's opponent could see his hand in the mirror and knew he was only holding a pair of deuces" and Nasser knew that his army is not prepared yet. "All of this was out of character...His tendencies in this regard may have been accentuated by diabetes... That was the only rational explanation for his actions in 1967".[240]

Antisemitism allegations

During an interview with Gerhard Frey in the German neo-Nazi newspaper National-Zeitung on May 1, 1964, Nasser said that "no person, not even the most simple one, takes seriously the lie of the six million Jews that were murdered [in the Holocaust]."[341][342][343] However, he is not known to have ever again publicly called the figure of six million into question, perhaps because his advisors and East German contacts had advised him on the subject.[344] Nasser, convinced of its authenticity, also encouraged the distribution of the antisemitic fabrication The Protocols of the Elders of Zion. He believed that the Jews greatly influenced the global financial market and that they ultimately strove for world domination. Nasser also hired former Nazi officials like Johann von Leers to distribute antisemitic propaganda. He is, however, thought to have been more moderate in that regard than contemporary political powers like Young Egypt or the Muslim Brotherhood.[345][346]

Regional leadership
Jaafar Nimeiry of Sudan (left), Nasser, and Muammar Gaddafi of Libya (right) at the Tripoli Airport, 1969. Nimeiry and Gaddafi were influenced by Nasser's pan-Arabist ideas and the latter sought to succeed him as "leader of the Arabs".

Through his actions and speeches, and because he was able to symbolize the popular Arab will, Nasser inspired several nationalist revolutions in the Arab world.[320] He defined the politics of his generation and communicated directly with the public masses of the Arab world, bypassing the various heads of states of those countries—an accomplishment not repeated by other Arab leaders.[335] The extent of Nasser's centrality in the region made it a priority for incoming Arab nationalist heads of state to seek good relations with Egypt, in order to gain popular legitimacy from their own citizens.[347]

To varying degrees,[38] Nasser's statist system of government was continued in Egypt and emulated by virtually all Arab republics,[348] namely Algeria, Syria, Iraq, Tunisia, Yemen, Sudan, and Libya.[38][348] Ahmed Ben Bella, Algeria's first president, was a staunch Nasserist.[349] Abdullah al-Sallal drove out the king of North Yemen in the name of Nasser's pan-Arabism.[199] Other coups influenced by Nasser included those that occurred in Iraq in July 1958 and Syria in 1963.[350] Muammar Gaddafi, who overthrew the Libyan monarchy in 1969, considered Nasser his hero and sought to succeed him as "leader of the Arabs".[351] Also in 1969, Colonel Gaafar Nimeiry, a supporter of Nasser, took power in Sudan.[352] The Arab Nationalist Movement (ANM) helped spread Nasser's pan-Arabist ideas throughout the Arab world, particularly among the Palestinians, Syrians, and Lebanese,[353][354] and in South Yemen, the Persian Gulf, and Iraq.[354] While many regional heads of state tried to emulate Nasser, Podeh opined that the "parochialism" of successive Arab leaders "transformed imitation [of Nasser] into parody".[348]

Portrayal in film

In 1963, Egyptian director Youssef Chahine produced the film El Nasser Salah El Dine ("Saladin The Victorious"), which intentionally drew parallels between Saladin, considered a hero in the Arab world, and Nasser and his pan-Arabist policies.[355] Nasser is played by Ahmed Zaki in Mohamed Fadel's 1996 Nasser 56. The film set the Egyptian box office record at the time, and focused on Nasser during the Suez Crisis.[356][357] It is also considered a milestone in Egyptian and Arab cinema as the first film to dramatize the role of a modern-day Arab leader.[358] Together with the 1999 Syrian biopic Gamal Abdel Nasser, the films marked the first biographical movies about contemporary public figures produced in the Arab world.[359] He is portrayed by Amir Boutrous in the Netflix television series The Crown. Nasser is also portrayed by Amr Saad in the 2025 Egyptian film El Sett, a biopic about the iconic Egyptian singer and actress Umm Kulthum.[360][361]

Personal life
Nasser and his family in Manshiyat al-Bakri, 1963. From left to right, his daughter Mona, his wife Tahia Kazem, daughter Hoda, son Abdel Hakim, son Khaled, son Abdel Hamid, and Nasser.

In 1944, Nasser married Tahia Kazem (1920–1992), the daughter of a wealthy Iranian father and an Egyptian mother, both of whom had died when she was young. She had been introduced to Nasser through her brother, Abdel Hamid Kazim, a merchant friend of Nasser's, in 1943.[362] After their wedding, the couple moved into a house in Manshiyat al-Bakri, a suburb of Cairo, where they lived for the rest of their lives. Nasser's entry into the officer corps in 1937 secured him relatively well-paid employment in a society where most people lived in poverty.[29] Nasser and Tahia would sometimes discuss politics at home, but for the most part Nasser kept his career separate from his family life. He preferred to spend most of his free time with his children.[363]

Nasser and Tahia had two daughters and three sons:[364]

Hoda, b. 1945.
Mona, b. 1947.
Khalid, 1949–2011. The most active politically. Said to have co-founded (with Egyptian diplomat Mahmoud Noureddin [ar]) a secret leftist organization, Egypt's Revolution [ar] (Thawrat Miṣr), which was accused of assassinating Israeli members of the Shin Bet stationed in Egypt in the late 1980s. Khalid took refuge in Yugoslavia and was eventually pardoned by President Hosni Mubarak.
Abd al-Hamid, b. 1951.
Abd al-Hakim, b. 1955. Appears regularly in Egyptian and regional media, heads the museum dedicated to the life of his father.

Although he was a proponent of secular politics, Nasser was an observant Muslim who made the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca in 1954 and 1965.[365][366] He was known to be personally incorruptible,[367][368][369][370] a characteristic which further enhanced his reputation among the citizens of Egypt and the Arab world.[369] Nasser's personal hobbies included playing chess, photography, watching American films, reading Arabic, English, and French magazines, and listening to classical music.[371][372]

Nasser practices photography at his home in Cairo, 1969

Nasser was a chain smoker.[292][368][373] He maintained 18-hour workdays and rarely took time off for vacations. The combination of smoking and working long hours contributed to his poor health. He was diagnosed with diabetes in the early 1960s and by the time of his death in 1970, he also had arteriosclerosis, heart disease, and high blood pressure. He suffered two major heart attacks (in 1966 and 1969), and was on bed rest for six weeks after the second episode. State media reported that Nasser's absence from the public view at that time was a result of influenza.[292]

## Abstract

![Image 10: sparkles](https://c.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)

The paper delves into the historical and cultural impact of Gamal Abdel Nasser's leadership in Egypt, particularly focusing on the nationalization of the Suez Canal and its connections to a broader narrative of Arab modernity and identity. It examines the aftermath of the 1967 Naksa (setback), which represents a critical moment in Arab history, revealing the fragility of Nasserist ideals and the subsequent disillusionment with nationalist fiction. The analysis reflects on how these themes resonate in contemporary movements for social and political change in the Arab world, emphasizing a search for authenticity and new agency in the wake of past failures.

Abstract: This article revisits the Nasserist project through the lens of haunting. It explores the afterlives of Nasserism, in particular in relation to Egypt’s move toward a free market economy from the 1970s onwards. To do this, I explore the Nasserist project in order to excavate some of the promises that were made and to trace the legacies these created. I argue that both these promises—only partially fulfilled—and the social violence they at times contained—continued to act as powerful political memories that limited Egyptian politics in the decades that followed. Thinking of Nasserism as a form of haunting allows for a deeper understanding of how different political projects seep into one another, problematizing the notion of a linear teleological or providential trajectory consisting of distinct eras. In distinction to work that has mobilised the concept of haunting (originally theorized by Jacques Derrida) in order to elaborate on the historical manifestation of damaging or violent legacies in the present, I argue that Nasserist forms of haunting should be read as both a productive and destructive normative force in the present. This article puts forward examples of both, particularly in relation to questions of social justice, socialism, and anti-imperialism.

From a comparative Arab, Palestinian and Jewish-Israeli perspective, our workshop offers to discuss the traces and evocations in the presence of two distinct past: the Shoah - "catastrophe" in Hebrew, a term used since the Second World War to designate the extermination of Jews in Europe and beyond, with the sometimes contested term "Holocaust" in English; and the Nakba - a concept derived from Arabic and also translated as "catastrophe", which refers to the process of expulsion, dispossession and deterritorialization of the majority of Palestinians in 1948. These two pasts involve different spaces, temporalities, facts and effects. They have given rise to policies, historical analyses, actions in the legal field and various memoirs. While some, here and there, both in the social and academic spheres, have tried to bring them closer together, their heterogeneity nevertheless makes any exercise of comparison perilous, burdening their own intelligibility. In their singular trajectories, the Shoah and Nakba sometimes cross jointly and sometimes in parallel, Israeli and Palestinian political speeches, academic works (Gilbert Ashcar; Bashir Bashir and Amos Goldberg...), Arab and Israeli literature (Avot Yeshurun, Rabai Al-Madhoun, Elias Khoury...) : while the first refers to a history that has taken place in other territories, it is nevertheless one of the major sources of Israel's identity (Ben Amos, 2012) and of identification in the present of Israelis, particularly in their relationship with the Palestinians; the second is instituted as a symbol of a Zionist policy, linked to other past colonial experiences. Beyond the discussions that get caught up in the system of evidence or focus on the legitimacy or illegitimacy of a comparison, it is the concrete modalities of this meeting and their (non-) coincidences that we wish to address in this panel. When, how, by whom, in what context has the "relationship to the Jewish tragedy" become more complex, in Israeli-Palestinian spaces, in the Middle East and beyond, "through its relationship with the Palestinian drama" (Ashcar, 2010:14)? Such complexity undoubtedly explains in part the still too marginal attention paid in France or abroad in academic studies to the reception of the Shoah in the Arab world and the Nakba in Israel and beyond. This workshop aims to overcome this, proposing a questioning in history, anthropology, political theory and literature on what is produced today, and in the long term, the meeting or not meeting Shoah-Nakba in the Middle East.

[Arie M Dubnov](https://gwu.academia.edu/ArieDubnov)

May 2018 marks the 70th anniversary of Israel’s Independence, as well as the 1948 War in Palestine/Israel. The war, which broke out in November 1947 in the wake of the UN General Assembly Resolution in favor of partition of Palestine into a Jewish and Arab states, was exceptionally cruel, leaving deep scars in both communities. To this day, it signifies different things for each side – a creation of a new, sovereign Israeli state for the Jews, and displacement, together with loss of land and home for the Palestinians. Indeed, even the different names used to mark the violent events and their aftermath – “Atzmaut” (Hebrew for Independence) and “Nakba” (Arabic for “Disaster” or “Catastrophe”) – capture this dissonance. The overall aim of the course is to explore the local, regional, and global contexts that produced the cataclysm of 1948, and to delve into the consequences and unresolved political, social, and cultural questions it left behind. To accomplish this overall aim, the students taking the class will be asked to engage in two connected, yet distinct types of scholarly inquiry: First, the course will introduce students to the major developments leading up to the war, the key personalities, events and various stages of the war, and some of the major historiographical debates which emerged in the last two decades. Second, switching from history to memory and “memory activism,” the course will analyze the way in which the war was narrated and remembered by Israelis and Palestinians, and the way in which this memory changed over the years. The course wishes not to avoid dealing with a controversial topic, but to do so in a scholarly and academic manner. It will provide a room for showcasing different narratives, historiographies and modes of interpretation, in a conscious attempt to go beyond political partisanship insofar as the topic permits. The timing is also auspicious. The class will run in tandem with multiple special events that will take place during the spring semester, and we intend to take advantage of this unique opportunity. Hence the class’s format is somewhat unconventional: first, in addition to the traditional class discussions, students will be also required to attend the movie series Cinema and the Memory of the 1948 War that will run parallel to the class during this semester (see dates below); second, students will be required to attend the one day conference entitled Nakba, Past & Present, that will take place on Friday, April 13 2017, at the Elliott School’s Institute for Middle East Studies.

1967 Arab-Israeli War is a historical turning point in the modern Middle East history. It was important for both Israel and Arab states: Israel proved itself as a stable and powerful nation within a hostile environment. On the contrary, the main centre against Israel in the region and the grassroot movement against colonialism, namely pan-Arabism or Arab nationalism or Arab socialism, had an absolute defeat and decline. After this war, postcolonial era of the Middle East (especially Egypt) opened a new chapter: Arab regimes, based on secularism and nationalism, loosened the strings of Islamism, gradually gave the etatist economy policies up, in foreign policy a shift from the USSR to the USA was clear, ideologically pan-Arabist themes started to be disappear. The losers of the so-called “Arab Cold War” clearly Gamal Abdel Nasser and Arab socialism, against Islamism and Saudi petro-dollars. Although Nasser physically died in 1970, his symbolic death occurred in 1967, after the Six-Day War. This striking moment was not an important point for military officials or politicians: It was a milestone also for Arab intellectuals.

This article explores how historical fiction in cinema has been used to disseminate and entrench the myth and aura of Jamāl ʿAbd an-Nāṣir (1918–1970) among Egyptians and the Arab world. These films project struggles for independence of the time into the past, thus arguably emphasizing the role of the Free Officers’ Revolution in rescuing Egypt from the corrupt and dystopian world of colonization. This portrayal also highlights internal enemies – leaders who legitimized this colonial universe. To do this, I explore the Nasserist project in order to excavate some of the promises that were made and to trace the legacies these created. I argue that both these promises—only partially fulfilled—and the social violence they at times contained—continued to act as powerful political memories that limited Egyptian politics in the decades that followed. Thinking of Nasserism as a form of haunting allows for a deeper understanding of how different political projects seep into one another, problematizing the notion of a linear teleological or providential trajectory consisting of distinct eras. In distinction to work that has mobilised the concept of haunting (originally theorized by Jacques Derrida) in order to elaborate on the historical manifestation of damaging or violent legacies in the present, I argue that Nasserist forms of haunting should be read as both a productive and destructive normative force in the present. This article puts forward examples of both, particularly in relation to questions of social justice, socialism, and anti-imperialism.

From a comparative Arab, Palestinian and Jewish-Israeli perspective, our workshop offers to discuss the traces and evocations in the presence of two distinct past: the Shoah - "catastrophe" in Hebrew, a term used since the Second World War to designate the extermination of Jews in Europe and beyond, with the sometimes contested term "Holocaust" in English; and the Nakba - a concept derived from Arabic and also translated as "catastrophe", which refers to the process of expulsion, dispossession and deterritorialization of the majority of Palestinians in 1948. These two pasts involve different spaces, temporalities, facts and effects. They have given rise to policies, historical analyses, actions in the legal field and various memoirs. While some, here and there, both in the social and academic spheres, have tried to bring them closer together, their heterogeneity nevertheless makes any exercise of comparison perilous, burdening their own intelligibility. In their singular trajectories, the Shoah and Nakba sometimes cross jointly and sometimes in parallel, Israeli and Palestinian political speeches, academic works (Gilbert Ashcar; Bashir Bashir and Amos Goldberg...), Arab and Israeli literature (Avot Yeshurun, Rabai Al-Madhoun, Elias Khoury...) : while the first refers to a history that has taken place in other territories, it is nevertheless one of the major sources of Israel's identity (Ben Amos, 2012) and of identification in the present of Israelis, particularly in their relationship with the Palestinians; the second is instituted as a symbol of a Zionist policy, linked to other past colonial experiences. Beyond the discussions that get caught up in the system of evidence or focus on the legitimacy or illegitimacy of a comparison, it is the concrete modalities of this meeting and their (non-) coincidences that we wish to address in this panel. When, how, by whom, in what context has the "relationship to the Jewish tragedy" become more complex, in Israeli-Palestinian spaces, in the Middle East and beyond, "through its relationship with the Palestinian drama" (Ashcar, 2010:14)? Such complexity undoubtedly explains in part the still too marginal attention paid in France or abroad in academic studies to the reception of the Shoah in the Arab world and the Nakba in Israel and beyond. This workshop aims to overcome this, proposing a questioning in history, anthropology, political theory and literature on what is produced today, and in the long term, the meeting or not meeting Shoah-Nakba in the Middle East.

The paper reveals that Nasser's narrative fostered a collective identity tied to aspirations of progress, culminating in an enduring emotional attachment even post-defeat in 1967. How did the 1967 Naksa alter public perception of Nasser?add

The paper illustrates that the Naksa transformed Nasser from a revered leader to a blameless child figure, eliciting unconditional love despite his admitted failures. This shift initiated a discourse of denial, shifting responsibility away from him and fostering conspiracy theories surrounding the defeat.

What role does iconography play in Sisi's political narrative?add

The research demonstrates that Sisi's iconography resurrects Nasserist themes, casting him as a historical savior invoking colonial undertones to legitimize his power. This narrative creates a contrast to the Muslim Brotherhood, depicted negatively, thus reinforcing Sisi's position as a unifying national figure.

What does the term 'generation of the Defeat' signify in this context?add

The paper identifies the 'generation of the Defeat' as a socio-political context, encompassing disillusionment following the 1967 war, with subsequent generations seeking to dissociate from this narrative. This concept reflects a longing for a new historical agency that opposes the stagnant ideologies of the past.

How do the Arab uprisings challenge previous Nasserist ideologies?add

The study indicates that the Arab uprisings sought to dismantle the stagnation associated with Nasser's legacy, advocating for dignity and a reinvigorated future. Despite initial enthusiasm, ongoing authoritarian practices, including Sisi's regime, continued to suppress these aspirations, complicating the uprisings' outcomes.

May 2018 marks the 70th anniversary of Israel’s Independence, as well as the 1948 War in Palestine/Israel. The war, which broke out in November 1947 in the wake of the UN General Assembly Resolution in favor of partition of Palestine into a Jewish and Arab states, was exceptionally cruel, leaving deep scars in both communities. To this day, it signifies different things for each side – a creation of a new, sovereign Israeli state for the Jews, and displacement, together with loss of land and home for the Palestinians. Indeed, even the different names used to mark the violent events and their aftermath – “Atzmaut” (Hebrew for Independence) and “Nakba” (Arabic for “Disaster” or “Catastrophe”) – capture this dissonance. The overall aim of the course is to explore the local, regional, and global contexts that produced the cataclysm of 1948, and to delve into the consequences and unresolved political, social, and cultural questions it left behind. To accomplish this overall aim, the students taking the class will be asked to engage in two connected, yet distinct types of scholarly inquiry: First, the course will introduce students to the major developments leading up to the war, the key personalities, events and various stages of the war, and some of the major historiographical debates which emerged in the last two decades. Second, switching from history to memory and “memory activism,” the course will analyze the way in which the war was narrated and remembered by Israelis and Palestinians, and the way in which this memory changed over the years. The course wishes not to avoid dealing with a controversial topic, but to do so in a scholarly and academic manner. It will provide a room for showcasing different narratives, historiographies and modes of interpretation, in a conscious attempt to go beyond political partisanship insofar as the topic permits. The timing is also auspicious. The class will run in tandem with multiple special events that will take place during the spring semester, and we intend to take advantage of this unique opportunity. Hence the class’s format is somewhat unconventional: first, in addition to the traditional class discussions, students will be also required to attend the movie series Cinema and the Memory of the 1948 War that will run parallel to the class during this semester (see dates below); second, students will be required to attend the one day conference entitled Nakba, Past & Present, that will take place on Friday, April 13 2017, at the Elliott School’s Institute for Middle East Studies.

1967 Arab-Israeli War is a historical turning point in the modern Middle East history. It was important for both Israel and Arab states: Israel proved itself as a stable and powerful nation within a hostile environment. On the contrary, the main centre against Israel in the region and the grassroot movement against colonialism, namely pan-Arabism or Arab nationalism or Arab socialism, had an absolute defeat and decline. After this war, postcolonial era of the Middle East (especially Egypt) opened a new chapter: Arab regimes, based on secularism and nationalism, loosened the strings of Islamism, gradually gave the etatist economy policies up, in foreign policy a shift from the USSR to the USA was clear, ideologically pan-Arabist themes started to be disappear. The losers of the so-called “Arab Cold War” clearly Gamal Abdel Nasser and Arab socialism, against Islamism and Saudi petro-dollars. ### Nasser, Nubia, and the Stories of a People

  

[with Alia Mossallam](https://eume-berlin.academia.edu/AliaMossallam)

 hosted by [Chris Gratien](https://history.virginia.edu/people/chris-gratien)

 | In 1952, a coup d'état led by Gamal Abdel Nasser ushered in a revolutionary period of Egyptian history in which sound played an integral role in shaping collective political consciousness. The culture of the 50s and 60s was dominated by songs by artists like Umm Kulthum and Abdel Halim Hafez that still resonate within national consciousness, but as we explore in this third installment of our four-part series on "[The Sound of Revolution in Modern Egypt](https://www.ottomanhistorypodcast.com/p/the-sound-of-revolution-in-modern-egypt.html)," the period produced spectacular sound as well as conspicous silence. As our guest Alia Mossallam explains, triumphant musical celebrations of the Egyptian state's signature achievement --- the construction of the Aswan High Dam --- shaped the terms through which Egyptians have come to remember this period. At the same time, songs of workers and Nubian villagers displaced by the dam captured subaltern sentiments beneath the surface of Nasserist cultural hegemony. We conclude our conversation with a reflection on the singular importance of sources like folk songs for writing histories erased by official sources.

 In 1952, a coup d'état led by Gamal Abdel Nasser ushered in a revolutionary period of Egyptian history in which sound played an integral role in shaping collective political consciousness. The culture of the 50s and 60s was dominated by songs by artists like Umm Kulthum and Abdel Halim Hafez that still resonate within national consciousness, but as we explore in this third installment of our four-part series on "[The Sound of Revolution in Modern Egypt](https://www.ottomanhistorypodcast.com/p/the-sound-of-revolution-in-modern-egypt.html)," the period produced spectacular sound as well as conspicous silence. As our guest Alia Mossallam explains, triumphant musical celebrations of the Egyptian state's signature achievement --- the construction of the Aswan High Dam --- shaped the terms through which Egyptians have come to remember this period. At the same time, songs of workers and Nubian villagers displaced by the dam captured subaltern sentiments beneath the surface of Nasserist cultural hegemony. We conclude our conversion with a reflection on the singular importance of sources like folk songs for writing histories erased by official sources.

  
  
  
  

 Contributor Bios

  

![Image 5](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEibvQu8_7vRJppuO5_Eu5hpxoE81UyyhbYr_4mHB6UqOkX6pdmWLdV4WGleegATVkPgUI9Y_DclB3xGFesjYE0vYotesnEjkmOaQib9srAaB5i0TkCj5YR3_q6QUnNlu0nEAQ8xoIXDon-Har3nd3o6czjXUXU5ZiTpL6jGefRNAa1b7zD-bPBQnNfGZgRO/s1600/s200_alia.mossallam.jpg)_[Alia Mossallam](https://eume-berlin.academia.edu/AliaMossallam) is a cultural historian, educator and writer interested in songs that tell stories and stories that tell of popular struggles behind the better-known events that shape world history. For her PhD she researched a popular history of Nasserist Egypt through the stories and experiences of the popular resistance in Port Said (1956) and Suez (1967-1974) and the construction of the Aswan High Dam through the experiences of its builders and the Nubian communities displaced by it. As a EUME fellow 2017-21 of the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation, she worked on her book on the visual and musical archiving practices of the builders of the Aswan High Dam and the Nubian communities displaced by it. Her new project at EUME (2021-24), “Tracing Emancipation Under Rubbles of War”, retrieves the physical and political journeys of Egyptian and North African workers on the various fronts of World War I through the songs and memoires that recount their struggles. Some of her research-based articles, essays and short-stories can be found in \_The Journal of Water History\_, \_The History Workshop Journal\_, the \_LSE Middle East Paper Series\_, \_Ma’azif\_, \_Bidayat\_, \_Mada Masr\_, \_Jadaliyya\_ and \_60 Pages\_. An experimentative pedagogue, she founded the site-specific public history project “Ihky ya Tarikh”, as well as having taught at the American University in Cairo, the Freie Universität in Berlin, and continuing to teach at the Cairo Institute for Liberal Arts._

His first book, \_[The Unsettled Plain: An Environmental History of the Late Ottoman Frontier](https://www.sup.org/books/title/?id=32948&bottom\\_ref=subject)\_, explores the social and environmental transformation of the Adana region of Southern Turkey during the 19th and 20th century._

### Nasser, Nubia, and the Stories of a People

  

[with Alia Mossallam](https://eume-berlin.academia.edu/AliaMossallam)

 hosted by [Chris Gratien](https://history.virginia.edu/people/chris-gratien)

 | In 1952, a coup d'état led by Gamal Abdel Nasser ushered in a revolutionary period of Egyptian history in which sound played an integral role in shaping collective political consciousness. The culture of the 50s and 60s was dominated by songs by artists like Umm Kulthum and Abdel Halim Hafez that still resonate within national consciousness, but as we explore in this third installment of our four-part series on "[The Sound of Revolution in Modern Egypt](https://www.ottomanhistorypodcast.com/p/the-sound-of-revolution-in-modern-egypt.html)," the period produced spectacular sound as well as conspicous silence. As our guest Alia Mossallam explains, triumphant musical celebrations of the Egyptian state's signature achievement --- the construction of the Aswan High Dam --- shaped the terms through which Egyptians have come to remember this period. At the same time, songs of workers and Nubian villagers displaced by the dam captured subaltern sentiments beneath the surface of Nasserist cultural hegemony. We conclude our conversation with a reflection on the singular importance of sources like folk songs for writing histories erased by official sources.

The culture of the 50s and 60s was dominated by songs by artists like Umm Kulthum and Abdel Halim Hafez that still resonate within national consciousness, but as we explore in this third installment of our four-part series on "[The Sound of Revolution in Modern Egypt](https://www.ottomanhistorypodcast.com/p/the-sound-of-revolution-in-modern-egypt.html)," the period produced spectacular sound as well as conspicous silence.  Contributor Bios

  

![Image 5](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEibvQu8_7vRJppuO5_Eu5hpxoE81UyyhbYr_4mHB6UqOkX6pdmWLdV4WGleegATVkPgUI9Y_DclB3xGFesjYE0vYotesnEjkmOaQib9srAaB5i0TkCj5YR3_q6QUnNlu0nEAQ8xoIXDon-Har3nd3o6czjXUXU5ZiTpL6jGefRNAa1b7zD-bPBQnNfGZgRO/s1600/s200_alia.mossallam.jpg)_[Alia Mossallam](https://eume-berlin.academia.edu/AliaMossallam) is a cultural historian, educator and writer interested in songs that tell stories and stories that tell of popular struggles behind the better-known events that shape world history. For her PhD she researched a popular history of Nasserist Egypt through the stories and experiences of the popular resistance in Port Said (1956) and Suez (1967-1974) and the construction of the Aswan High Dam through the experiences of its builders and the Nubian communities displaced by it. As a EUME fellow 2017-21 of the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation, she worked on her book on the visual and musical archiving practices of the builders of the Aswan High Dam and the Nubian communities displaced by it. Her new project at EUME (2021-24), “Tracing Emancipation Under Rubbles of War”, retrieves the physical and political journeys of Egyptian and North African workers on the various fronts of World War I through the songs and memoires that recount their struggles. Some of her research-based articles, essays and short-stories can be found in \_The Journal of Water History\_, \_The History Workshop Journal\_, the \_LSE Middle East Paper Series\_, \_Ma’azif\_, \_Bidayat\_, \_Mada Masr\_, \_Jadaliyya\_ and \_60 Pages\_. An experimentative pedagogue, she founded the site-specific public history project “Ihky ya Tarikh”, as well as having taught at the American University in Cairo, the Freie Universität in Berlin, and continuing to teach at the Cairo Institute for Liberal Arts._

## Extract

Although the effects of the Revolution of 23 July 1952 on Egyptian politics and the economy are well known, its impact on Egyptian culture has not yet been satisfactorily explained. Politically and economically, the Revolution has gone thrsough two more or less distinct phases. During the first decade of its existence, it moved cautiously on all fronts, and its spokesmen were fond of pointing out that their ‘ideology’ was experimental, pragmatic, and flexible rather than bound to any set of predetermined ideas. Then in 1961 the government veered sharply to the left. The so-called Socialist Laws were issued, altering profoundly the ownership and distribution of wealth in Egypt.

Al-Râfi'î's study of 'Urâbî, on the other hand, is quite critical at points, and al-Râfî'î's feeling that ‘Urâbî should have left politics to the politicians cannot have been welcome to President Nasser. ## Extract

Although the effects of the Revolution of 23 July 1952 on Egyptian politics and the economy are well known, its impact on Egyptian culture has not yet been satisfactorily explained. Politically and economically, the Revolution has gone thrsough two more or less distinct phases. During the first decade of its existence, it moved cautiously on all fronts, and its spokesmen were fond of pointing out that their ‘ideology’ was experimental, pragmatic, and flexible rather than bound to any set of predetermined ideas. Then in 1961 the government veered sharply to the left. The so-called Socialist Laws were issued, altering profoundly the ownership and distribution of wealth in Egypt.

Al-Râfi'î's study of 'Urâbî, on the other hand, is quite critical at points, and al-Râfî'î's feeling that ‘Urâbî should have left politics to the politicians cannot have been welcome to President Nasser. # When Ma ḥfūẓ wrote about the 1967 defeat 

(Re)reading Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla (1969) and al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar (1973, 2023) 

Naglaa Waly 

The 1967 defeat remains one of the most dreadful moments in modern Arab history. Rapid and violent, it shook the foundations of the political order and dismantled the myth of Nasser and his anti-colonial project. This crisis had lasting consequences on the trajectory of post-1967 Arab literature and intellectual thought. This article seeks to explore Ma ḥfūẓ ’s depiction of national trauma through a close reading of two of his works written in the aftermath of the defeat: the short story Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla (‘Under the Bus Shelter,’ 1969) and the novel al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar (‘Love in the Rain,’ 1973, 2023). I argue that re-reading these works through the lens of trauma theory offers an essential dimension to their literary analysis, deepening our understanding of their significance. In applying trauma theory to this new reading, I draw on the studies by Neal (1998, 2005), Alexander et al. (2004), LaCapra (2001, 2014) and those related to decolonized trauma theory by Visser (2014), as well as studies applying a sociological approach to Arabic literature (Mehrez 1994; Jacquemond 2008), which have been fundamental resources. Both works exemplify Ma ḥfūẓ ’s sincere commitment to the socio-political realities of his country, as well as his innovative narrative techniques that capture the complexities of the world he seeks to portray.

Introduction In his Writing history, writing trauma (2001, 2014), Dominick LaCapra suggests that forms of literature or art can provide a more expansive space, “in psychoanalytic terms, a relatively safe haven” (LaCapra 2014: 185), for investigating modes of response to trauma, such as the role of affect and the tendency to repeat traumatic events. Elsewhere, in the same volume, he explains the merits of using literature to claim trauma, as narrative fiction can convey the ‘feel’ of traumatic experience, without necessarily aiming to reproduce the facts: 

> One might argue that narratives in fiction may also involve truth claims on a structural or general level by providing insight into phenomena such as slavery or the Holocaust, by offering a reading of a process or period, or by giving at least a plausible “feel” for experience and emotion which may be difficult to arrive at through restricted documentary methods (LaCapra 2014: 13-14).

LaCapra cites, among other literary works, Camus’s The Fall (1956) and Morrison’s Beloved (1987), as examples of fiction that effectively communicate the experience of mass trauma. Analogously, many Arabic literary works have served as privileged spaces, or ‘safe havens,’ for the claiming of trauma, particularly over the past six decades, amid the enduring crises in the Middle East that have generated multifaceted forms of suffering. Moreover, the recent rise in awareness of the intersection between trauma theory and literature—as a means to gain deeper insight into literary texts and to illuminate the political and social realities of the Arab region—has firmly placed trauma studies on the ongoing agenda of many literary scholars (cf. Milich and Moghnieh 2018). Against this backdrop, the following pages will aim to adopt a broader prism through which to explore the representation of traumatic events in Arabic literature, a topic I have previously examined in two earlier articles focusing on post-2011 works (Waly 2023a, 2023b). While the representation of trauma in the aftermath of 2011 has been widely discussed by many scholars (cf. Bianco 2023, Sala 2025), a glance at the literary production in the Arab world since 1948 reveals that Arabic literature has long been shaped by recurring aftermaths and deep disenchantments. One of the most devastating moments in modern Arab history was undoubtedly the humiliating defeat of 1967. 1 The event was rapid and violent, shattering the foundations of the established political order, the myth of Nasser and his anti-colonial project. Arthur Neal (1998) defines a traumatic event as a ‘national trauma’ in terms of its ‘enduring effects’ and as referring to events “which cannot be easily dismissed, which will be played over again and again in individual consciousness” (Eyerman 2004: 61) and which then become “ingrained in collective memory.” In this account, a national trauma must be understood, explained, and made coherent through public reflection and discourse. Eyerman (2004: 61, 62) elucidates this definition, illustrating that trauma necessarily refers to something that is experienced in psychological accounts, calling that experience traumatic requires interpretation. National trauma is rooted in an event or series of events, but not necessarily in their direct experience. Such experience is mediated, for example through newspapers, radio or television, which implies a spatial and temporal distance between the event and its experience. Thus, national or cultural trauma always involves a “struggle for meaning,” a “grappling with an event that involves identifying the nature of the pain and the nature of the victim and the attribution of responsibility” (Alexander 2004: 15). 4

Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla : the storyline The story is written in a surreal style, with episodes of a dream-like nature and exaggerated scenes of horror, which seem very unusual for Ma ḥfūẓ ’s literary style when compared to his earlier works. The story unfolds in a surreal atmosphere, with a group of people gathered under a bus shelter in the rain. Some of them are waiting for a bus that will never come, while others seek shelter from the rain. Suddenly, they witness a group of people chasing a thief. As soon as they catch him, they immediately start beating him. The group under the shelter is concerned about the thief's fate. A series of bizarre situations and disconnected scenes of bloodshed then unfold before them: violent car crashes, explosions, deaths, presence of a judge, Bedouins, foreigners, the former thief dancing completely naked in the rain, and even sexual acts performed over a dead body. This insanity takes place in front of a policeman who is completely uninterested. The spectators remain neutral, seeking a reasonable explanation for all this chaos, convincing themselves that this is a film shoot and that there is a director controlling the scenes. When they observe a robust man commenting on the scenes, they assume he is the director and ask him for an explanation, but he departs without answering. At this moment, they think it might be a terrible nightmare. As the events become more violent, the rain intensifies, and the horror reaches its climax when a man's head slides between their feet. However, no one takes action. When the people under the bus shelter request the policeman’s intervention, he first asks them to show their ID cards. He then accuses them of an illegal gathering and subsequently shoots them to death. Naglaa Waly – When Ma ḥfūẓ wrote about the 1967 defeat: (Re)reading Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla and al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar

3.1. Narrative technique and claiming trauma As aforementioned, Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla is labelled by El-Enany (1993), as Ma ḥfūẓ ’s first aesthetic response to the defeat. Given that the collection of short stories was published in 1969, it can be considered a belated response to the national trauma of 1967 (Caruth 1996). In this context, the choice of a surrealist narrative replete with tragic events appears to be a very apt mode of expression to expose the trauma of a war aftermath, as Allmer (2022: 10) explains: 

> Surrealism was always already a response to the traumatic experience of early twentieth century history. Forged in the wake of, and haunted by the experiences of, the First World War, and motivated in part by disgust at that war […] the radical aesthetics of surrealism responded overtly and covertly to the cultural and psychic effects of the war’s change on individual and cultural consciousness—both the wider cultural impact of wartime suffering and the experiences of people who lived through it.

Furthermore, I believe that the deployment of surrealism, as an allegorical art, fulfils two key functions: first, it creates a distance between the writer and the situation; second, it provides an indirect narrative mode to represent this trauma. According to Hartman (1996), establishing an indirect relationship between the texts and the traumas they filter is a sort of authorial ‘coldness’ that one must adopt when approaching psychic anguish on a personal or collective level. 

Ma ḥfūẓ also succeeds in engaging the readers’ cognitive and emotional responses through the use of cinematic writing with a concise, dry dialogue, concentrating on picturing the events in a camera-eye style; the implication of this technique is that no one recounts the events, which instead just unfold before our eyes. Thus, the readers are drawn inside the story, they share the heroes’ consternation and amazement at the unfolding events, and subsequently, they feel the same apathy and disengagement. In addition, the story's tragic end increases the readers' involvement, as they can recognize the situation of those under the shelter as their own. Interestingly, Ma ḥfūẓ ’s portrayal of the heroes’ attitudes and their collective emotional responses aligns with the social mood sequences triggered by traumatizing conditions as described by Sztompka (2004: 166):  

> First, there is a general climate of anxiety, insecurity, and uncertainty (Wilkinson 1999), which sometimes manifests itself in the phenomenon of ‘moral panics’ (Thompson 1998). Second, there is a prevailing syndrome of distrust, both toward people and institutions (Sztompka 1999). Third, there is a disorientation concerning collective identity. Fourth, there is widespread apathy, passivism, and helplessness. Fifth, there is pessimism concerning the future, matched with nostalgic images of the past. Of course, not all these symptoms accompany every case of trauma, and not all these symptoms are equally manifested by various groups or subgroups within a society. Historicising public mourning When Ma ḥfūẓ published the collection Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla in 1969, literary critics (El-Enany 1993) were surprised by his sudden leap into surreal and absurd modes of expression. They agreed that he had abandoned his earlier themes and his commitment to external reality. In Mehrez’s interpretation (Mehrez1994), this heavy resort to symbolism was his tool to circumvent censorship. Nonetheless, Ma ḥfūẓ himself asserts his political and social commitment even in these surreal writings: 

however, my insistence on social commitment spoiled their absurdity in those works, I painted a world that was confused, fragmented and devoid of logic or reason. But it was apparent, despite this, that there was a certain meaning that I was driving at (el-Enany 1993: 204) 

In this respect, we can read this short story as an allegorisation of Egyptian reality in the immediate aftermath of 1967. The literary construction of that memory is obviously not a ‘literal retrieval but a statement of a different sort.’ 10 Here, Ma ḥfūẓ employed allegory in Benjamin’s sense as “a form of expression” (Benjamin 1928, quoted in Cowan 1981: 112). Ma ḥfūẓ published al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-Ma ṭar in 1973, addressing social and political issues that had touched upon briefly in his earlier experimental novel al-Mar āyā (‘Mirrors’), published the previous year. Unlike many of his previous works, however, al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar faced significant censorship. 14 Initially, the novel was serialized in al-Šab āb newspaper after al-Ahram refused to serialize it. During the serialization in al-Šab āb, beginning specifically with the ninth chapter, the state censors requested the deletion of certain passages. Later, when the novel was to be published as a book, the compromise was even greater: “an entire section was removed with Ma ḥfūẓ ’s knowledge and consent ˮ (cf. Mehrez 1994). Subsequently, the novel was re-published in 1983, with some censored passages restored. Later, in 2022, the journalist and literary critic Mu ḥammad Šuʿayyir (b. 1974) received the original manuscript from the widow of Ra ǧāʾ al-Naqq āš , literary critic and former editor-in-chief of al-Šab āb.This led to another edition being published in 2023. Thus, the novel has been published in three different versions. Šuʿayyir, who carefully compared the first two versions with the original manuscript, identified the censored parts. He observed that the censors tended to remove passages highlighting the people’s apathy towards the war, as well as overt critiques of the regime. 15 

4.1. Synopsis, structure and themes The novel is set presumably between 1967 and 1970, as there is no mention of Nasser’s death in September 1970. It is divided into forty-five short chapters. In this densely populated narrative featuring twenty-one characters, Ḥusn ī Ḥiǧā zī emerges as a central figure, closely connected to most of the other protagonists. Amidst a tapestry of intertwining narratives and characters, we encounter two homicides, along with the misfortunes and disillusionments of many protagonists, particularly among the younger generation. In an open-ended closure, the final chapter explores a conversation

The novel presents archetypes of different strata of Egyptian society: working-class, petit-bourgeoisie, intellectuals, former aristocrats and youth. These characters encapsulate roughly three generations or age-groups (the elderly, the middle-aged and youth). However, the sheer number of characters introduced within a relatively short novel (188 pages) limits the depth of their development. They are depicted, in fragmented ways, mainly through their present circumstances, with only minimal insight into their pasts. The novel emphasizes themes of frustration, apathy, and disillusionment among the people of Cairo in the aftermath of 1967. Ma ḥfūẓ addresses many urgent issues of that historical moment, such as the sense of exile and disengagement among intellectuals, the disillusionment of youth and their desire to emigrate, torture in prisons, and the resentment of former landowners toward the regime of the Free Officers. Rather than presenting a detailed analysis of the novel, which has already been done (LeGassick 1975, Allen 1977 and El-Enany 1993), the following section will investigate the narrative strategies that convey the characters’ traumas and the writer’s counter-narrative on that period in Egyptian history. 4.2. Another defining feature of Ma ḥfūẓ 's narrative technique in the novel, identified by both Le Gassick (1975) and Allen (1977), is its cinematic style, characterised by concise dialogue and rapid scene changes. This objective language, stripped of emotion, may reflect the pervasive sense of apathy within the narrative. Indeed, the novel is almost entirely constructed through dialogue, with the characters' conversations forming its backbone. These dialogues are framed by the omniscient narrator’s discourse, who introduces the conversations, and provides minimal descriptions of the setting and the characters’ appearances. Thus, it is safe to say that Mahfouz relies considerably on dialogues to move the plot forward, to delineate characters and express their points of view in fragmented accounts. Furthermore, by juxtaposing multiple voices, the novel embodies the polyphonic quality, as defined in Bakhtin’s conception of the polyphonic text (Bakhtin 1973; quoted in Rimmon-Kenan 1983: 4). Mehrez (1994), in her analysis of Ma ḥfūẓ ’s Yawm qutila al-za ʿī m (‘The Day the Leader Was Killed,’ 1985) notes that the use of a multi-point narrative serves Ma ḥfūẓ on multiple levels. On the one hand, it allows him to address a wide range of narrative content or discontent, whether generational, social, or ideological, within the constraints of the novel's space and form. On the other hand, it enables him “to pose as the ‘objective’ historian who simply records rather than takes sides” (Mehrez 1994: 91). This technique is similarly evident in al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , where we can perceive the author’s neutrality in many of the characters’ stances. However, this is not always the case, as the author’s presence is felt in certain dialogues, particularly through the use of free indirect discourse. The presence of the author becomes particularly perceptible in the political stances expressed by Ḥiǧā zī and Ḥam ūda. In these moments, Ma ḥfūẓ employs what Chaitin (1999: 1025) terms the ‘dual voice,’ a narrative technique that “captures the individuality of the character's speech and thought, while at the same time allowing the narrator to express his or her interpretation and evaluation of that speech.” 5. Egyptians’ suffering vs. the flaws of the regime From the very first sentences, we perceive Ma ḥfūẓ ’s attempt to paint a comprehensive portrait of Egyptian society, encompassing its diverse political views and social classes. He attempts to capture the full picture within the diegesis by creating a plethora of characters and placing Ḥusn ī Ḥiǧā zī in direct contact with the lively social context of the café. In my re-reading of the novel, I argue that Ma ḥfūẓ , through al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-Ma ṭar, exposes the national trauma of the post 1967 as the culmination of the multiple traumas experienced under Naglaa Waly – When Ma ḥfūẓ wrote about the 1967 defeat: (Re)reading Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla and al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar

In this context, themes such as apathy, hopelessness, alienation, sexuality, resentment, and violence emerge as symptoms of enduring national trauma. Resilience, in contrast, emerges as a positive response to trauma. These themes are clearly traceable in the conversations of the novel’s characters, who represent different generations. The theme of helplessness, as “physiological responses to traumatic events ˮ

(Neal 1998: 3), is foregrounded and well perceived in Ḥiǧā zī's dialogue with the older generation, such as ʿAbd ū, the waiter and ʿAšmāwī, the former Futawwa who ended up working as a shoe-shiner. The conversation between Ḥiǧā zī and ʿAbd ū illustrates a deep sense of helplessness and diminished human agency, shaped by abject poverty and personal tragedy, specifically, the blindness of ʿAbd ū’s son during the war. Intriguingly, Ḥiǧā zī's critique of their moral stance resonates Nietzsche’s condemnation of herd mentality (Young 2014). He highlights the contradictions in their ethical framework by pointing out that they accept systemic injustice yet react with indignation to carnal love, perceiving it as a transgression of societal norms.

In the novel, hopelessness and frustration are transformed into alienation, a defining trait among the characters of the second and third generations. Ma ḥfūẓ ’s depiction of alienated intellectuals and ‘organic intellectuals,’ in Gramsci’s notions (1996), demonstrates how the defeat in 1967 exacerbated the sense of frustration and disillusionment that had already afflicted many intellectuals over the previous two decades. The crisis of intellectuals post-1952 has its roots in the regime’s political policies, as explained by Abd al-Malek (1968): 

> A general state law prohibits all political parties […] While no other political parties have been allowed, the regime has proved itself unable to inspire and organize its own party. The result has been a growing and widespread political apathy, in a country that hitherto was notably ebullient. If the state insists on doing everything by itself, and by order, then why not watch from afar? (Abd al-Malek 1968: 24-25).

The most representative example of alienation in the novel is found in the character of Ḥiǧā zī, who is arguably the only central figure. He is portrayed as emotionally detached and indifferent to societal expectations and norms. He engages in multiple affairs with young women and is obsessed with pornographic films. He even spends considerable time at the In šir āḥ Café, where the waiter happens to be the father of one of his mistresses. Ḥiǧā zī appears to embody the features of alienation as described by Seeman (1959: 783): “powerlessness, meaninglessness, normlessness, isolation, and self-estrangement.” Even when he frequents the café in an attempt to gain a sense of belonging, he remains passive, listening to ʿAšmāwī’s enthusiasm about the war but unable to genuinely engage. And when, after the murder of Samra āʼ , he is confronted with the fear of revealing his affairs with these girls, he decides to flee to Lebanon. The alienation of Ḥiǧā zī is juxtaposed with the easy-going life of Ṣafwat Mar ǧā n, the opportunist journalist who mouths the ideological slogans of the regime for his own interests. These two figures reflect a synthesis, offered by Sam āḥ Idr īs (1992), describing how the regime was systematically isolating and silencing intellectuals—except for those willing to offer unconditional support. Another symptom of trauma in the novel is expressed by the sexual behaviour of the protagonists. Indeed, sexuality as a defence against painful affects has been widely discussed by several scholars (cf.Kohut 1971). In al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , the theme of sexuality is a foregrounded theme throughout the narrative. Eroticism, for instance, plays a central role in Ḥiǧā zī’s life, a pattern that is also reflected in the cases of the two film directors, Ra šwān and ʾAḥmad. Wen-chin Ouyang (2012), in her study on Ma ḥfūẓ ’s Trilogy, draws a connection between political inaction and the abundance of sexual or romantic relationships. In al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , sexual activity functions not only as a substitute for political action, but also as a form of psychological escapism, a kind of drug, as seen in the character of 

ʿAliyy āt who, after a painful break-up, has sex with a stranger and becomes pregnant. Notably, the female characters in the novel display considerable sexual permissiveness: with the exception of Muna and Mar ǧā n’s wife, they all engage in relationships in exchange for money or gifts. However, Ma ḥfūẓ does not moralise or dramatize this behaviour; rather, he portrays it without condemnation, judgement or melodrama. Although most of the female protagonists have independent agency and are not depicted as ‘fallen women,’ they rarely speak about real employment or professional aspirations, despite their education—at least three are university graduates. Here, Ma ḥfūẓ 

appears to satirize the Nasserist vision of working women as central to the socialist and post-colonial national project. It is worth noting that both murders in the novel are rooted in issues of sexuality. The first occurs when Muna's brother kills the director Ra šwān after he makes sexual advances towards her; the second involves ʿAliyy āt’s father killing Samr āʾ after she reveals to him that her unmarried daughter has had an abortion. Although the novel was written in 1973, prior to the formal recognition of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in the DSM-III in 1980, Ma ḥfūẓ 's depiction of his characters’ irritability and aggressive reactions is closely aligned with the symptoms later identified in that diagnostic framework. In this sense, the novel also reflects the psychological consequences of the 1967 defeat, as outlined by 

ʿĪ sā (1972) in his seminal article. Ma ḥfūẓ also highlights a theme closely associated with trauma, namely apathy. As Cvetkovich (2003: 41) notes: “traumatic experiences and their consequences can be characterised not only by too much feeling, or hyperarousal, but also by an absence of feeling, or numbness. ˮ This emotional numbness is evident in Ḥiǧā zī, when he recounts the absurd death of his nephew, whose mother sent him to Canada to avoid military service.
