Instances of resilience In her study on trauma and power in postcolonial literary studies, Irene Visser (2014) underlines Erikson’s thesis (1994) on the inherent intricacy of trauma, asserting that it should be understood not only as acute and event-based, but also as chronic and non-event-based. Thus, “it can be debilitating and disruptive to individuals and communities, but it can also create a stronger social cohesion and a renewed sense of identity” (Visser2014: 110). She adds that literature, as a venue for the narratives that emerge after an overwhelming social event, has the ability to mirror and construct that complexity. In al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , we find vivid examples of the complex nature of trauma, as articulated by Visser (2014). Throughout the narrative, Ma ḥfūẓ highlights not only the disruptive impact of this collective trauma, but also presents instances of positive adaptation in response to such harsh experiences. The first example is encountered in Muna's father, “whose patriotism has been strengthened and revitalised by the defeat ˮ (Ma ḥfūẓ 2011: 38). Therefore, he was pained when his sons told him about their desire to immigrate and he tries to stir up their patriotic sentiments. The second example is represented by ʿAliyy āt’s brother, ʾAḥmad, the soldier who lost his sight during the war. Despite this tragic experience, he exhibits a psychologically healthy response to trauma, namely, resilience (Luckhurst 2008 and Visser 2014); ʾAḥmad starts a new life, thanks to his fiancée Saniyya, and continues their marriage project. The third example can be tracked down in Ḥā mid, who not only lost an eye but also the chance to continue his university education after being arrested and tortured by the regime's security forces due to false accusations of communism. Nevertheless, Ḥā mid regains his life, starts working and continues his studies independently, becomes an active communist and shows moral integrity when he decides to support his fiancé ʿAliyy āt, despite the scandal surrounding her abortion. 5.2. Ma ḥfūẓ as an underground historian Ma ḥfūẓ is fully aware of his role as a writer and intellectual in Egypt, where it is difficult to dissociate politics from art. Through the dialogues of the characters, we can observe the author’s intention to create a dialectical and ideological relationship between the text and the world it represents, each developing the other, and to fill in the lacunae and silences of official history or, in Jacquemond’s words, how he becomes the “underground historian or “parallel sociologist” of his country (Jacquemond 2008: 90). For instance, we can note that all the characters use the word haz īma , in referring to the 1967 defeat. None of them resorts even once to the word naksa (‘setback’), largely used by Egyptian media and first introduced by Nasser in his speech on 9 June 196, as a euphemism for defeat. This term, as noted by (al-

By employing the word haz īma (‘defeat’) in a bold tone, Ma ḥfūẓ assigns the responsibility for this humiliating defeat to Nasser and his regime. At first glance, Ma ḥfūẓ portrays a wounded post-1967 society. For instance, through his meticulous portrayal of ʿAbd ū and ʿAšmāwī’s abject poverty, he dismantles the state’s official discourse that claims to guarantee a dignified standard of living for its citizens. Conclusions In this article, I attempted to re-read, through the lens of trauma theory, two of Na ǧī b Ma ḥfūẓ ’s indirect and direct representations of the 1967 debacle: the short story Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla (1969), and the realist novel al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar (1973). The short story is, inasmuch, his first response to the harsh event and reveals many narrative traits that reflect the struggles faced by the traumatized when trying to articulate the source of their trauma. Ma ḥfūẓ , in a surrealistic narrative, uses symbolism in an ingenious way to represent the state of mourning experienced by Egyptians in the wake of the defeat. The realist novel al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-Ma ṭar , written four years later, delves into the wounds inflicted on Egyptian society in the aftermath of the 1967 defeat. It subtly critiques Nasser’s regime and illustrates the traumatic effects of its policies. # When Ma ḥfūẓ wrote about the 1967 defeat 

(Re)reading Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla (1969) and al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar (1973, 2023) 

Naglaa Waly 

The 1967 defeat remains one of the most dreadful moments in modern Arab history. Rapid and violent, it shook the foundations of the political order and dismantled the myth of Nasser and his anti-colonial project. This crisis had lasting consequences on the trajectory of post-1967 Arab literature and intellectual thought. This article seeks to explore Ma ḥfūẓ ’s depiction of national trauma through a close reading of two of his works written in the aftermath of the defeat: the short story Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla (‘Under the Bus Shelter,’ 1969) and the novel al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar (‘Love in the Rain,’ 1973, 2023). I argue that re-reading these works through the lens of trauma theory offers an essential dimension to their literary analysis, deepening our understanding of their significance. In applying trauma theory to this new reading, I draw on the studies by Neal (1998, 2005), Alexander et al. (2004), LaCapra (2001, 2014) and those related to decolonized trauma theory by Visser (2014), as well as studies applying a sociological approach to Arabic literature (Mehrez 1994; Jacquemond 2008), which have been fundamental resources. Both works exemplify Ma ḥfūẓ ’s sincere commitment to the socio-political realities of his country, as well as his innovative narrative techniques that capture the complexities of the world he seeks to portray. 

Keywords: 1967 defeat, Na ǧī b Ma ḥfūẓ , Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla, al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , trauma theory. Defeat goes deeper into the human soul than victory. Introduction In his Writing history, writing trauma (2001, 2014), Dominick LaCapra suggests that forms of literature or art can provide a more expansive space, “in psychoanalytic terms, a relatively safe haven” (LaCapra 2014: 185), for investigating modes of response to trauma, such as the role of affect and the tendency to repeat traumatic events. Elsewhere, in the same volume, he explains the merits of using literature to claim trauma, as narrative fiction can convey the ‘feel’ of traumatic experience, without necessarily aiming to reproduce the facts: 

> One might argue that narratives in fiction may also involve truth claims on a structural or general level by providing insight into phenomena such as slavery or the Holocaust, by offering a reading of a process or period, or by giving at least a plausible “feel” for experience and emotion which may be difficult to arrive at through restricted documentary methods (LaCapra 2014: 13-14).

LaCapra cites, among other literary works, Camus’s The Fall (1956) and Morrison’s Beloved (1987), as examples of fiction that effectively communicate the experience of mass trauma. Analogously, many Arabic literary works have served as privileged spaces, or ‘safe havens,’ for the claiming of trauma, particularly over the past six decades, amid the enduring crises in the Middle East that have generated multifaceted forms of suffering. Moreover, the recent rise in awareness of the intersection between trauma theory and literature—as a means to gain deeper insight into literary texts and to illuminate the political and social realities of the Arab region—has firmly placed trauma studies on the ongoing agenda of many literary scholars (cf. Milich and Moghnieh 2018). Against this backdrop, the following pages will aim to adopt a broader prism through which to explore the representation of traumatic events in Arabic literature, a topic I have previously examined in two earlier articles focusing on post-2011 works (Waly 2023a, 2023b). While the representation of trauma in the aftermath of 2011 has been widely discussed by many scholars (cf. Bianco 2023, Sala 2025), a glance at the literary production in the Arab world since 1948 reveals that Arabic literature has long been shaped by recurring aftermaths and deep disenchantments. One of the most devastating moments in modern Arab history was undoubtedly the humiliating defeat of 1967. 1 The event was rapid and violent, shattering the foundations of the established political order, the myth of Nasser and his anti-colonial project. The spectators remain neutral, seeking a reasonable explanation for all this chaos, convincing themselves that this is a film shoot and that there is a director controlling the scenes. 3.1. Narrative technique and claiming trauma As aforementioned, Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla is labelled by El-Enany (1993), as Ma ḥfūẓ ’s first aesthetic response to the defeat. Given that the collection of short stories was published in 1969, it can be considered a belated response to the national trauma of 1967 (Caruth 1996). In this context, the choice of a surrealist narrative replete with tragic events appears to be a very apt mode of expression to expose the trauma of a war aftermath, as Allmer (2022: 10) explains: 

> Surrealism was always already a response to the traumatic experience of early twentieth century history. Forged in the wake of, and haunted by the experiences of, the First World War, and motivated in part by disgust at that war […] the radical aesthetics of surrealism responded overtly and covertly to the cultural and psychic effects of the war’s change on individual and cultural consciousness—both the wider cultural impact of wartime suffering and the experiences of people who lived through it.

Furthermore, I believe that the deployment of surrealism, as an allegorical art, fulfils two key functions: first, it creates a distance between the writer and the situation; second, it provides an indirect narrative mode to represent this trauma. According to Hartman (1996), establishing an indirect relationship between the texts and the traumas they filter is a sort of authorial ‘coldness’ that one must adopt when approaching psychic anguish on a personal or collective level. 

Ma ḥfūẓ also succeeds in engaging the readers’ cognitive and emotional responses through the use of cinematic writing with a concise, dry dialogue, concentrating on picturing the events in a camera-eye style; the implication of this technique is that no one recounts the events, which instead just unfold before our eyes. Thus, the readers are drawn inside the story, they share the heroes’ consternation and amazement at the unfolding events, and subsequently, they feel the same apathy and disengagement. In addition, the story's tragic end increases the readers' involvement, as they can recognize the situation of those under the shelter as their own. Interestingly, Ma ḥfūẓ ’s portrayal of the heroes’ attitudes and their collective emotional responses aligns with the social mood sequences triggered by traumatizing conditions as described by Sztompka (2004: 166):  

> First, there is a general climate of anxiety, insecurity, and uncertainty (Wilkinson 1999), which sometimes manifests itself in the phenomenon of ‘moral panics’ (Thompson 1998). Second, there is a prevailing syndrome of distrust, both toward people and institutions (Sztompka 1999). Third, there is a disorientation concerning collective identity. Fourth, there is widespread apathy, passivism, and helplessness. Fifth, there is pessimism concerning the future, matched with nostalgic images of the past. Of course, not all these symptoms accompany every case of trauma, and not all these symptoms are equally manifested by various groups or subgroups within a society. Historicising public mourning When Ma ḥfūẓ published the collection Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla in 1969, literary critics (El-Enany 1993) were surprised by his sudden leap into surreal and absurd modes of expression. They agreed that he had abandoned his earlier themes and his commitment to external reality. In Mehrez’s interpretation (Mehrez1994), this heavy resort to symbolism was his tool to circumvent censorship. Nonetheless, Ma ḥfūẓ himself asserts his political and social commitment even in these surreal writings: 

however, my insistence on social commitment spoiled their absurdity in those works, I painted a world that was confused, fragmented and devoid of logic or reason. But it was apparent, despite this, that there was a certain meaning that I was driving at (el-Enany 1993: 204) 

In this respect, we can read this short story as an allegorisation of Egyptian reality in the immediate aftermath of 1967. The literary construction of that memory is obviously not a ‘literal retrieval but a statement of a different sort.’ 10 Here, Ma ḥfūẓ employed allegory in Benjamin’s sense as “a form of expression” (Benjamin 1928, quoted in Cowan 1981: 112). Thus, the short story can be read as an allegory of the chaos and confusion of Egyptian society, at the moment when Nasser, in his resignation speech on 9 June, publicly acknowledged the defeat of 1967. 11 The people were waking up in a nightmare, as the idea of defeat was completely banished from

Ma ḥfūẓ published al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-Ma ṭar in 1973, addressing social and political issues that had touched upon briefly in his earlier experimental novel al-Mar āyā (‘Mirrors’), published the previous year. Unlike many of his previous works, however, al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar faced significant censorship. 14 Initially, the novel was serialized in al-Šab āb newspaper after al-Ahram refused to serialize it. During the serialization in al-Šab āb, beginning specifically with the ninth chapter, the state censors requested the deletion of certain passages. Later, when the novel was to be published as a book, the compromise was even greater: “an entire section was removed with Ma ḥfūẓ ’s knowledge and consent ˮ (cf. Mehrez 1994). Subsequently, the novel was re-published in 1983, with some censored passages restored. Later, in 2022, the journalist and literary critic Mu ḥammad Šuʿayyir (b. 1974) received the original manuscript from the widow of Ra ǧāʾ al-Naqq āš , literary critic and former editor-in-chief of al-Šab āb.This led to another edition being published in 2023. Thus, the novel has been published in three different versions. Šuʿayyir, who carefully compared the first two versions with the original manuscript, identified the censored parts. He observed that the censors tended to remove passages highlighting the people’s apathy towards the war, as well as overt critiques of the regime. 15 

4.1. Synopsis, structure and themes The novel is set presumably between 1967 and 1970, as there is no mention of Nasser’s death in September 1970. It is divided into forty-five short chapters. In this densely populated narrative featuring twenty-one characters, Ḥusn ī Ḥiǧā zī emerges as a central figure, closely connected to most of the other protagonists. Amidst a tapestry of intertwining narratives and characters, we encounter two homicides, along with the misfortunes and disillusionments of many protagonists, particularly among the younger generation. The novel presents archetypes of different strata of Egyptian society: working-class, petit-bourgeoisie, intellectuals, former aristocrats and youth. These characters encapsulate roughly three generations or age-groups (the elderly, the middle-aged and youth). However, the sheer number of characters introduced within a relatively short novel (188 pages) limits the depth of their development. They are depicted, in fragmented ways, mainly through their present circumstances, with only minimal insight into their pasts. The novel emphasizes themes of frustration, apathy, and disillusionment among the people of Cairo in the aftermath of 1967. Ma ḥfūẓ addresses many urgent issues of that historical moment, such as the sense of exile and disengagement among intellectuals, the disillusionment of youth and their desire to emigrate, torture in prisons, and the resentment of former landowners toward the regime of the Free Officers. Rather than presenting a detailed analysis of the novel, which has already been done (LeGassick 1975, Allen 1977 and El-Enany 1993), the following section will investigate the narrative strategies that convey the characters’ traumas and the writer’s counter-narrative on that period in Egyptian history. 4.2. Another defining feature of Ma ḥfūẓ 's narrative technique in the novel, identified by both Le Gassick (1975) and Allen (1977), is its cinematic style, characterised by concise dialogue and rapid scene changes. This objective language, stripped of emotion, may reflect the pervasive sense of apathy within the narrative. Indeed, the novel is almost entirely constructed through dialogue, with the characters' conversations forming its backbone. These dialogues are framed by the omniscient narrator’s discourse, who introduces the conversations, and provides minimal descriptions of the setting and the characters’ appearances. Thus, it is safe to say that Mahfouz relies considerably on dialogues to move the plot forward, to delineate characters and express their points of view in fragmented accounts. Furthermore, by juxtaposing multiple voices, the novel embodies the polyphonic quality, as defined in Bakhtin’s conception of the polyphonic text (Bakhtin 1973; quoted in Rimmon-Kenan 1983: 4). Mehrez (1994), in her analysis of Ma ḥfūẓ ’s Yawm qutila al-za ʿī m (‘The Day the Leader Was Killed,’ 1985) notes that the use of a multi-point narrative serves Ma ḥfūẓ on multiple levels. On the one hand, it allows him to address a wide range of narrative content or discontent, whether generational, social, or ideological, within the constraints of the novel's space and form. On the other hand, it enables him “to pose as the ‘objective’ historian who simply records rather than takes sides” (Mehrez 1994: 91). This technique is similarly evident in al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , where we can perceive the author’s neutrality in many of the characters’ stances. However, this is not always the case, as the author’s presence is felt in certain dialogues, particularly through the use of free indirect discourse. The presence of the author becomes particularly perceptible in the political stances expressed by Ḥiǧā zī and Ḥam ūda. In these moments, Ma ḥfūẓ employs what Chaitin (1999: 1025) terms the ‘dual voice,’ a narrative technique that “captures the individuality of the character's speech and thought, while at the same time allowing the narrator to express his or her interpretation and evaluation of that speech.” 5. Egyptians’ suffering vs. the flaws of the regime From the very first sentences, we perceive Ma ḥfūẓ ’s attempt to paint a comprehensive portrait of Egyptian society, encompassing its diverse political views and social classes. He attempts to capture the full picture within the diegesis by creating a plethora of characters and placing Ḥusn ī Ḥiǧā zī in direct contact with the lively social context of the café. In my re-reading of the novel, I argue that Ma ḥfūẓ , through al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-Ma ṭar, exposes the national trauma of the post 1967 as the culmination of the multiple traumas experienced under Naglaa Waly – When Ma ḥfūẓ wrote about the 1967 defeat: (Re)reading Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla and al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar 

64 

tyrannical rule. A chain of disappointments had rendered Egyptian society more trauma prone 17 in the aftermath of 1967 than at any other moment in its modern history. In this context, themes such as apathy, hopelessness, alienation, sexuality, resentment, and violence emerge as symptoms of enduring national trauma. Resilience, in contrast, emerges as a positive response to trauma. These themes are clearly traceable in the conversations of the novel’s characters, who represent different generations. The theme of helplessness, as “physiological responses to traumatic events ˮ

(Neal 1998: 3), is foregrounded and well perceived in Ḥiǧā zī's dialogue with the older generation, such as ʿAbd ū, the waiter and ʿAšmāwī, the former Futawwa who ended up working as a shoe-shiner. The conversation between Ḥiǧā zī and ʿAbd ū illustrates a deep sense of helplessness and diminished human agency, shaped by abject poverty and personal tragedy, specifically, the blindness of ʿAbd ū’s son during the war. Intriguingly, Ḥiǧā zī's critique of their moral stance resonates Nietzsche’s condemnation of herd mentality (Young 2014). He highlights the contradictions in their ethical framework by pointing out that they accept systemic injustice yet react with indignation to carnal love, perceiving it as a transgression of societal norms.

These include retreating into a glorified past and exalting its virtues; denying personal agency in shaping history; and attributing defeat to divine punishment for abandoning Islamic principles. In the novel, hopelessness and frustration are transformed into alienation, a defining trait among the characters of the second and third generations. Ma ḥfūẓ ’s depiction of alienated intellectuals and ‘organic intellectuals,’ in Gramsci’s notions (1996), demonstrates how the defeat in 1967 exacerbated the sense of frustration and disillusionment that had already afflicted many intellectuals over the previous two decades. The crisis of intellectuals post-1952 has its roots in the regime’s political policies, as explained by Abd al-Malek (1968): 

> A general state law prohibits all political parties […] While no other political parties have been allowed, the regime has proved itself unable to inspire and organize its own party. The result has been a growing and widespread political apathy, in a country that hitherto was notably ebullient. If the state insists on doing everything by itself, and by order, then why not watch from afar? (Abd al-Malek 1968: 24-25).

The most representative example of alienation in the novel is found in the character of Ḥiǧā zī, who is arguably the only central figure. He is portrayed as emotionally detached and indifferent to societal expectations and norms. He engages in multiple affairs with young women and is obsessed with pornographic films. He even spends considerable time at the In šir āḥ Café, where the waiter happens to be the father of one of his mistresses. Ḥiǧā zī appears to embody the features of alienation as described by Seeman (1959: 783): “powerlessness, meaninglessness, normlessness, isolation, and self-estrangement.” Even when he frequents the café in an attempt to gain a sense of belonging, he remains passive, listening to ʿAšmāwī’s enthusiasm about the war but unable to genuinely engage. And when, after the murder of Samra āʼ , he is confronted with the fear of revealing his affairs with these girls, he decides to flee to Lebanon. The alienation of Ḥiǧā zī is juxtaposed with the easy-going life of Ṣafwat Mar ǧā n, the opportunist journalist who mouths the ideological slogans of the regime for his own interests. These two figures reflect a synthesis, offered by Sam āḥ Idr īs (1992), describing how the regime was systematically isolating and silencing intellectuals—except for those willing to offer unconditional support. Another symptom of trauma in the novel is expressed by the sexual behaviour of the protagonists. Indeed, sexuality as a defence against painful affects has been widely discussed by several scholars (cf.Kohut 1971). In al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , the theme of sexuality is a foregrounded theme throughout the narrative. Eroticism, for instance, plays a central role in Ḥiǧā zī’s life, a pattern that is also reflected in the cases of the two film directors, Ra šwān and ʾAḥmad. Wen-chin Ouyang (2012), in her study on Ma ḥfūẓ ’s Trilogy, draws a connection between political inaction and the abundance of sexual or romantic relationships. In al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , sexual activity functions not only as a substitute for political action, but also as a form of psychological escapism, a kind of drug, as seen in the character of 

ʿAliyy āt who, after a painful break-up, has sex with a stranger and becomes pregnant. Notably, the female characters in the novel display considerable sexual permissiveness: with the exception of Muna and Mar ǧā n’s wife, they all engage in relationships in exchange for money or gifts. However, Ma ḥfūẓ does not moralise or dramatize this behaviour; rather, he portrays it without condemnation, judgement or melodrama. Although most of the female protagonists have independent agency and are not depicted as ‘fallen women,’ they rarely speak about real employment or professional aspirations, despite their education—at least three are university graduates. Here, Ma ḥfūẓ 

appears to satirize the Nasserist vision of working women as central to the socialist and post-colonial national project. It is worth noting that both murders in the novel are rooted in issues of sexuality. The first occurs when Muna's brother kills the director Ra šwān after he makes sexual advances towards her; the second involves ʿAliyy āt’s father killing Samr āʾ after she reveals to him that her unmarried daughter has had an abortion. Although the novel was written in 1973, prior to the formal recognition of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in the DSM-III in 1980, Ma ḥfūẓ 's depiction of his characters’ irritability and aggressive reactions is closely aligned with the symptoms later identified in that diagnostic framework. In this sense, the novel also reflects the psychological consequences of the 1967 defeat, as outlined by 

ʿĪ sā (1972) in his seminal article. Ma ḥfūẓ also highlights a theme closely associated with trauma, namely apathy. 5.1. Instances of resilience In her study on trauma and power in postcolonial literary studies, Irene Visser (2014) underlines Erikson’s thesis (1994) on the inherent intricacy of trauma, asserting that it should be understood not only as acute and event-based, but also as chronic and non-event-based. Thus, “it can be debilitating and disruptive to individuals and communities, but it can also create a stronger social cohesion and a renewed sense of identity” (Visser2014: 110). She adds that literature, as a venue for the narratives that emerge after an overwhelming social event, has the ability to mirror and construct that complexity. In al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , we find vivid examples of the complex nature of trauma, as articulated by Visser (2014). Throughout the narrative, Ma ḥfūẓ highlights not only the disruptive impact of this collective trauma, but also presents instances of positive adaptation in response to such harsh experiences. The first example is encountered in Muna's father, “whose patriotism has been strengthened and revitalised by the defeat ˮ (Ma ḥfūẓ 2011: 38). Therefore, he was pained when his sons told him about their desire to immigrate and he tries to stir up their patriotic sentiments. The second example is represented by ʿAliyy āt’s brother, ʾAḥmad, the soldier who lost his sight during the war. Despite this tragic experience, he exhibits a psychologically healthy response to trauma, namely, resilience (Luckhurst 2008 and Visser 2014); ʾAḥmad starts a new life, thanks to his fiancée Saniyya, and continues their marriage project. The third example can be tracked down in Ḥā mid, who not only lost an eye but also the chance to continue his university education after being arrested and tortured by the regime's security forces due to false accusations of communism. Nevertheless, Ḥā mid regains his life, starts working and continues his studies independently, becomes an active communist and shows moral integrity when he decides to support his fiancé ʿAliyy āt, despite the scandal surrounding her abortion. 5.2. Ma ḥfūẓ as an underground historian Ma ḥfūẓ is fully aware of his role as a writer and intellectual in Egypt, where it is difficult to dissociate politics from art. Thus, writing at that crucial time in history gives him an alternative political action within fiction’s space, highlighting the function of the novel as a site of opposition and dissent. Through the dialogues of the characters, we can observe the author’s intention to create a dialectical and ideological relationship between the text and the world it represents, each developing the other, and to fill in the lacunae and silences of official history or, in Jacquemond’s words, how he becomes the “underground historian or “parallel sociologist” of his country (Jacquemond 2008: 90). For instance, we can note that all the characters use the word haz īma , in referring to the 1967 defeat. None of them resorts even once to the word naksa (‘setback’), largely used by Egyptian media and first introduced by Nasser in his speech on 9 June 196, as a euphemism for defeat. This term, as noted by (al-

ʿAẓm 2007), was employed by Nasser to absolve himself of any responsibility and place the blame for the defeat on the world. By employing the word haz īma (‘defeat’) in a bold tone, Ma ḥfūẓ assigns the responsibility for this humiliating defeat to Nasser and his regime. At first glance, Ma ḥfūẓ portrays a wounded post-1967 society. However, by explicitly and implicitly intertwining social and political issues throughout the narratives of the novel’s characters, he connects their suffering to the broader failures of the regime’s policies, thereby articulating his political critique. For instance, through his meticulous portrayal of ʿAbd ū and ʿAšmāwī’s abject poverty, he dismantles the state’s official discourse that claims to guarantee a dignified standard of living for its citizens. In doing so, he exposes the failure of the social transformation promised by Nasser and the 1952 revolution. 20 Furthermore, through Ḥā mid’s account, he denounces the brutality inflicted

Here, Ma ḥfūẓ creates a counter-discourse that challenges the dominant representation of the landowning class in the Egyptian narrative in those years. Moreover, the novel implicitly critiques the regime by juxtaposing the alienated identity and absence of national spirit among the younger generation, ‘children of the revolution,’ with the fervent patriotism and strong Egyptian identity of the older generation, shaped prior to 1952. This older group, described by the narrator as the 1919 generation, embodies a ‘pure’ nationalism rooted in an anti-colonial struggle and civic responsibility. In al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar , Ma ḥfūẓ evokes a sense of nostalgia for the era of the 1919 Revolution, a theme he had previously explored in Mīrāmār, in which a stark moral contrast is drawn between the pre- and post-revolutionary generations. 7. Conclusions In this article, I attempted to re-read, through the lens of trauma theory, two of Na ǧī b Ma ḥfūẓ ’s indirect and direct representations of the 1967 debacle: the short story Ta ḥt al-mi ẓalla (1969), and the realist novel al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-ma ṭar (1973). The short story is, inasmuch, his first response to the harsh event and reveals many narrative traits that reflect the struggles faced by the traumatized when trying to articulate the source of their trauma. Ma ḥfūẓ , in a surrealistic narrative, uses symbolism in an ingenious way to represent the state of mourning experienced by Egyptians in the wake of the defeat. The realist novel al-Ḥubb ta ḥt al-Ma ṭar , written four years later, delves into the wounds inflicted on Egyptian society in the aftermath of the 1967 defeat. It subtly critiques Nasser’s regime and illustrates the traumatic effects of its policies. Interestingly, the cinematic milieu is foregrounded in both works: in the short story, people initially believe that the scenes they witness are part of a film, while in the novel, much of the action unfolds within a film studio, populated by directors and actors. This emphasis on cinematic settings may be interpreted through Tarek El-Ariss’s observation (2014) that Nasser, as a political figure, was constructed by the state propaganda machine as a heroic character within a fictionalized national narrative. al-Ariss argues that the defeat constitutes “an interruption, if not collapse, of a particular kind of fiction associated with Nasser. Naksa […] revealed what was behind the curtain, taking the Arab viewers backstage” (El Ariss 2014: 6). This hypothesis provides a further evidence of the sophistication with which Ma ḥfūẓ depicts the political realm in the two works discussed in this article. The short story and novel discussed in this article are both excellent examples of Ma ḥfūẓ ’s commitment to addressing the socio-political issues of his country. They also exemplify his innovative narrative strategies, through which he effectively captures and reflects the complex realities of the worlds he depicts. By portraying this anatomy of 1952 failures, Ma ḥfūẓ denudes and subverts much of the official history of Nasser’s era. Thus, he conveys in these works, what he called the “writer’s voice,” or rather, “the voice of truth” (Mehrez 1995: 95). Lastly, by juxtaposing sociological and psychological scholarship on the 1967 aftermath with Ma ḥfūẓ ’s texts, we can clearly reassert literature’s primacy over psychological and social notions (cf. # Remembering the Egyptian Novelist Sonallah Ibrahim: “Taking a Scalpel to the Communist Dream”

September 30, 2025

_by_[Gretchen McCullough](https://worldliteraturetoday.org/author/gretchen-mccullough)

This page is available to subscribers. [Click here to sign in or get access](https://my.worldlit.org/).

![Image 4: Sonallah Ibrahim with the cover to several of his books](https://worldliteraturetoday.org/sites/worldliteraturetoday.org/files/McCullough-anchor.jpg)
_The author pays tribute to the prolific Egyptian writer Sonallah Ibrahim, best known as a leftist writer who began his career in the 1960s, during the reign of President Nasser._

When I first met Sonallah Ibrahim (August 3, 1937–August 13, 2025) in 2016—the Egyptian novelist with his shock of bushy white hair, granny glasses, and bemused expression—I was charmed by his quirkiness, wry humor, and wide knowledge of history, politics, and literature. I was interviewing him about his then-new novel, Berlin 69, which was published in Arabic in 2014. He came over for a few Stella beers at our place in Cairo—the interview felt like an informal chat between writers. He liked my book of bilingual short stories, _Three Stories from Cairo_ (2011), which was translated into Arabic by the Egyptian poet Mohamed Metwalli, my husband. Offbeat expatriate characters clash with Cairo and traditional Egypt in humorous ways in my book: a theme that interested Ibrahim.

In the Arabic-speaking world, Ibrahim is best known as a leftist writer of the “Sixties Generation” who began his career during the period of President Gamal Abdel Nasser. Prolific, he published seventeen novels, four short-story collections, six children’s books, and three translations. Nine of his books have been translated into English: _The Smell of It and Other Stories_; _The Committee_; _Beirut, Beirut_; _Zaat_; _Warda_; _Stealth_; _The Turban and the Hat_; _Ice_;and _1970: The Last Days_.

Ibrahim was born in 1937 during the waning years of the British occupation. His novel _Stealth_ (2007)—translated by Hosam Aboul-Ela (2014) and narrated in present tense from a small child’s point of view—gives readers an insight into this era.

During our interview, Sonallah chose to sit in a large, comfy armchair with his back to the door. He mentioned that this choice was an exception. Normally, he sat with his back to the wall if he was outside of his house. Arrested in 1959 for distributing Communist leaflets and imprisoned for five years during Nasser’s rule, he was still traumatized from the experience. He said, “State security put me in front with the driver and the officer in the back kept beating me. Afterward, (it) was torture in prison for five years.”

Soon after he was released from prison in 1964, he published _The Smell of It and Other Stories_(1966), which was first translated by Denys Johnson Davies in 1971. The novel describes a disillusioned political prisoner who wanders around Cairo in a daze, alienated from daily life, like one of the Seven Sleepers of the Cave. The book was retranslated in 2013 by Robyn Creswell as _That Smell_ with the addition of _Notes from Prison_—Ibrahim’s notes on cigarette papers written in prison.

Since we were talking about _Berlin 69_ for the interview, I asked him: “Did your experience in East Germany and Russia (1969–74) give you a useful perspective on Nasser’s version of socialism?”

“The dream was fantastic, but it remains a dream,” he said, waving his hands expansively.

He explained that other factors spoiled the Communist dream. “Other factors were not seen before, at the beginning of the experience—like the role of the state and the idea of one-party rule, defined as the vanguard class,” he commented.“People were enjoying the basic necessities, and you would never see a man sleeping on the street. Everyone had a job. You don’t enjoy freedom of expression; that is the dilemma.”

His novel[_Ice_](https://www.seagullbooks.org/ice/) (2011), translated by Margaret Litvin (2019), uses a diary format to take a scalpel to the “fantastic dream” of communism through the eagle eyes of a sardonic Egyptian narrator who has come to study in Russia. The novel echoes some of the themes of _Berlin 69_: coping with paranoia and the fear of intelligence services, nostalgia for Egypt, transient relationships with foreign women, the hunt for scarce commodities, and a corrupt party elite. Ibrahim lived in Moscow during a crucial period in Egypt’s history, following the 1967 defeat and Egypt’s 1973 victory over Israel. Ibrahim observed that living abroad was beneficial for him as a writer. “It’s useful to look at your country from the outside,” he said, “to be in contact with other cultures and psychologies. Not to see your country as the center of the world.”

He toyed with the idea of staying in East Germany but said he was not comfortable writing in either German or English: “If you master the language, you can write in it. But one also has to understand the psychology and traditions of the culture. There are exceptions, like Nabokov.” Ultimately, he decided to return to Egypt.

The main character in _Berlin 69_ is a young Egyptian journalist who finds it difficult to write creatively in East Germany. When I asked him if being a journalist had stymied his own creativity, he said no. Instead, he pointed out the positive influence that journalism has had on literature “starting with Hemingway—he used the simple reporting in his telegraphic style and used different dimensions of texts.”

Besides _The Smell of It_ and _Ice_, the novels _Warda_ and _The Turban and the Hat_ also utilize the diary form.

One of my favorites is[_Warda_](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300228656/warda/) (2000), translated by Hosam Aboul-Ela (2021). The novel tells the little-known political story of the Dhofar Liberation Front, a Marxist group, whose main goal was to expel the British from Oman and Yemen after Egypt’s setback of 1967. (The Soviets and Chinese funded proxy wars in the Gulf in the 1960s and ’70s to gain influence there.)Rushdy, the main character, is a middle-aged writer searching for “Warda,” or Rose, the _nom de guerre_ for an Omani activist he fell in love with while he was a student at Cairo University in the late 1950s.Rushdy visits his cousin in Oman to find out what happened to Warda. He receives her diary in a brand-name plastic bag in a series of mysterious handoffs. The novel alternates between Rushdy’s point of view in the 1990s and Warda’s in the 1960s (up until the end of the Dhofar Rebellion in the mid-1970s). Her diary gives the reader an insider’s view of a female rebel in a volatile political movement: an eclectic bunch, consisting of local tribespeople, herders, and Arab intellectuals.

The novel[_The Turban and the Hat_](https://seagullbooks.org/products/the-turban-and-the-hat) (2008), translated by Bruce Fudge in 2022, is an enjoyable read that gives modern-day readers the texture of everyday life in Egypt during Napoleon’s occupation of Egypt (1798–1801) and is informed by extensive historical research and Al-Jabarti’s chronicles. (Al-Jabarti was an Egyptian historian who wrote a firsthand account of the French invasion of Egypt in 1798.) The “diarist” in _The Turban and the Hat_ is a student of Al-Jabarti’s who describes the struggle between French and Turkish forces for control of Egypt, the abuse of civilians by the occupiers, the lively intellectual atmosphere of Napoleon’s scientific expedition, the fear and the enforced quarantines during the bubonic plague, the collaboration of the Egyptian elite with the French occupiers, and Napoleon’s disastrous campaign in Syria. The narrator is sexually initiated by Pauline, a Frenchwoman who traveled with the expedition, who was reported to have an affair with Napoleon.

Ibrahim’s best-known novel in Egypt is probably _Zaat_ (1992), which means “self” and was translated by Tony Calderbank in (2001). In it,Ibrahim alternated chapters of third-person narrative with newspaper headlines of the era,foregrounding politics with his use of headlines, sandwiching banal advertisements, scandals, and mundane details of daily life with big political events to highlight the hypocrisy of narratives promoted by the media. (The American writer William Burroughs used the “cut-up” technique, arranging bits of information to reflect a certain absurdity. This experimental approach was popular during the 1960s.)The novel was popularized by the entertaining television series _Zaat_ (2013), with star Nelly Karim acting as the lead character Zaat, an ordinary Egyptian girl who struggles to complete her education during Nasser’s reign. Instead of marrying her sweetheart, she marries Abdel Mageed, an unimaginative dolt who seems to have better economic prospects. Against the backdrop of the Peace Agreement with Israel in 1979 and Sadat’s Open-Door Policy, it shows how ordinary Egyptians were squeezed by rising prices, unable to afford the deluge of consumer goods. Those who immigrate to the Gulf bring back Wahabi ideas about Islam, transforming Egyptian society in surprising ways that seem incompatible with the Egyptian spirit. The television series made Zaat’s story accessible to a mainstream Egyptian audience, who might not have read the experimental novel.

On the other hand, an international audience might be more familiar with _The Committee_ (1984), translated in 2001 by Charlene Constable and Mary St. Germaine, reminiscent of Kafka, which focuses on the adventures of an unreliable narrator who is driven crazy by the byzantine bureaucracy during the time of Nasser.

_Beirut, Beirut_ (1984), translated by Chip Rossetti in 2014, focuses on the Lebanese Civil War and also uses collage: newspaper headlines and excerpts from a film script.In one informal conversation, Ibrahim acknowledged to me how difficult it was for outsiders to penetrate the labyrinth of Lebanese politics and society.

This novel intersperses newspaper headlines with the private musings of President Nasser from a second-person point of view in the last days before his death. One yearns for the point of view of others in the Free Officers’ Movement, however. Perhaps even Mohamed Naguib, one of the Free Officers who was sidelined and put under house arrest by Nasser, whose story has not been widely told.

Sonallah sent me a copy of the translation _1970: The Last Days_ last year with a short dedication that must have taken some effort because of his poor health. Frequently, he used to send us copies of books in Arabic from the avant-garde publishing house Dar El-Thakafa El-Gadidda, which he had run since 2008, when Mohamed Youssef El-Guendy, his wife’s first husband, had died. El-Guendy established the publishing house in 1968.

I remembered our visit to his flat in Heliopolis in 2017. He had written a blurb for my novel, and we were going to pick it up. We didn’t know if we should go or not because it was raining—a minor catastrophe in Egypt! He called and urged us to come: “It’s not raining here!”

A rope with a vegetable basket—known as a _sabat_—dangled from the stairwell. Many apartment dwellers lower the _sabat_ down to those below for deliveries. Much public housing built during the Nasser era did not have elevators—later, landlords refused to spend the money to install them. We started the climb to the seventh floor. He and his wife, Laila, had lived there for decades—and his stepdaughter, Nadia, remembered how he had carried her up the stairs when she was little.

Laila had long, white hair, intelligent eyes, and a pleasant smile, and it wasn’t hard to imagine her as a young woman. She was self-deprecating and claimed she was “just a housewife,” but she was fluent in English and held a degree in English literature and Egyptology from Cairo University. She shared Sonallah’s left-wing political sympathies, and they had married in 1975. While Laila was away working as a tour guide, Sonallah cared for his stepdaughter, Nadia, since he was at home, writing. He read her bedtime stories when she was young and later encouraged her to pursue her doctorate in molecular biology.

“Sonallah was in the kitchen all afternoon!” Laila said. “I hope you’re hungry.”

It was a modest flat, with books stacked in every nook and cranny. We sat in a cozy living room in front of a low coffee table. The table was crammed with a variety of delicious mezze dishes. I was touched that he had gone to so much trouble since his ankles were swollen. He longed for a beer. “I’m on medication,” he said, pointing to his ankles. “All we do is go to doctors.” But he kept popping open the beers for me and my husband. He believed my novel was good—and would eventually be published.

When the novel was published in 2022, we arranged to visit him and give him a copy of the book, _Confessions of a Knight Errant_, and a copy of our translation of Mohamed’s collection of poetry, _A Song by the Aegean Sea_. Nadia and her husband had helped Sonallah and Laila move from Heliopolis to their building in Mokattam Hills during the Covid pandemic in 2020. We got lost and had to call Nadia to find the building. Sadly, Laila had recently died.

It was an airy flat with nice light; a sliding glass door led to a large terrace.

He couldn’t hear well, and it was difficult to communicate with him. Nadia explained that he didn’t like to wear his hearing aid! He was very frail.

His ten-year-old granddaughter was also there, playing with a cat.

Sonallah directed us to the terrace with his cane. “I prefer the fresh air here.”

We stood outside for a moment and looked at the expansive sky, the Mokattam plateau in the distance. The sunlight was dimming.

# Remembering the Egyptian Novelist Sonallah Ibrahim: “Taking a Scalpel to the Communist Dream”

September 30, 2025

_by_[Gretchen McCullough](https://worldliteraturetoday.org/author/gretchen-mccullough)

This page is available to subscribers. [Click here to sign in or get access](https://my.worldlit.org/).

![Image 4: Sonallah Ibrahim with the cover to several of his books](https://worldliteraturetoday.org/sites/worldliteraturetoday.org/files/McCullough-anchor.jpg)
_The author pays tribute to the prolific Egyptian writer Sonallah Ibrahim, best known as a leftist writer who began his career in the 1960s, during the reign of President Nasser._

When I first met Sonallah Ibrahim (August 3, 1937–August 13, 2025) in 2016—the Egyptian novelist with his shock of bushy white hair, granny glasses, and bemused expression—I was charmed by his quirkiness, wry humor, and wide knowledge of history, politics, and literature. I was interviewing him about his then-new novel, Berlin 69, which was published in Arabic in 2014. He came over for a few Stella beers at our place in Cairo—the interview felt like an informal chat between writers. He liked my book of bilingual short stories, _Three Stories from Cairo_ (2011), which was translated into Arabic by the Egyptian poet Mohamed Metwalli, my husband. Offbeat expatriate characters clash with Cairo and traditional Egypt in humorous ways in my book: a theme that interested Ibrahim.

In the Arabic-speaking world, Ibrahim is best known as a leftist writer of the “Sixties Generation” who began his career during the period of President Gamal Abdel Nasser. Prolific, he published seventeen novels, four short-story collections, six children’s books, and three translations. Nine of his books have been translated into English: _The Smell of It and Other Stories_; _The Committee_; _Beirut, Beirut_; _Zaat_; _Warda_; _Stealth_; _The Turban and the Hat_; _Ice_;and _1970: The Last Days_.

Ibrahim was born in 1937 during the waning years of the British occupation. His novel _Stealth_ (2007)—translated by Hosam Aboul-Ela (2014) and narrated in present tense from a small child’s point of view—gives readers an insight into this era.

During our interview, Sonallah chose to sit in a large, comfy armchair with his back to the door. He mentioned that this choice was an exception. Normally, he sat with his back to the wall if he was outside of his house. Arrested in 1959 for distributing Communist leaflets and imprisoned for five years during Nasser’s rule, he was still traumatized from the experience. He said, “State security put me in front with the driver and the officer in the back kept beating me. Afterward, (it) was torture in prison for five years.”

Soon after he was released from prison in 1964, he published _The Smell of It and Other Stories_(1966), which was first translated by Denys Johnson Davies in 1971. The novel describes a disillusioned political prisoner who wanders around Cairo in a daze, alienated from daily life, like one of the Seven Sleepers of the Cave. The book was retranslated in 2013 by Robyn Creswell as _That Smell_ with the addition of _Notes from Prison_—Ibrahim’s notes on cigarette papers written in prison.

Since we were talking about _Berlin 69_ for the interview, I asked him: “Did your experience in East Germany and Russia (1969–74) give you a useful perspective on Nasser’s version of socialism?”

“The dream was fantastic, but it remains a dream,” he said, waving his hands expansively.

He explained that other factors spoiled the Communist dream. “Other factors were not seen before, at the beginning of the experience—like the role of the state and the idea of one-party rule, defined as the vanguard class,” he commented.“People were enjoying the basic necessities, and you would never see a man sleeping on the street. Everyone had a job. You don’t enjoy freedom of expression; that is the dilemma.”

His novel[_Ice_](https://www.seagullbooks.org/ice/) (2011), translated by Margaret Litvin (2019), uses a diary format to take a scalpel to the “fantastic dream” of communism through the eagle eyes of a sardonic Egyptian narrator who has come to study in Russia. The novel echoes some of the themes of _Berlin 69_: coping with paranoia and the fear of intelligence services, nostalgia for Egypt, transient relationships with foreign women, the hunt for scarce commodities, and a corrupt party elite. Ibrahim lived in Moscow during a crucial period in Egypt’s history, following the 1967 defeat and Egypt’s 1973 victory over Israel. Ibrahim recounts many details about the difficulties of living in Russia.For example, shortages of goods and commodities in a state-controlled economy led to absurd situations and bizarre behavior. When the main character is getting medical treatment, the doctor clearly states that he needs a new tire for his car!

_Ice_ uses a diary format to take a scalpel to the “fantastic dream” of communism through the eagle eyes of a sardonic Egyptian narrator who has come to study in Russia.

Ibrahim observed that living abroad was beneficial for him as a writer. “It’s useful to look at your country from the outside,” he said, “to be in contact with other cultures and psychologies. Not to see your country as the center of the world.”

He toyed with the idea of staying in East Germany but said he was not comfortable writing in either German or English: “If you master the language, you can write in it. But one also has to understand the psychology and traditions of the culture. There are exceptions, like Nabokov.” Ultimately, he decided to return to Egypt.

The main character in _Berlin 69_ is a young Egyptian journalist who finds it difficult to write creatively in East Germany. When I asked him if being a journalist had stymied his own creativity, he said no. Instead, he pointed out the positive influence that journalism has had on literature “starting with Hemingway—he used the simple reporting in his telegraphic style and used different dimensions of texts.”

Besides _The Smell of It_ and _Ice_, the novels _Warda_ and _The Turban and the Hat_ also utilize the diary form.

One of my favorites is[_Warda_](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300228656/warda/) (2000), translated by Hosam Aboul-Ela (2021). The novel tells the little-known political story of the Dhofar Liberation Front, a Marxist group, whose main goal was to expel the British from Oman and Yemen after Egypt’s setback of 1967. (The Soviets and Chinese funded proxy wars in the Gulf in the 1960s and ’70s to gain influence there.)Rushdy, the main character, is a middle-aged writer searching for “Warda,” or Rose, the _nom de guerre_ for an Omani activist he fell in love with while he was a student at Cairo University in the late 1950s.Rushdy visits his cousin in Oman to find out what happened to Warda. He receives her diary in a brand-name plastic bag in a series of mysterious handoffs. The novel alternates between Rushdy’s point of view in the 1990s and Warda’s in the 1960s (up until the end of the Dhofar Rebellion in the mid-1970s). Her diary gives the reader an insider’s view of a female rebel in a volatile political movement: an eclectic bunch, consisting of local tribespeople, herders, and Arab intellectuals.

Warda’s diary gives the reader an insider’s view of a female rebel in a volatile political movement: an eclectic bunch, consisting of local tribespeople, herders, and Arab intellectuals.

The novel[_The Turban and the Hat_](https://seagullbooks.org/products/the-turban-and-the-hat) (2008), translated by Bruce Fudge in 2022, is an enjoyable read that gives modern-day readers the texture of everyday life in Egypt during Napoleon’s occupation of Egypt (1798–1801) and is informed by extensive historical research and Al-Jabarti’s chronicles. (Al-Jabarti was an Egyptian historian who wrote a firsthand account of the French invasion of Egypt in 1798.) The “diarist” in _The Turban and the Hat_ is a student of Al-Jabarti’s who describes the struggle between French and Turkish forces for control of Egypt, the abuse of civilians by the occupiers, the lively intellectual atmosphere of Napoleon’s scientific expedition, the fear and the enforced quarantines during the bubonic plague, the collaboration of the Egyptian elite with the French occupiers, and Napoleon’s disastrous campaign in Syria. The narrator is sexually initiated by Pauline, a Frenchwoman who traveled with the expedition, who was reported to have an affair with Napoleon.

Ibrahim’s best-known novel in Egypt is probably _Zaat_ (1992), which means “self” and was translated by Tony Calderbank in (2001). In it,Ibrahim alternated chapters of third-person narrative with newspaper headlines of the era,foregrounding politics with his use of headlines, sandwiching banal advertisements, scandals, and mundane details of daily life with big political events to highlight the hypocrisy of narratives promoted by the media. (The American writer William Burroughs used the “cut-up” technique, arranging bits of information to reflect a certain absurdity. This experimental approach was popular during the 1960s.)The novel was popularized by the entertaining television series _Zaat_ (2013), with star Nelly Karim acting as the lead character Zaat, an ordinary Egyptian girl who struggles to complete her education during Nasser’s reign. Instead of marrying her sweetheart, she marries Abdel Mageed, an unimaginative dolt who seems to have better economic prospects. Against the backdrop of the Peace Agreement with Israel in 1979 and Sadat’s Open-Door Policy, it shows how ordinary Egyptians were squeezed by rising prices, unable to afford the deluge of consumer goods. Those who immigrate to the Gulf bring back Wahabi ideas about Islam, transforming Egyptian society in surprising ways that seem incompatible with the Egyptian spirit. The television series made Zaat’s story accessible to a mainstream Egyptian audience, who might not have read the experimental novel.

On the other hand, an international audience might be more familiar with _The Committee_ (1984), translated in 2001 by Charlene Constable and Mary St. Germaine, reminiscent of Kafka, which focuses on the adventures of an unreliable narrator who is driven crazy by the byzantine bureaucracy during the time of Nasser.

_Beirut, Beirut_ (1984), translated by Chip Rossetti in 2014, focuses on the Lebanese Civil War and also uses collage: newspaper headlines and excerpts from a film script.In one informal conversation, Ibrahim acknowledged to me how difficult it was for outsiders to penetrate the labyrinth of Lebanese politics and society.

[_1970: The Last Days_](https://seagullbooks.org/products/1970) (2024) was just translated by Eleanor Ellis. This novel intersperses newspaper headlines with the private musings of President Nasser from a second-person point of view in the last days before his death. One yearns for the point of view of others in the Free Officers’ Movement, however. Perhaps even Mohamed Naguib, one of the Free Officers who was sidelined and put under house arrest by Nasser, whose story has not been widely told.

Sonallah sent me a copy of the translation _1970: The Last Days_ last year with a short dedication that must have taken some effort because of his poor health. Frequently, he used to send us copies of books in Arabic from the avant-garde publishing house Dar El-Thakafa El-Gadidda, which he had run since 2008, when Mohamed Youssef El-Guendy, his wife’s first husband, had died. El-Guendy established the publishing house in 1968.

I remembered our visit to his flat in Heliopolis in 2017. He had written a blurb for my novel, and we were going to pick it up. We didn’t know if we should go or not because it was raining—a minor catastrophe in Egypt! He called and urged us to come: “It’s not raining here!”

A rope with a vegetable basket—known as a _sabat_—dangled from the stairwell. Many apartment dwellers lower the _sabat_ down to those below for deliveries. Much public housing built during the Nasser era did not have elevators—later, landlords refused to spend the money to install them. We started the climb to the seventh floor. He and his wife, Laila, had lived there for decades—and his stepdaughter, Nadia, remembered how he had carried her up the stairs when she was little.

Laila had long, white hair, intelligent eyes, and a pleasant smile, and it wasn’t hard to imagine her as a young woman. She was self-deprecating and claimed she was “just a housewife,” but she was fluent in English and held a degree in English literature and Egyptology from Cairo University. She shared Sonallah’s left-wing political sympathies, and they had married in 1975. While Laila was away working as a tour guide, Sonallah cared for his stepdaughter, Nadia, since he was at home, writing. He read her bedtime stories when she was young and later encouraged her to pursue her doctorate in molecular biology.

“Sonallah was in the kitchen all afternoon!” Laila said. “I hope you’re hungry.”

It was a modest flat, with books stacked in every nook and cranny. We sat in a cozy living room in front of a low coffee table. The table was crammed with a variety of delicious mezze dishes. I was touched that he had gone to so much trouble since his ankles were swollen. He longed for a beer. “I’m on medication,” he said, pointing to his ankles. “All we do is go to doctors.” But he kept popping open the beers for me and my husband. He believed my novel was good—and would eventually be published.

The table was crammed with a variety of delicious mezze dishes. I was touched that Sonallah had gone to so much trouble since his ankles were swollen.

When the novel was published in 2022, we arranged to visit him and give him a copy of the book, _Confessions of a Knight Errant_, and a copy of our translation of Mohamed’s collection of poetry, _A Song by the Aegean Sea_. Nadia and her husband had helped Sonallah and Laila move from Heliopolis to their building in Mokattam Hills during the Covid pandemic in 2020. We got lost and had to call Nadia to find the building. Sadly, Laila had recently died.

It was an airy flat with nice light; a sliding glass door led to a large terrace.

He couldn’t hear well, and it was difficult to communicate with him. Nadia explained that he didn’t like to wear his hearing aid! He was very frail.

His ten-year-old granddaughter was also there, playing with a cat.

Sonallah directed us to the terrace with his cane. “I prefer the fresh air here.”

We stood outside for a moment and looked at the expansive sky, the Mokattam plateau in the distance. The sunlight was dimming.

_Cairo_

ABSTRACT 

CHARISMATIC LEADERSHIP IN EGYPT: GAMAL ABDEL NASSER 

ALTUN, Tuğba 

M.A., The Department of Middle East Studies 

Supervisor: Prof. Dr. Meliha BENLİ ALTUNIŞIK 

December 2022, 111 pages 

During the years between 1952 and 1970, Egypt was almost the most influential country in the Arab world. Gamal Abdel Nasser’s powerful image in the eyes of the Egyptians and among the Arabs in general as the president of Egypt at that time was influential. Nasser strongly supported Arab nationalism and unity in the Arab world. Also, he was passionately against colonialism and the bipolar system in the world. Therefore, he created a powerful charismatic leadership with his ideas and policies among the Arabs. However, it was interesting to note that he domestic and regional support continued even after the defeats in Yemen and in 1967 War. Thus, this study focuses on understanding how Nasser was able to continue his rule even after the defeats. It is argued that his suppressive policies at home does not explain wholly his popularity in Egypt and beyond. Instead, the thesis claims that the charismatic leadership of Nasser was one of the main reasons for the continuation of Nasser’s rule and his popularity. Therefore, the study suggests that Nasser was able to continue his rule and popularity with charismatic leadership by explaining the features of v

charismatic leadership, Nasser’s domestic and foreign policies, and the process of the establishment of his charismatic leadership. 

Keywords: Nasser, Charismatic Leadership, Egypt, Arab nationalism vi

Nasır, Arap milliyetçiliğinin ve Arap birliğinin güçlü bir destekçisi olarak ön plana çıkmıştır. Ayrıca Nasır, sömürgeciliğe ve dünyadaki çift kutuplu sisteme şiddetli bir şekilde karşı çıkmıştır. Bu sayede Nasır, Arap dünyasındaki fikirleri ve politikalarıyla güçlü bir karizmatik liderlik oluşturmuştur. Nasır’ın Yemen Savaşı ve 1967 Arap-İsrail savaşında yaşanan yenilgilerin ardından bile halk tarafından desteklenmeye devam etmesi dikkat çekici olmuştur. Bu çalışma da Nasır’ın yaşadığını yenilgilerin ardından bile yönetimini nasıl sürdürebildiğini anlamaya odaklanıyor. Nasır’ın baskıcı politikaları Mısır’da ve tüm Arap dünyasında devam eden popularitesini tam olarak açıklamamktadır. Bu tez, Nasır’ın yönetiminin devamı için karizmatik liderliğin en önemli nedenlerden biri olduğu savunuyor. Özellikle bu çalışma, karizmatik liderliğin özellikleri, Nasır’ın iç ve dış politikası, karizmatik liderlik oluşma sürecini inceleyerek Nasır’ın karizmatik liderliği sayesinde yönetimini ve popülerliğini sürdürdüğünü öne sürüyor.
