Abstract:
Background:
Morocco launched an appeal in 2002 to develop a fundamental law on Basic Medical Coverage. Two systems have been put in place: Compulsory
Health Insurance (AMO) based on solidarity and social security contributions; and a Medical Assistance Scheme based on the principle of social
protection. The objective of these systems is to achieve Universal Health Coverage (UHC) to attain equity and equality in access to health care.
In the international trend, access to economic and social rights has become a significant concern in public policies. This concept, based on the
value of “equity” is now essential in evaluating equal opportunities in social and health systems. More importantly, there is a need to clarify the
difference between the terms equality and equity in health. In most cases, reference is made to the definition used in Anglo-Saxon literature
(equity, equality, fairness). Therefore, not all inequalities are inequities. The difference between equality and equity lies in that the first term gives
the result of comparison without value judgment, while the second makes a judgment that qualifies the result as fair or unfair.

Our study aims to analyze the specific problems related to the healthcare policy focused on allocating the supply of care, and efforts to improve
financial accessibility specifically by developing medical coverage. We will present results that reflect the availability and quality of care in
Morocco and shed light on the problem of not seeking healthcare for financial, geographical, and other reasons. In addition, we will discuss the
difficulties related to the use of care by Moroccan citizens.
The findings of this paper can potentially inform national healthcare policy and add to the small but growing literature on this subject in Morocco.

Methodology:
The methodology is based on research & data taken from official institutional publications from Morocco & United Nations organizations (gray
literature) and data derived from articles published in scientific journals.

Results:
Morocco continues to suffer from disparities in the distribution of health practitioners due to an imbalanced distribution of health infrastructure and
human resources between rural and urban areas. The Health Map developed by the Ministry of Health and Social Protection in 2016 is a very good
tool to monitor the distribution of public health needs in each region, plan the delivery of care, regulate spending, and consolidate regionalization
policy to ensure equity in supply and access to health care. At the end of 2021, the national average ratios were 7.3 physicians and 10 beds per
10000 inhabitants. In 2018, more than 60% of the Moroccan population enjoyed basic medical coverage and the Moroccan Government is
committed to reaching 100% of Universal Health Coverage (UHC) by 2030.

Conclusion:
The health map will make it possible to control health expenditure by allocating human and financial resources according to needs and will
determine the future location of health facilities to establish equity in the offer and access to health care.

**Mohammed al-Khamis bin Yusef bin Hassan al-Alawi**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-1) better known simply as **Mohammed V**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-2) (10 August 1909 – 26 February 1961), was the ruler of Morocco from 1927 to 1961, except for a two-year period in exile during the 1950s. He reigned as [sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_of_Morocco "Sultan of Morocco") until 1957, and afterwards as the first [king of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Morocco "King of Morocco"). A member of the [Alawi dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alawi_dynasty "Alawi dynasty"), he played an instrumental role in restoring the independence of Morocco from the French and Spanish protectorates.

Mohammed was enthroned as sultan upon the death of his father [Yusef bin Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusef_of_Morocco "Yusef of Morocco") in 1927. Early in his reign, his approval of the [Berber Dahir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_Dahir "Berber Dahir") drew widespread backlash and spurred an upsurge of [Moroccan nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_nationalism "Moroccan nationalism") and opposition to [continued French rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_protectorate_in_Morocco "French protectorate in Morocco"). Initially more amenable to colonial authorities, Mohammed grew increasingly supportive of the nationalist movement later on. During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") he supported the [Allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II"), participated in the 1943 [Anfa Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca_Conference "Casablanca Conference") and has been widely credited with protecting [Morocco’s Jewish population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Jews "Moroccan Jews") during World War II, as he reportedly resisted [Vichy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France") efforts to impose anti-Jewish measures and deport Jews, and emphasized that all Moroccan Jews were under his protection as subjects of the crown.

Mohammed became a central figure of the independence cause after the war. In 1947, he delivered a [historic speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier_Speech "Tangier Speech") in [Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier_International_Zone "Tangier International Zone"), in which he made an open appeal for Moroccan independence and emphasized the country's ties with the rest of the [Arab world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_world "Arab world"). His relationship with the French became increasingly strained afterwards as colonial rule grew more repressive. In 1953, French authorities deposed Mohammed, exiled him to [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") (later transferring him to [Madagascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar "Madagascar")) and installed his first cousin once removed [Mohammed Ben Aarafa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Ben_Aarafa "Mohammed Ben Aarafa") as sultan. The deposition sparked active opposition to the French protectorate and two years later, faced with rising violence in Morocco, the French government allowed Mohammed's return. In 1956, he successfully negotiated with France and Spain for Moroccan independence, and in the following year he assumed the title of king. Mohammed died in 1961 at the age of 51 and was succeeded by his eldest son, who took the throne as [Hassan II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_II_of_Morocco "Hassan II of Morocco").

Mohammed is often described by historians as a moderate and unifying figure whose leadership style was marked by restraint and a generally gentle and conciliatory approach, contributing to his reputation as a widely respected and principled monarch.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Sidi Mohammed bin Yusef was born on 10 August 1909 in [Fes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fez,_Morocco "Fez, Morocco") to Sultan [Yusef of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusef_of_Morocco "Yusef of Morocco") and [Lalla Yacout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Yacout "Lalla Yacout"), and was his father's third and youngest son.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-3)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:22-4) In March 1912, the [Treaty of Fes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fes "Treaty of Fes") was signed, turning Morocco into a French protectorate after a [French invasion from the west](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardment_of_Casablanca_(1907) "Bombardment of Casablanca (1907)") and the east, resulting in an eventual capture of the capital, Fes.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Yusef was enthroned as sultan by the French in September 1912.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-5)

Sidi Mohammed began his education in Fes, inside the palace grounds of his home, _qasr al-amami_ (front palace). There he learned to read and write and received his first lessons in the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:2-6)

When his father established [Rabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabat "Rabat") as the capital of the kingdom and of the administration, he transferred Sidi Mohammed there, with most of his brothers. There, he continued his studies with private teachers. In Rabat, he continued to study [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic "Arabic") and the Quran until he became a [_hafiz_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafiz_(Quran) "Hafiz (Quran)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:2-6) He also studied [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-7) under [Mohammed Mammeri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Mammeri?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mohammed Mammeri (page does not exist)"), who gave him special attention. After he became Sultan, Mammeri remained in his service for a long time as head of protocol.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:3-8)

Sidi Mohammed then continued his education in a public school in Rabat.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:2-6)

## Reign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Reign")]

### Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early years")]

On 18 November 1927, a "young and timid" 17-year-old Muhammad bin Yusef was enthroned after the death of his father and the departure of [Hubert Lyautey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Lyautey "Hubert Lyautey").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10)

At the time of Mohammed's enthronement, the French colonial authorities were "pushing for a more assertive 'native policy.'"[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10) On 16 May 1930, Sultan Muhammad V signed the [Berber Dahir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_Dahir "Berber Dahir"), which changed the legal system in parts of Morocco where [Berber languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_languages "Berber languages") were primarily spoken (_[Bled es-Siba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bled\_es-Siba "Bled es-Siba")_), while the legal system in the rest of the country (_Bled al-Makhzen_) remained the way it had been before the [French invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_conquest_of_Morocco "French conquest of Morocco").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-11) Although the sultan was under no duress, he was then only twenty years old.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10) This [_dahir_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Dahir "Moroccan Dahir") "electrified the nation"; it was sharply criticized by [Moroccan nationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_nationalism "Moroccan nationalism") and catalyzed the [Moroccan Nationalist Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Nationalist_Movement "Moroccan Nationalist Movement").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10)

### World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: World War II")]

Sultan Mohammed participated in the [Anfa Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca_Conference "Casablanca Conference") hosted in [Casablanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca "Casablanca") during World War II.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10) On 22 January 1943, he met privately with the US president [Franklin Delano Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Delano_Roosevelt "Franklin Delano Roosevelt") and the Prime Minister of the UK [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10) At this dinner, Roosevelt assured the sultan that "the post-war scene and the pre-war scene would ... sharply differ, especially as they related to the colonial question." The sultan's 14-year-old son and future king of Morocco, Hassan II, also attended and later stated that Roosevelt said, "Ten years from now your country will be independent."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10)

"There are competing accounts of exactly what Mohammed V did or did not do for the [Moroccan Jewish community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Jews "Moroccan Jews")" during [the Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Marglin-12) However, "though a subject of debate, most scholars stress the benevolence of Mohammed V toward the Jews" during the [Vichy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France") era.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-13) Mohammed reportedly refused to sign off on efforts by Vichy officials to impose [anti-Jewish legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_anti-Jewish_legislation "Vichy anti-Jewish legislation") upon Morocco and deport the country's 250,000 Jews to their deaths in [Nazi concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_concentration_camp "Nazi concentration camp") and [extermination camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extermination_camp "Extermination camp") in Europe. The sultan's stand was "based as much on the insult the Vichy _[diktats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diktat "Diktat")_ posed to his claim of sovereignty over all his subjects, including the Jews, as on his humanitarian instincts." Partial Nazi race measures were enacted in Morocco over Mohammed's objection,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Miller-14) and Mohammed did sign, under the instructions of Vichy officials, two decrees that barred Jews from certain schools and positions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Bouasria-15)

Nevertheless, Mohammed is highly esteemed by Moroccan Jews who credit him for protecting their community from [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") and the Vichy French government,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Marglin-12) and he has been honored by Jewish organizations for his role in protecting his Jewish subjects during the Holocaust.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-16) Some historians maintain that Mohammed's anti-Nazi role has been exaggerated; historian [Michel Abitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Abitol "Michel Abitol") writes that while Mohammed was compelled by Vichy officials to sign the anti-Jewish dahirs, "he was more passive than [Moncef Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_VII_al-Munsif "Muhammad VII al-Munsif") ([ruler of Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Beys_of_Tunis "List of Beys of Tunis") during the Second World War) in that he did not take any side and did not engage in any public act that could be interpreted as a rejection of Vichy's policy."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Bouasria-15)

### Struggle for independence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Struggle for independence")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Editing_File-Franklin_D._Roosevelt%2C_Winston_Churchill%2C_Mohammed_V_and_Hassan_II_at_the_Casablanca_Conference.jpg/250px-Editing_File-Franklin_D._Roosevelt%2C_Winston_Churchill%2C_Mohammed_V_and_Hassan_II_at_the_Casablanca_Conference.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Editing_File-Franklin_D._Roosevelt,_Winston_Churchill,_Mohammed_V_and_Hassan_II_at_the_Casablanca_Conference.jpg)

Sultan Mohammed seated with [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") and [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill") during the 1943 [Casablanca Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca_Conference "Casablanca Conference"); his son [Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_II_of_Morocco "Hassan II of Morocco") is pictured standing behind him.

Sultan Mohammad was a central figure in the independence movement in Morocco, also known as the [Revolution of the King and the People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolution_of_the_King_and_the_People "Revolution of the King and the People") (ثورة الملك والشعب). The [Moroccan Nationalist Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Nationalist_Movement "Moroccan Nationalist Movement") grew from protests regarding the [Berber Dahir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_Dahir "Berber Dahir") of 16 May 1930. He was critical of early movements for reform in French colonial administration in Morocco before becoming a supporter of independence later on.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-17)

His central position in the [Proclamation of Independence of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_Independence_of_Morocco "Proclamation of Independence of Morocco") further boosted his image as a national symbol. On 9 and 10 April 1947, he delivered two momentous speeches respectively at the [Mendoubia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendoubia "Mendoubia") and [Grand Mosque of Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_of_Tangier "Grand Mosque of Tangier"), together known as the [Tangier Speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier_Speech "Tangier Speech"), appealing for the independence of Morocco without calling out specific colonial powers.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-18)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-19)

In 1947, the rapid progress of the nationalist movement prompted Sidi Mohammed to demand independence for the first time during the [Tangier speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier_Speech "Tangier Speech"), where he also called for the union of the Arabs and Morocco's membership of the [Arab League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_League "Arab League") which was founded in 1945, in which he praised, emphasized the close ties between Morocco and the rest of the [Arab world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_world "Arab world"). This rapprochement between the monarchy and the nationalist movement, whose projects differ, can be explained, according to historian Bernard Cubertafond, by the fact that "each side needs the other: the national movement sees the growing popularity of the king and his prudent but gradual emancipation from a protector who, in fact, left the treaty of 1912 to come to direct administration; the king cannot, except to discredit himself, cut himself off from a nationalist movement bringing together the living forces of his country and the elite of his youth, and he needs this power of protest to impose changes on France”.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:1-20)

From then on, relations became strained with the French authorities, in particular with the new Resident General, General [Alphonse Juin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Juin "Alphonse Juin"), who applied severe measures and pressured the sultan to disavow the Istiqlal and distance himself from nationalist claims. The break with France was consummated in 1951 and Mohammed formed a pact with the nationalists in Tangier to fight for independence. The appointment of a new Resident General, General [Augustin Guillaume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustin_Guillaume "Augustin Guillaume"), accentuated the dissension between Mohammed and France. Further demonstrations in Morocco culminated in riots in 1952, notably in Casablanca, and Mohammed addressed the United Nations to publicize the Moroccan cause with the support of the United States.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:1-20)

### Deposition and exile

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Deposition and exile")]

On 20 August 1953 (the eve of [Eid al-Adha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eid_al-Adha "Eid al-Adha")), the [French colonial authorities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_French_residents-general_in_Morocco "List of French residents-general in Morocco") forced Mohammed V, an important national symbol in the growing Moroccan independence movement, into exile in [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") along with his family. His first cousin once removed, [Mohammed Ben Aarafa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Ben_Aarafa "Mohammed Ben Aarafa"), called the "French sultan," was made a [puppet monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppet_monarch "Puppet monarch") and placed on the throne. In response, [Muhammad Zarqtuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Zarqtuni "Muhammad Zarqtuni") bombed Casablanca's [Central Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Market_(Casablanca) "Central Market (Casablanca)") on Christmas Eve of that year.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:0-21)

Mohammed and his family were then transferred to [Madagascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar "Madagascar") in January 1954. Mohammed returned from exile on 16 November 1955, and was again recognized as Sultan after active opposition to the French protectorate. His triumphant return was for many the sign of the end of the colonial era.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-22) The situation became so tense that in 1955, the Moroccan nationalists, who enjoyed support in [Libya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Libya "Kingdom of Libya"), [Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria "Algeria") (with the [FLN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Liberation_Front_(Algeria) "National Liberation Front (Algeria)")) and [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Egypt_under_Gamal_Abdel_Nasser#Republic_of_Egypt_(1953%E2%80%931958) "History of Egypt under Gamal Abdel Nasser") forced the French government to negotiate and recall the sultan. In February 1956 he successfully negotiated with [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and Spain for the independence of Morocco.

### After independence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: After independence")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Sultan_Mohammed_V_on_TIME_Magazine%2C_April_22%2C_1957.jpg/250px-Sultan_Mohammed_V_on_TIME_Magazine%2C_April_22%2C_1957.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sultan_Mohammed_V_on_TIME_Magazine,_April_22,_1957.jpg)

On the [cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_covers_of_Time_magazine_(1950s)#1957 "List of covers of Time magazine (1950s)") of [_Time_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)"), 22 April 1957

Mohammed supported the Algerian [National Liberation Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Liberation_Front_(Algeria) "National Liberation Front (Algeria)") (FLN) in the struggle for Algerian Independence and offered to facilitate the participation of FLN leaders in a conference with [Habib Bourguiba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habib_Bourguiba "Habib Bourguiba") in Tunis.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:032-23) On October 22, 1956, [French forces hijacked a Moroccan airplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_hijacking_of_Moroccan_plane "French hijacking of Moroccan plane") carrying leaders of the FLN during the ongoing [Algerian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algerian_War "Algerian War").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:032-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:142-25) The plane, which was carrying [Ahmed Ben Bella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_Ben_Bella "Ahmed Ben Bella"), [Hocine Aït Ahmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hocine_A%C3%AFt_Ahmed "Hocine Aït Ahmed"), and [Mohamed Boudiaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Boudiaf "Mohamed Boudiaf"), was destined to leave from [Palma de Mallorca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palma_de_Mallorca "Palma de Mallorca") for [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"), but French forces redirected the flight to occupied [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers"), where the FLN leaders were arrested.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:032-23)

In 1957, he took the title of [king of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Morocco "King of Morocco"), to symbolise the unity of the country despite divisions between [Arabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs") and [Berbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbers "Berbers"). In terms of domestic policy, upon his return he allowed the first congress of the [Istiqlal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istiqlal_Party "Istiqlal Party"), which formed various governments under his reign. He authorized the creation of trade unions, but the unrest and the strikes lead him to take full power in the last years of his reign.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:1-20) His state visit to the United States later that year "strengthened his position as the kingdom's sole legitimate representative". This way he managed to replace the members of the nationalist movement on the global stage and turned his trip into a great publicity success. This visit marked a strategic effort to align Morocco closely with the US, showcasing the monarchy's importance on the global stage. He used various techniques to project the royal authority, such as personally thanking the nationalist movement's former supporters in the name of the Moroccan people.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Globalizing_Morocco_:_transnational-26) Mohammed also acted as patron to the _International Meetings_, conferences on contemporary issues and interfaith dialogue hosted at the [Benedictine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedictines "Benedictines")[monastery of Toumliline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastery_of_Toumliline "Monastery of Toumliline") that attracted scholars and intellectuals from all over the world.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-27)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Gamal_Abdel_Nasser_in_Morocco.jpg/250px-Gamal_Abdel_Nasser_in_Morocco.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gamal_Abdel_Nasser_in_Morocco.jpg)

Mohamed V receiving Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser in Casablanca, 1961

During his reign, the [Moroccan Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Army_of_Liberation "Moroccan Army of Liberation") waged [war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ifni_War "Ifni War") against Spain and France, and successfully captured most of [Ifni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ifni "Ifni") as well as [Cape Juby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Juby "Cape Juby") and parts of [Spanish Sahara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Sahara "Spanish Sahara"). With the [treaty of Angra de Cintra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Angra_de_Cintra "Treaty of Angra de Cintra"), Morocco annexed [Cape Juby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Juby "Cape Juby") and the surroundings of [Ifni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ifni "Ifni"), while the rest of the remaining colony was ceded by Spain in 1969.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-28)

## Illness and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Illness and death")]

In the final years of his life, Mohammed suffered from an ear illness for which doctors advised him to undergo a [tonsillectomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonsillectomy "Tonsillectomy") in August 1959.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-29) On 26 February 1961, Mohammed underwent a second banal surgery on the [nasal septum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_septum "Nasal septum") in relation to his illness, conducted by a surgeon from [Lausanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lausanne "Lausanne"). Shortly after the operation was completed, Mohammed suffered a fatal cardiac arrest resulting from complications of the surgery.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-30)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:4-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-33)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Funeral_of_Mohammed_V_4.jpg/250px-Funeral_of_Mohammed_V_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Funeral_of_Mohammed_V_4.jpg)

Funeral prayer held in the Hassan Tower platform

His death was announced on national radio by his son, crown prince Moulay Hassan, who succeeded him as King [Hassan II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_II_of_Morocco "Hassan II of Morocco").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:4-32) A seven-day period of national mourning was then declared.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-34) The [state funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_funeral "State funeral") was rescheduled two days later, only to invite foreign leaders to attend. Hundreds of thousands of mourners reportedly attended, including Moroccan Jews who revered the King and saw his death as a unifying tragedy. Following a military parade, the king’s coffin was placed on a [bier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bier "Bier") in the [Royal Palace of Rabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Palace_of_Rabat "Royal Palace of Rabat") gardens for a [lying in state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lying_in_state "Lying in state"), the coffin was then loaded into a [caisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caisson_(vehicle) "Caisson (vehicle)") and transported across the capital to the [Hassan Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_Tower "Hassan Tower") platform where the [Islamic funeral prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_funeral_prayer "Islamic funeral prayer") was held.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-36)

The tomb was buried in the Royal Palace grounds until [a mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_Mohammed_V "Mausoleum of Mohammed V") was built in 1971 to accommodate his remains.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-37)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Inside_Mohammed_V_mausoleum.jpg/250px-Inside_Mohammed_V_mausoleum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Inside_Mohammed_V_mausoleum.jpg)

Tomb of Mohammed V inside [his mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_Mohammed_V "Mausoleum of Mohammed V")

The [Mohammed V International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_International_Airport "Mohammed V International Airport"), [Stade Mohammed V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_Mohammed_V "Stade Mohammed V") and [Mohammed V Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_Square "Mohammed V Square") in [Casablanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca "Casablanca"), the [Mohammed V Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_Mohammed_V,_Rabat "Avenue Mohammed V, Rabat"), [Mohammed V University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_University "Mohammed V University") and [Mohammadia School of Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammadia_School_of_Engineering "Mohammadia School of Engineering") in Rabat, the [Mohammed V Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_Mosque,_Tangier "Mohammed V Mosque, Tangier") in [Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier "Tangier"), and the [Mohammed V Foundation for Solidarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_Foundation_for_Solidarity "Mohammed V Foundation for Solidarity") are among numerous buildings, locales and institutions named after him. The mausoleum where he is buried bears the name of [Mohammed V Mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_Mohammed_V "Mausoleum of Mohammed V"). There is an Avenue Mohammed V in nearly every Moroccan city and a major one in [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"), [Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia "Tunisia"), and in [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers"), [Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria "Algeria"). The Mohammed V Palace in [Conakry, Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conakry,_Guinea "Conakry, Guinea") is named in his honour.

The [Istiqlal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istiqlal_Party "Istiqlal Party"), after his death, considered him "a universal hero as well as a national hero" and praised his "struggle to liberate Morocco, Algeria and all of Africa."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-38)

In December 2007, _[The Jewish Daily Forward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jewish\_Daily\_Forward "The Jewish Daily Forward")_ reported on a secret diplomatic initiative by the Moroccan government to have Mohammed V admitted to the [Righteous Among the Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Righteous_Among_the_Nations "Righteous Among the Nations").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-39)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/King_of_Morocco_with_members_of_his_family_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-King_of_Morocco_with_members_of_his_family_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_of_Morocco_with_members_of_his_family_(cropped).jpg)

Mohammed V with daughters Princesses Malika, Aïcha and Nuzha, and son Moulay Abdellah, c. 1950

His first wife was [Hanila bint Mamoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Hanila_bint_Mamoun "Lalla Hanila bint Mamoun"). They married in 1925.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-40)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-41) She was the mother of his first daughter [Fatima Zohra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Fatima_Zohra "Lalla Fatima Zohra").

His second wife was his first cousin [Abla bint Tahar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Abla_bint_Tahar "Lalla Abla bint Tahar"). She was the daughter of [Mohammed Tahar bin Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Tahar_bin_Hassan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mohammed Tahar bin Hassan (page does not exist)"), son of [Hassan I of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_I_of_Morocco "Hassan I of Morocco"). She married Mohammed V in 1928 and died in [Rabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabat "Rabat") on 1 March 1992. She gave birth to five children: the future King [Hassan II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_II_of_Morocco "Hassan II of Morocco"), [Aisha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Lalla_Aicha_of_Morocco "Princess Lalla Aicha of Morocco"), [Malika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Lalla_Malika_of_Morocco "Princess Lalla Malika of Morocco"), [Abdallah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Moulay_Abdallah_of_Morocco "Prince Moulay Abdallah of Morocco") and [Nuzha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Lalla_Nuzha_of_Morocco "Princess Lalla Nuzha of Morocco").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-42)

His third wife was [Bahia bint Antar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Bahia "Lalla Bahia"), with whom he had a daughter [Amina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Lalla_Amina_of_Morocco "Princess Lalla Amina of Morocco").

**Mohammed al-Khamis bin Yusef bin Hassan al-Alawi**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-1) better known simply as **Mohammed V**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-2) (10 August 1909 – 26 February 1961), was the ruler of Morocco from 1927 to 1961, except for a two-year period in exile during the 1950s. He reigned as [sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_of_Morocco "Sultan of Morocco") until 1957, and afterwards as the first [king of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Morocco "King of Morocco"). A member of the [Alawi dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alawi_dynasty "Alawi dynasty"), he played an instrumental role in restoring the independence of Morocco from the French and Spanish protectorates.

Mohammed was enthroned as sultan upon the death of his father [Yusef bin Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusef_of_Morocco "Yusef of Morocco") in 1927. Early in his reign, his approval of the [Berber Dahir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_Dahir "Berber Dahir") drew widespread backlash and spurred an upsurge of [Moroccan nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_nationalism "Moroccan nationalism") and opposition to [continued French rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_protectorate_in_Morocco "French protectorate in Morocco"). Initially more amenable to colonial authorities, Mohammed grew increasingly supportive of the nationalist movement later on. During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") he supported the [Allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II"), participated in the 1943 [Anfa Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca_Conference "Casablanca Conference") and has been widely credited with protecting [Morocco’s Jewish population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Jews "Moroccan Jews") during World War II, as he reportedly resisted [Vichy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France") efforts to impose anti-Jewish measures and deport Jews, and emphasized that all Moroccan Jews were under his protection as subjects of the crown.

Mohammed became a central figure of the independence cause after the war. In 1947, he delivered a [historic speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier_Speech "Tangier Speech") in [Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier_International_Zone "Tangier International Zone"), in which he made an open appeal for Moroccan independence and emphasized the country's ties with the rest of the [Arab world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_world "Arab world"). His relationship with the French became increasingly strained afterwards as colonial rule grew more repressive. In 1953, French authorities deposed Mohammed, exiled him to [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") (later transferring him to [Madagascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar "Madagascar")) and installed his first cousin once removed [Mohammed Ben Aarafa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Ben_Aarafa "Mohammed Ben Aarafa") as sultan. The deposition sparked active opposition to the French protectorate and two years later, faced with rising violence in Morocco, the French government allowed Mohammed's return. In 1956, he successfully negotiated with France and Spain for Moroccan independence, and in the following year he assumed the title of king. Mohammed died in 1961 at the age of 51 and was succeeded by his eldest son, who took the throne as [Hassan II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_II_of_Morocco "Hassan II of Morocco").

Mohammed is often described by historians as a moderate and unifying figure whose leadership style was marked by restraint and a generally gentle and conciliatory approach, contributing to his reputation as a widely respected and principled monarch.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Sidi Mohammed bin Yusef was born on 10 August 1909 in [Fes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fez,_Morocco "Fez, Morocco") to Sultan [Yusef of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusef_of_Morocco "Yusef of Morocco") and [Lalla Yacout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Yacout "Lalla Yacout"), and was his father's third and youngest son.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-3)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:22-4) In March 1912, the [Treaty of Fes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fes "Treaty of Fes") was signed, turning Morocco into a French protectorate after a [French invasion from the west](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardment_of_Casablanca_(1907) "Bombardment of Casablanca (1907)") and the east, resulting in an eventual capture of the capital, Fes.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Yusef was enthroned as sultan by the French in September 1912.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-5)

Sidi Mohammed began his education in Fes, inside the palace grounds of his home, _qasr al-amami_ (front palace). There he learned to read and write and received his first lessons in the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:2-6)

When his father established [Rabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabat "Rabat") as the capital of the kingdom and of the administration, he transferred Sidi Mohammed there, with most of his brothers. There, he continued his studies with private teachers. In Rabat, he continued to study [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic "Arabic") and the Quran until he became a [_hafiz_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafiz_(Quran) "Hafiz (Quran)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:2-6) He also studied [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-7) under [Mohammed Mammeri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Mammeri?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mohammed Mammeri (page does not exist)"), who gave him special attention. After he became Sultan, Mammeri remained in his service for a long time as head of protocol.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:3-8)

Sidi Mohammed then continued his education in a public school in Rabat.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:2-6)

## Reign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Reign")]

### Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early years")]

On 18 November 1927, a "young and timid" 17-year-old Muhammad bin Yusef was enthroned after the death of his father and the departure of [Hubert Lyautey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Lyautey "Hubert Lyautey").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10)

At the time of Mohammed's enthronement, the French colonial authorities were "pushing for a more assertive 'native policy.'"[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10) On 16 May 1930, Sultan Muhammad V signed the [Berber Dahir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_Dahir "Berber Dahir"), which changed the legal system in parts of Morocco where [Berber languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_languages "Berber languages") were primarily spoken (_[Bled es-Siba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bled\_es-Siba "Bled es-Siba")_), while the legal system in the rest of the country (_Bled al-Makhzen_) remained the way it had been before the [French invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_conquest_of_Morocco "French conquest of Morocco").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-11) Although the sultan was under no duress, he was then only twenty years old.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10) This [_dahir_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Dahir "Moroccan Dahir") "electrified the nation"; it was sharply criticized by [Moroccan nationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_nationalism "Moroccan nationalism") and catalyzed the [Moroccan Nationalist Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Nationalist_Movement "Moroccan Nationalist Movement").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10)

### World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: World War II")]

Sultan Mohammed participated in the [Anfa Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca_Conference "Casablanca Conference") hosted in [Casablanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca "Casablanca") during World War II.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10) On 22 January 1943, he met privately with the US president [Franklin Delano Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Delano_Roosevelt "Franklin Delano Roosevelt") and the Prime Minister of the UK [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10) At this dinner, Roosevelt assured the sultan that "the post-war scene and the pre-war scene would ... sharply differ, especially as they related to the colonial question." The sultan's 14-year-old son and future king of Morocco, Hassan II, also attended and later stated that Roosevelt said, "Ten years from now your country will be independent."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:02-10)

"There are competing accounts of exactly what Mohammed V did or did not do for the [Moroccan Jewish community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Jews "Moroccan Jews")" during [the Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Marglin-12) However, "though a subject of debate, most scholars stress the benevolence of Mohammed V toward the Jews" during the [Vichy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France") era.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-13) Mohammed reportedly refused to sign off on efforts by Vichy officials to impose [anti-Jewish legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_anti-Jewish_legislation "Vichy anti-Jewish legislation") upon Morocco and deport the country's 250,000 Jews to their deaths in [Nazi concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_concentration_camp "Nazi concentration camp") and [extermination camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extermination_camp "Extermination camp") in Europe. The sultan's stand was "based as much on the insult the Vichy _[diktats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diktat "Diktat")_ posed to his claim of sovereignty over all his subjects, including the Jews, as on his humanitarian instincts." Partial Nazi race measures were enacted in Morocco over Mohammed's objection,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Miller-14) and Mohammed did sign, under the instructions of Vichy officials, two decrees that barred Jews from certain schools and positions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Bouasria-15)

Nevertheless, Mohammed is highly esteemed by Moroccan Jews who credit him for protecting their community from [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") and the Vichy French government,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Marglin-12) and he has been honored by Jewish organizations for his role in protecting his Jewish subjects during the Holocaust.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-16) Some historians maintain that Mohammed's anti-Nazi role has been exaggerated; historian [Michel Abitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Abitol "Michel Abitol") writes that while Mohammed was compelled by Vichy officials to sign the anti-Jewish dahirs, "he was more passive than [Moncef Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_VII_al-Munsif "Muhammad VII al-Munsif") ([ruler of Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Beys_of_Tunis "List of Beys of Tunis") during the Second World War) in that he did not take any side and did not engage in any public act that could be interpreted as a rejection of Vichy's policy."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Bouasria-15)

### Struggle for independence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Struggle for independence")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Editing_File-Franklin_D._Roosevelt%2C_Winston_Churchill%2C_Mohammed_V_and_Hassan_II_at_the_Casablanca_Conference.jpg/250px-Editing_File-Franklin_D._Roosevelt%2C_Winston_Churchill%2C_Mohammed_V_and_Hassan_II_at_the_Casablanca_Conference.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Editing_File-Franklin_D._Roosevelt,_Winston_Churchill,_Mohammed_V_and_Hassan_II_at_the_Casablanca_Conference.jpg)

Sultan Mohammed seated with [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") and [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill") during the 1943 [Casablanca Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca_Conference "Casablanca Conference"); his son [Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_II_of_Morocco "Hassan II of Morocco") is pictured standing behind him.

Sultan Mohammad was a central figure in the independence movement in Morocco, also known as the [Revolution of the King and the People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolution_of_the_King_and_the_People "Revolution of the King and the People") (ثورة الملك والشعب). The [Moroccan Nationalist Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Nationalist_Movement "Moroccan Nationalist Movement") grew from protests regarding the [Berber Dahir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_Dahir "Berber Dahir") of 16 May 1930. He was critical of early movements for reform in French colonial administration in Morocco before becoming a supporter of independence later on.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-17)

His central position in the [Proclamation of Independence of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_Independence_of_Morocco "Proclamation of Independence of Morocco") further boosted his image as a national symbol. On 9 and 10 April 1947, he delivered two momentous speeches respectively at the [Mendoubia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendoubia "Mendoubia") and [Grand Mosque of Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_of_Tangier "Grand Mosque of Tangier"), together known as the [Tangier Speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier_Speech "Tangier Speech"), appealing for the independence of Morocco without calling out specific colonial powers.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-18)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-19)

In 1947, the rapid progress of the nationalist movement prompted Sidi Mohammed to demand independence for the first time during the [Tangier speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier_Speech "Tangier Speech"), where he also called for the union of the Arabs and Morocco's membership of the [Arab League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_League "Arab League") which was founded in 1945, in which he praised, emphasized the close ties between Morocco and the rest of the [Arab world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_world "Arab world"). This rapprochement between the monarchy and the nationalist movement, whose projects differ, can be explained, according to historian Bernard Cubertafond, by the fact that "each side needs the other: the national movement sees the growing popularity of the king and his prudent but gradual emancipation from a protector who, in fact, left the treaty of 1912 to come to direct administration; the king cannot, except to discredit himself, cut himself off from a nationalist movement bringing together the living forces of his country and the elite of his youth, and he needs this power of protest to impose changes on France”.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:1-20)

From then on, relations became strained with the French authorities, in particular with the new Resident General, General [Alphonse Juin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Juin "Alphonse Juin"), who applied severe measures and pressured the sultan to disavow the Istiqlal and distance himself from nationalist claims. The break with France was consummated in 1951 and Mohammed formed a pact with the nationalists in Tangier to fight for independence. The appointment of a new Resident General, General [Augustin Guillaume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustin_Guillaume "Augustin Guillaume"), accentuated the dissension between Mohammed and France. Further demonstrations in Morocco culminated in riots in 1952, notably in Casablanca, and Mohammed addressed the United Nations to publicize the Moroccan cause with the support of the United States.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:1-20)

### Deposition and exile

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Deposition and exile")]

On 20 August 1953 (the eve of [Eid al-Adha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eid_al-Adha "Eid al-Adha")), the [French colonial authorities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_French_residents-general_in_Morocco "List of French residents-general in Morocco") forced Mohammed V, an important national symbol in the growing Moroccan independence movement, into exile in [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") along with his family. His first cousin once removed, [Mohammed Ben Aarafa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Ben_Aarafa "Mohammed Ben Aarafa"), called the "French sultan," was made a [puppet monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppet_monarch "Puppet monarch") and placed on the throne. In response, [Muhammad Zarqtuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Zarqtuni "Muhammad Zarqtuni") bombed Casablanca's [Central Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Market_(Casablanca) "Central Market (Casablanca)") on Christmas Eve of that year.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:0-21)

Mohammed and his family were then transferred to [Madagascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar "Madagascar") in January 1954. Mohammed returned from exile on 16 November 1955, and was again recognized as Sultan after active opposition to the French protectorate. His triumphant return was for many the sign of the end of the colonial era.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-22) The situation became so tense that in 1955, the Moroccan nationalists, who enjoyed support in [Libya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Libya "Kingdom of Libya"), [Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria "Algeria") (with the [FLN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Liberation_Front_(Algeria) "National Liberation Front (Algeria)")) and [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Egypt_under_Gamal_Abdel_Nasser#Republic_of_Egypt_(1953%E2%80%931958) "History of Egypt under Gamal Abdel Nasser") forced the French government to negotiate and recall the sultan. In February 1956 he successfully negotiated with [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and Spain for the independence of Morocco.

### After independence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: After independence")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Sultan_Mohammed_V_on_TIME_Magazine%2C_April_22%2C_1957.jpg/250px-Sultan_Mohammed_V_on_TIME_Magazine%2C_April_22%2C_1957.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sultan_Mohammed_V_on_TIME_Magazine,_April_22,_1957.jpg)

On the [cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_covers_of_Time_magazine_(1950s)#1957 "List of covers of Time magazine (1950s)") of [_Time_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)"), 22 April 1957

Mohammed supported the Algerian [National Liberation Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Liberation_Front_(Algeria) "National Liberation Front (Algeria)") (FLN) in the struggle for Algerian Independence and offered to facilitate the participation of FLN leaders in a conference with [Habib Bourguiba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habib_Bourguiba "Habib Bourguiba") in Tunis.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:032-23) On October 22, 1956, [French forces hijacked a Moroccan airplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_hijacking_of_Moroccan_plane "French hijacking of Moroccan plane") carrying leaders of the FLN during the ongoing [Algerian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algerian_War "Algerian War").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:032-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:142-25) The plane, which was carrying [Ahmed Ben Bella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_Ben_Bella "Ahmed Ben Bella"), [Hocine Aït Ahmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hocine_A%C3%AFt_Ahmed "Hocine Aït Ahmed"), and [Mohamed Boudiaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Boudiaf "Mohamed Boudiaf"), was destined to leave from [Palma de Mallorca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palma_de_Mallorca "Palma de Mallorca") for [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"), but French forces redirected the flight to occupied [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers"), where the FLN leaders were arrested.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:032-23)

In 1957, he took the title of [king of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Morocco "King of Morocco"), to symbolise the unity of the country despite divisions between [Arabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs") and [Berbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbers "Berbers"). In terms of domestic policy, upon his return he allowed the first congress of the [Istiqlal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istiqlal_Party "Istiqlal Party"), which formed various governments under his reign. He authorized the creation of trade unions, but the unrest and the strikes lead him to take full power in the last years of his reign.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:1-20) His state visit to the United States later that year "strengthened his position as the kingdom's sole legitimate representative". This way he managed to replace the members of the nationalist movement on the global stage and turned his trip into a great publicity success. This visit marked a strategic effort to align Morocco closely with the US, showcasing the monarchy's importance on the global stage. He used various techniques to project the royal authority, such as personally thanking the nationalist movement's former supporters in the name of the Moroccan people.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-Globalizing_Morocco_:_transnational-26) Mohammed also acted as patron to the _International Meetings_, conferences on contemporary issues and interfaith dialogue hosted at the [Benedictine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedictines "Benedictines")[monastery of Toumliline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastery_of_Toumliline "Monastery of Toumliline") that attracted scholars and intellectuals from all over the world.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-27)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Gamal_Abdel_Nasser_in_Morocco.jpg/250px-Gamal_Abdel_Nasser_in_Morocco.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gamal_Abdel_Nasser_in_Morocco.jpg)

Mohamed V receiving Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser in Casablanca, 1961

During his reign, the [Moroccan Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Army_of_Liberation "Moroccan Army of Liberation") waged [war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ifni_War "Ifni War") against Spain and France, and successfully captured most of [Ifni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ifni "Ifni") as well as [Cape Juby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Juby "Cape Juby") and parts of [Spanish Sahara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Sahara "Spanish Sahara"). With the [treaty of Angra de Cintra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Angra_de_Cintra "Treaty of Angra de Cintra"), Morocco annexed [Cape Juby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Juby "Cape Juby") and the surroundings of [Ifni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ifni "Ifni"), while the rest of the remaining colony was ceded by Spain in 1969.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-28)

## Illness and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Illness and death")]

In the final years of his life, Mohammed suffered from an ear illness for which doctors advised him to undergo a [tonsillectomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonsillectomy "Tonsillectomy") in August 1959.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-29) On 26 February 1961, Mohammed underwent a second banal surgery on the [nasal septum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_septum "Nasal septum") in relation to his illness, conducted by a surgeon from [Lausanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lausanne "Lausanne"). Shortly after the operation was completed, Mohammed suffered a fatal cardiac arrest resulting from complications of the surgery.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-30)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:4-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-33)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Funeral_of_Mohammed_V_4.jpg/250px-Funeral_of_Mohammed_V_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Funeral_of_Mohammed_V_4.jpg)

Funeral prayer held in the Hassan Tower platform

His death was announced on national radio by his son, crown prince Moulay Hassan, who succeeded him as King [Hassan II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_II_of_Morocco "Hassan II of Morocco").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-:4-32) A seven-day period of national mourning was then declared.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-34) The [state funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_funeral "State funeral") was rescheduled two days later, only to invite foreign leaders to attend. Hundreds of thousands of mourners reportedly attended, including Moroccan Jews who revered the King and saw his death as a unifying tragedy. Following a military parade, the king’s coffin was placed on a [bier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bier "Bier") in the [Royal Palace of Rabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Palace_of_Rabat "Royal Palace of Rabat") gardens for a [lying in state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lying_in_state "Lying in state"), the coffin was then loaded into a [caisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caisson_(vehicle) "Caisson (vehicle)") and transported across the capital to the [Hassan Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_Tower "Hassan Tower") platform where the [Islamic funeral prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_funeral_prayer "Islamic funeral prayer") was held.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-36)

The tomb was buried in the Royal Palace grounds until [a mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_Mohammed_V "Mausoleum of Mohammed V") was built in 1971 to accommodate his remains.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-37)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Inside_Mohammed_V_mausoleum.jpg/250px-Inside_Mohammed_V_mausoleum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Inside_Mohammed_V_mausoleum.jpg)

Tomb of Mohammed V inside [his mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_Mohammed_V "Mausoleum of Mohammed V")

The [Mohammed V International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_International_Airport "Mohammed V International Airport"), [Stade Mohammed V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_Mohammed_V "Stade Mohammed V") and [Mohammed V Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_Square "Mohammed V Square") in [Casablanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca "Casablanca"), the [Mohammed V Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_Mohammed_V,_Rabat "Avenue Mohammed V, Rabat"), [Mohammed V University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_University "Mohammed V University") and [Mohammadia School of Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammadia_School_of_Engineering "Mohammadia School of Engineering") in Rabat, the [Mohammed V Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_Mosque,_Tangier "Mohammed V Mosque, Tangier") in [Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier "Tangier"), and the [Mohammed V Foundation for Solidarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_Foundation_for_Solidarity "Mohammed V Foundation for Solidarity") are among numerous buildings, locales and institutions named after him. The mausoleum where he is buried bears the name of [Mohammed V Mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_Mohammed_V "Mausoleum of Mohammed V"). There is an Avenue Mohammed V in nearly every Moroccan city and a major one in [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"), [Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia "Tunisia"), and in [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers"), [Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria "Algeria"). The Mohammed V Palace in [Conakry, Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conakry,_Guinea "Conakry, Guinea") is named in his honour.

The [Istiqlal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istiqlal_Party "Istiqlal Party"), after his death, considered him "a universal hero as well as a national hero" and praised his "struggle to liberate Morocco, Algeria and all of Africa."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-38)

In December 2007, _[The Jewish Daily Forward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jewish\_Daily\_Forward "The Jewish Daily Forward")_ reported on a secret diplomatic initiative by the Moroccan government to have Mohammed V admitted to the [Righteous Among the Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Righteous_Among_the_Nations "Righteous Among the Nations").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-39)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_V_of_Morocco&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/King_of_Morocco_with_members_of_his_family_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-King_of_Morocco_with_members_of_his_family_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_of_Morocco_with_members_of_his_family_(cropped).jpg)

Mohammed V with daughters Princesses Malika, Aïcha and Nuzha, and son Moulay Abdellah, c. 1950

His first wife was [Hanila bint Mamoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Hanila_bint_Mamoun "Lalla Hanila bint Mamoun"). They married in 1925.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-40)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-41) She was the mother of his first daughter [Fatima Zohra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Fatima_Zohra "Lalla Fatima Zohra").

His second wife was his first cousin [Abla bint Tahar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Abla_bint_Tahar "Lalla Abla bint Tahar"). She was the daughter of [Mohammed Tahar bin Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Tahar_bin_Hassan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mohammed Tahar bin Hassan (page does not exist)"), son of [Hassan I of Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_I_of_Morocco "Hassan I of Morocco"). She married Mohammed V in 1928 and died in [Rabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabat "Rabat") on 1 March 1992. She gave birth to five children: the future King [Hassan II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_II_of_Morocco "Hassan II of Morocco"), [Aisha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Lalla_Aicha_of_Morocco "Princess Lalla Aicha of Morocco"), [Malika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Lalla_Malika_of_Morocco "Princess Lalla Malika of Morocco"), [Abdallah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Moulay_Abdallah_of_Morocco "Prince Moulay Abdallah of Morocco") and [Nuzha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Lalla_Nuzha_of_Morocco "Princess Lalla Nuzha of Morocco").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_V_of_Morocco#cite_note-42)

His third wife was [Bahia bint Antar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalla_Bahia "Lalla Bahia"), with whom he had a daughter [Amina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Lalla_Amina_of_Morocco "Princess Lalla Amina of Morocco").
