### Abstract

This paper aims to investigate Gamal Abdel Nasser’s 1967 stepping down speech using Fairclough’s [1] model of critical discourse analysis. The paper focuses on the dimension of text, which contains lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors. The analysis shows how Abdel Nasser employs all of these linguistic tools to his favor and shows a thematic use of the lexical items. Also, the analysis exhibits the use of rhetorical devices such as euphemism, which serves as a means of mitigating the intensity of the situation. Other rhetorical devices include dysphemism, digression, and rhetorical questions. Metaphors are used to describe the defeat, to glorify the revolution, or to describe the sacrifices of the fallen soldiers on the battlefield. This study is limited to the dimension of text; therefore, recommendations are due for further analysis that includes all the dimensions of Fairclough's [1] model.

**Keywords:**[critical discourse analysis](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=critical%20discourse%20analysis)[text](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=text)[lexical items](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=lexical%20items)[rhetoric](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=rhetoric)[and metaphors](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=and%20metaphors)

### 1. Introduction

To present a comprehensible analysis of Abdel Nasser’s speech, it is essential to have a closer look into the audience who has received it. A great way to do so is by looking at the society and the political waves that spread at the time of the war and after the defeat, or what Abdel Nasser has promoted as ‘al-Naksa’. Dr. Sadik Jalal al-Azm 2 introduces in his book _Self-Criticism After the Defeat_ a subjective image of the Arab nation and the mainstream notions that spread before and during the war. Al-Azm claims that prior to declaring the war, the public masses of Arab countries have taken a stand pro-war, and have supported Abdel Nasser as the new hero that will lead Arabs into victory. He mentions the glorification and aggrandizement of Abdel Nasser as a leader, and Egypt as an invincible military force, and argues that this exaggeration is an irreverence of the enemy's strength and is, therefore, one of the reasons that lead to defeat. On that matter, Al-Azm refers to what Mohammed Hasanin Haikal has written back on June 2 nd, 1967 -a few days prior to declaring war- in Al-Ahram newspaper. Haikal states that whatever happens, and without anticipation, Israel is about to collapse from the inside and the outside (2, para. 2-3).

With this in mind, and with the image of the audience that has been emotionally charged with dreams of pan-Arabism, it is hard to imagine the state of mind and heart that these people have gone through when they have had to face the defeat. Al-Azm mentions the state of denial that overshadows all Arab countries after the defeat, and documents a specific incidence with the Lebanese journalist Mohsen Ibrahim, in Al-Hureyya magazine back on June 14 th 1967, where he denies the defeat by a headline that says “kallā lam yuḫṭiʾ ʿabdel Nasser w lam yuhzam al-ʿrab”, which is roughly translated to: “No, Abdel Nasser did not make a mistake, and the Arab did not lose” (2, forward). Another case of this denial is what Mohammed Saeed Tayeb -a Saudi activist- remembers about the war, he mentions that between the 6 th and 9 th of June, western radio stations have been talking about the defeat, while Sawt Al-Arab (Egyptian radio station) talks about the victory 3.

Moreover, the geographical face of the Arab countries changes with this defeat, and Israel succeeds to occupy Sinai Peninsula, The Golan Heights, and the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and Gaza strip 3. Still, with all the disappointment, denial, and anger, Abdel Nasser manages to lure the public out to the streets to cheer him on and encourage him to stay in his position as a president of Egypt and a leader to the Arabs. He manages to do that with his speech and his linguistic intuition.

### 2. Significance of the Study

The incredible response to Abdel Nasser's speech is what makes this discourse critical and of importance. Abdel Nasser is completely responsible for the 1967's defeat and is also responsible for losing Sinai Peninsula, the Golan Heights, and the West Bank. However, people have flooded into the streets asking him to retreat from stepping down after he gives his speech. The speech and Abdel Nasser's deceiving charisma are essential factors in the construction of the audience's reaction. This agrees with Diong’s 4 views on the importance of the rhetorical devices that Abdel Nasser uses. Moreover, Diong acknowledges the importance of Sawt Al-Arab (the radio station) in endorsing Abdel Nasser’s ideologies before, during, and after 1967. Despite the thorough analysis, Diong does not analyze the lexical items of this discourse, which this paper attempts to do.

Al-Ahmad 5 describes the language Abdel Nasser uses and explains the shift between sympathy and aggression in all of his speeches. This is also applicable to this speech, in which Abdel Nasser talks about the enemy in an aggressive and strong language. He uses a language that can be described as propitiated when he talks about himself and his role in the war. Equally of importance is Abdel Latif's 6 views in his linguistic analysis of Abdel Nasser’s speech in which he indicates the reason behind the response it receives. However, to the best of the researcher's knowledge, this paper is the first to use Fairclough's 1 model of critical discourse analysis to analyze Abdel Nasser's speech.

### 3. Research Objectives

This research aims to investigate Gamal Abdel Nasser’s 1967 stepping down speech using Fairclough’s 1 model of critical discourse analysis. The focus of the paper will be on the text level, including the analysis of lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors.

### 4. Research Questions

1. What is the nature of the lexical items used in the speech?

2. Which rhetorical devices does Abdel Nasser use in his speech?

3. In which contexts have metaphors been used in the speech?

### 5. Review of Literature

**5.1. Critical Discourse Analysis**
Fairclough 7 sets primary characteristics of critical discourse analysis (CDA) to establish the dimensions in which CDA operates. First, CDA is not just an analysis of a text or a discourse, it is the practice of linking the analysis to social processes. Second, it needs to be a systematic analysis, not just a commentary. Last but not least, CDA “is not just descriptive, it is also normative. It addresses social wrongs in their discursive aspects and possible ways of righting or mitigating them” (11). Withdrawing from that, Gee 8 explains the two tasks of any discourse analysis, one examines meaning and the other one examines situated meaning. The first one as Gee puts it, is what he calls utterance-type meaning task, which studies the links between form (words, phrases, morphemes, and syntactic structure) and function which is the meaning or the communicative purpose (24). The other task is utterance-token meaning, which is concerned with the link between form and meaning in the framework of situation. Simply put, in utterance-token meaning studies analysis, the analyst needs to discover the situations and contexts surrounding the utterance in order to decode the actual meaning. Gee emphasizes the importance of differentiating between these two tasks, to conduct a valid analysis.

Fairclough 1 creates a model of discourse analysis that depends on three basic dimensions of analysis; text, discursive practice, and social practice. Fairclough insists on the absence of a clear division between these three dimensions, because of the overlapping nature of all three features. Text as an analytical tool focuses on the linguistic features of any discourse and urges to describe and analyze lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors before delving into the other two dimensions. The second dimension focuses on the shared knowledge between the producer of the discourse and the audience receiving it. To take a close look into the discursive practice of the discourse, we look at the shared knowledge, intertextuality, and the production of the discourse in question and how the audience receives and comprehends it. The third dimension is the social practice, which looks into the several social statuses in a society, the social identities, ideologies, hegemony, and the social relationship between the producer of the discourse and the audience (Fairclough 1, 62-100).

**5.2. Political Discourse**
Wilson 9 differentiates between two types of political discourse. The first one focuses on political discourse that has an authentic association to politics, and the second type -which he withdraws from Shapiro 10- that claims all discourse as political regardless of its actual relation to political content or context. Wilson suggests that this confusion stems from the fact that the conditions upon which any discourse is considered political are very common in most of the discourses; these conditions involve power, control, conflict, or dominance. However, this broad definition of political discourse is not practical in the field of linguistics, which is why Wilson resorts to limiting the definition of political discourse into formal and informal political context and political actors, i.e. “politicians, political institutions, governments, political media, and political supporters operating in political environments to achieve political goals” (398).

Moreover, Wilson refers to Orwell’s 11 remarks on political discourse, and to the way politicians formulate language to deliver more peaceful and acceptable messages. For instance, he refers to the use of ‘pacification’ instead of ‘invasion’, which politicians use to mask the horrors and hostilities of invasions. The issue that presents itself here is the manipulation of language that blinds the masses to the negativity that might surround them, which is the case in every political statement or speech, and Abdel Nasser’s speeches are no exception.

Wilson acknowledges the essential ties between linguistics and socio-politics and highlights the efforts in combining both in any political discourse analysis. He insists to focus on the language as the main tool of analysis, and still manages to emphasize the importance of sociopolitical analysis claiming the language-based analysis do not consider answering ‘why’; why does this politician arrange his sentences in this manner, or what formulates his word choices? and so on.

**5.3. Previous Studies**
Bajri and Othman 12 conduct a comparative critical discourse analysis of Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech ‘I have a Dream’ and Malcolm X's speech ‘A Message to the Grassroots’. They use Fairclough's 3D model to deconstruct both discourses into their basic features, and divide the analysis into three major headlines; text, discursive practice, and social practice. Under each headline, a few other sublines talking specifically about certain features that fall under the headlines. For example, headline: text, subline: lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors. Bajri and Othman highlight the importance of the devices in both speeches -especially rhetorical-, and conclude on the importance of style in changing societies and perspectives, and point to the massive change that these discourses have inflected.

Equally as important is the work of Lahlali 13, in which he touches on pan-Arabism in Abdel Nasser’s speeches. According to Lahlali, Abdel Nasser uses words like ‘Arab unity’ and ‘Arab values’ to promote for pan-Arabism in order to gain support for his image as a leader of the Arab nation. Lahlali suggests that with his charisma and mastery of the Arabic language, Abdel Nasser manages to make the audience across Arab countries feel like one family. This mirrors what Diong 4 notices of Abdel Nasser's rhetoric techniques, whereby she asserts the importance of Abdel Nasser's word choices in the broadcasting of his propaganda and ideology. She states that the word choices “[are] made specifically to target the West and to spread anti-colonial sentiments amongst those who heard his speeches” (4). Diong withdraws from Al-Ahmed's 5 study that discusses Abdel Nasser’s use of language, in which Al-Ahmad states that his language has had waves of sympathy and aggression.

### 6. Methodology

**6.1. Theoretical Framework**
This paper utilizes Fairclough’s 1 model of critical discourse analysis to investigate Gamal Abdel Nasser’s 1967 speech.

**6.2. Data Collection**
The paper will analyze Gamal Abdel Nasser's stepping down speech, which has been delivered on June 9 th, 1967 through Sawt Al-Arab radio station from his office in Kubbeh palace in Cairo. The text has been retrieved from an online source dedicated to all of Abdel Nasser’s speeches.

**6.3. Data Analysis**
To analyze the data, application and discussion section will focus on the first dimension of Fairclough’s 1 3D model, which is text. Under text umbrella falls three subcategories; lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors.

### 7. Application and Discussion

**7.1. Text**  
**7.1.1. Lexical Items**
Linguistic etiquette -according to Allan and Burridge 14- is used in implicit and indirect discourse and is found in our everyday speech. It includes “euphemism, swearing, polite talk, slang and political correctness", and it gives an indication of the speaker's attitude and intentions. Furthermore, linguistic etiquette -specifically talking about euphemism here- is a way of leveling the message, and delivering by masking the negativity in it 14.

Euphemism occurs repeatedly in Abdel Nasser’s stepping down speech. He mentions the word ‘al-naksa’ which is translated to ‘the setback’ four times, serving as a substitute for the word ‘defeat’. This word, in particular, is what frees Abdel Nasser from any consequences following his action that lead to the war and to losing the war.

As shown in Table 1, Abdel Nasser's speech is thematic; words reoccur in different synonyms and different stems from the same root. The main themes that appear in the speech are as follows:

1- Brotherhood: This theme is assembled in the word ‘brothers’ reoccurs many times in the speech to spread a feeling of intimacy and closeness among the audience.

2- Nationalism: As previously mentioned in the literature review, Pan-Arabism and the ideology of the Arab nation is heavily pushed in all of Abdel Nasser's speeches. In fact, Abdel Nasser himself mentions this ideology inflection in this very particular speech, wherein he states that the opposing forces of pan-Arabism talk about it as if it is Abdel Nasser's own empire -which he denies.

3- Togetherness and Honesty: Again, this speech is loaded with intimate words that Abdel Nasser tucks in, to draw a friendly, warm, and informal image. He uses his words to paint an image of himself and the public sitting ‘together’ and talking ‘together’, and getting accustomed to being honest ‘together’. He talks about ‘open hearts’ and ‘professing the truth’, which help him create an atmosphere of trust and closeness among his audience.

4- Righteousness: As a person who is responsible for the upsetting defeat, Abdel Nasser insists that his path is the right path, and his choice is the right choice. He mentions ‘victory’ and ‘righteous road’ as if the defeat is a natural catastrophe that happens despite all forces. Which is what Al-Azm 2 builds his argument around. Al-Azm claims that when Abdel Nasser uses the word of ‘al-naksa’ instead of defeat, he means to strip himself of any responsibility and to throw this defeat on the worlds' shoulders (2, forward)

5- Courage and Arab values: Abdel Nasser mentions a few traits that all Arabs value, such as ‘courage’, ‘honor’, ‘pride’, and ‘manliness’. These are a few traits that are deeply rooted in the psychology and history of Arabs. Abdel Nasser emphasizes on these word choices to be connect more with his audience; Arabs all over the world.

8- Revolution: ‘Revolution’ is Abdel Nasser’s background and validation. It is how he has come into power, and it is how he gains authority, so it is not strange that he mentions it for validity in almost all of his speeches. In this discourse, Abdel Nasser mentions ‘revolution’ in the context of achievements. He advertises for himself through the accomplishments of the revolution. He states that the revolution -represented in his own persona- has evacuated colonialism, brought independence to Egypt, defined Egypt’s Arabic character, retrieved the Suez channel, built the High Dam, and used petroleum resources. This is a short version of the long list that Abdel Nasser mentions in his speech as achievements of the revolution. Moreover, he asserts in every other sentence that these achievements have come after a long time of waiting. Abdel Nasser, being a communist, is proud in his speech that he has brought communism into Egypt and established its grounds.

9- Unity: Assertion on unity –‘Arabs unity’ and ‘Egyptians unity’- is another recurrent theme in the speech. In which Abdel Nasser manages to include all Arabs when the context revolves around the nation and manages to include all spectrums of society when the context revolves around Egypt.

  
**7.1.2. Rhetorical Devices**
The first rhetorical device in this discourse is ‘euphemism’ as mentioned in the previous section. On that matter, Abdel Latif 6 comments that the use of the word ‘al-naksa’ as an alternative for defeat comes of important significance. This is because Abdel Nasser and the while Egyptian media devices have promoted victory before and during the war, and the use of any words that indicate loss will harm his image (152). Abdel Latif mentions another rhetoric device in the speech, which is ‘dysphemism’. Examples for that is when Abdul Nasser uses the word ‘aggression’ instead of words like ‘invasion’, ‘occupation’, and ‘war’ to further emphasize the injustice and vices of the enemy (154).

Another rhetorical device is ‘digression’, which is heavily used in the discourse at hand. According to Shahatah 15, ‘digression’ is of important significance in Arabic rhetoric because it is used by highly fluent people, and it is used as a sudden and surprising element. This style stimulates the receiver and charges his senses into paying closer attention to what is being said (3119). The following table contains a few examples of this rhetorical device.

Rhetorical questions are another style that Abdel Nasser uses in his speech. A rhetorical question, according to Harris 16 is a question that does not need answering, because the answer is self-evident, and it is usually implied in the question itself (171). An example of this is Abdel Nasser’s question: “Does this mean that we have no responsibility for the consequences of this setback?”, in which the answer is implied in the question so he does not need to assert on it.

  
**7.1.3. Metaphors**
Abdel Nasser's speech does not carry a lot of metaphors, perhaps for the urgency of the matter, and the hardships that accompany the topic. However, it is not totally empty of metaphors, and the first metaphor is ‘no matter how dim the light is’, which comes in the context where Abdel Nasser talks about the defeat. The other metaphors serve as eloquent style employed to tackle emotions like the metaphors that talks about the achievements of the revolution. For example, ‘an individual is a tool in the hands of popular will’, and the High Dam was built to spread fertile greenery over the desert’. He also uses metaphors to talk about the fallen soldiers, e.g. ‘glorious tournaments written by officers and soldiers of our armed forces with their blood’, and these tournaments ‘will remain a torch of light intact in our history’, along with: soldiers ‘defended the grains of sand in the desert to the last drop of their blood’.

### 8. Conclusion

The analysis shows the linguistic tools that Abdel Nasser uses in his speech on the text level. The nature of the lexical items he uses can be distributed into themes; brotherhood, nationalism -to assert on Pan-Arabism-, togetherness, and honesty - a tool to gain sympathetic reactions-, righteousness -to endorse his image as a leader-, courage and Arab values -to relate to all the masses in Arab countries using their values and identity-, revolution, and unity. The analysis also focuses on rhetorical devices and finds the main devices Abdel Nasser uses, such as euphemism, dysphemism, digression, and rhetorical questions. Some of these are used to mitigate the intensity of the defeat or magnify the enemy's responsibilities for what has happened, and the other devices are used to strengthen the speech. Regarding metaphors, the speech is not heavily loaded, but it contains some metaphors that serve as a tool to tackle emotions like the metaphors that talks about the achievements of the revolution. Other metaphors are used to describe the sacrifices and heroism of the fallen soldiers on the battlefield. All of these linguistic tools are of essence to Abdel Nasser to turn the tables in his favor. These tools are a part of the reasons why people have flooded into the streets to cheer for him despite his failure and despite the aftermath of this defeat. With that in mind, this analysis although thorough is not complete yet, since it does not cover the other dimensions of Fairclough’s 1 model, which are discursive and social practices. This limitation is due to the lack of time, but further study will be conducted to cover the rest of the dimensions.

### Abstract

This paper aims to investigate Gamal Abdel Nasser’s 1967 stepping down speech using Fairclough’s [1] model of critical discourse analysis. The paper focuses on the dimension of text, which contains lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors. The analysis shows how Abdel Nasser employs all of these linguistic tools to his favor and shows a thematic use of the lexical items. Also, the analysis exhibits the use of rhetorical devices such as euphemism, which serves as a means of mitigating the intensity of the situation. Other rhetorical devices include dysphemism, digression, and rhetorical questions. Metaphors are used to describe the defeat, to glorify the revolution, or to describe the sacrifices of the fallen soldiers on the battlefield. This study is limited to the dimension of text; therefore, recommendations are due for further analysis that includes all the dimensions of Fairclough's [1] model.

**Keywords:**[critical discourse analysis](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=critical%20discourse%20analysis)[text](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=text)[lexical items](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=lexical%20items)[rhetoric](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=rhetoric)[and metaphors](http://www.sciepub.com/portal/search?q=and%20metaphors)

### 1. Introduction

To present a comprehensible analysis of Abdel Nasser’s speech, it is essential to have a closer look into the audience who has received it. A great way to do so is by looking at the society and the political waves that spread at the time of the war and after the defeat, or what Abdel Nasser has promoted as ‘al-Naksa’. Dr. Sadik Jalal al-Azm 2 introduces in his book _Self-Criticism After the Defeat_ a subjective image of the Arab nation and the mainstream notions that spread before and during the war. Al-Azm claims that prior to declaring the war, the public masses of Arab countries have taken a stand pro-war, and have supported Abdel Nasser as the new hero that will lead Arabs into victory. He mentions the glorification and aggrandizement of Abdel Nasser as a leader, and Egypt as an invincible military force, and argues that this exaggeration is an irreverence of the enemy's strength and is, therefore, one of the reasons that lead to defeat. On that matter, Al-Azm refers to what Mohammed Hasanin Haikal has written back on June 2 nd, 1967 -a few days prior to declaring war- in Al-Ahram newspaper. Haikal states that whatever happens, and without anticipation, Israel is about to collapse from the inside and the outside (2, para. 2-3).

With this in mind, and with the image of the audience that has been emotionally charged with dreams of pan-Arabism, it is hard to imagine the state of mind and heart that these people have gone through when they have had to face the defeat. Al-Azm mentions the state of denial that overshadows all Arab countries after the defeat, and documents a specific incidence with the Lebanese journalist Mohsen Ibrahim, in Al-Hureyya magazine back on June 14 th 1967, where he denies the defeat by a headline that says “kallā lam yuḫṭiʾ ʿabdel Nasser w lam yuhzam al-ʿrab”, which is roughly translated to: “No, Abdel Nasser did not make a mistake, and the Arab did not lose” (2, forward). Another case of this denial is what Mohammed Saeed Tayeb -a Saudi activist- remembers about the war, he mentions that between the 6 th and 9 th of June, western radio stations have been talking about the defeat, while Sawt Al-Arab (Egyptian radio station) talks about the victory 3.

Moreover, the geographical face of the Arab countries changes with this defeat, and Israel succeeds to occupy Sinai Peninsula, The Golan Heights, and the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and Gaza strip 3. Still, with all the disappointment, denial, and anger, Abdel Nasser manages to lure the public out to the streets to cheer him on and encourage him to stay in his position as a president of Egypt and a leader to the Arabs. He manages to do that with his speech and his linguistic intuition.

### 2. Significance of the Study

The incredible response to Abdel Nasser's speech is what makes this discourse critical and of importance. Abdel Nasser is completely responsible for the 1967's defeat and is also responsible for losing Sinai Peninsula, the Golan Heights, and the West Bank. However, people have flooded into the streets asking him to retreat from stepping down after he gives his speech. The speech and Abdel Nasser's deceiving charisma are essential factors in the construction of the audience's reaction. This agrees with Diong’s 4 views on the importance of the rhetorical devices that Abdel Nasser uses. Moreover, Diong acknowledges the importance of Sawt Al-Arab (the radio station) in endorsing Abdel Nasser’s ideologies before, during, and after 1967. Despite the thorough analysis, Diong does not analyze the lexical items of this discourse, which this paper attempts to do.

Al-Ahmad 5 describes the language Abdel Nasser uses and explains the shift between sympathy and aggression in all of his speeches. This is also applicable to this speech, in which Abdel Nasser talks about the enemy in an aggressive and strong language. He uses a language that can be described as propitiated when he talks about himself and his role in the war. Equally of importance is Abdel Latif's 6 views in his linguistic analysis of Abdel Nasser’s speech in which he indicates the reason behind the response it receives. However, to the best of the researcher's knowledge, this paper is the first to use Fairclough's 1 model of critical discourse analysis to analyze Abdel Nasser's speech.

### 3. Research Objectives

This research aims to investigate Gamal Abdel Nasser’s 1967 stepping down speech using Fairclough’s 1 model of critical discourse analysis. The focus of the paper will be on the text level, including the analysis of lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors.

### 4. Research Questions

1. What is the nature of the lexical items used in the speech?

2. Which rhetorical devices does Abdel Nasser use in his speech?

3. In which contexts have metaphors been used in the speech?

### 5. Review of Literature

**5.1. Critical Discourse Analysis**
Fairclough 7 sets primary characteristics of critical discourse analysis (CDA) to establish the dimensions in which CDA operates. First, CDA is not just an analysis of a text or a discourse, it is the practice of linking the analysis to social processes. Second, it needs to be a systematic analysis, not just a commentary. Last but not least, CDA “is not just descriptive, it is also normative. It addresses social wrongs in their discursive aspects and possible ways of righting or mitigating them” (11). Withdrawing from that, Gee 8 explains the two tasks of any discourse analysis, one examines meaning and the other one examines situated meaning. The first one as Gee puts it, is what he calls utterance-type meaning task, which studies the links between form (words, phrases, morphemes, and syntactic structure) and function which is the meaning or the communicative purpose (24). The other task is utterance-token meaning, which is concerned with the link between form and meaning in the framework of situation. Simply put, in utterance-token meaning studies analysis, the analyst needs to discover the situations and contexts surrounding the utterance in order to decode the actual meaning. Gee emphasizes the importance of differentiating between these two tasks, to conduct a valid analysis.

Fairclough 1 creates a model of discourse analysis that depends on three basic dimensions of analysis; text, discursive practice, and social practice. Fairclough insists on the absence of a clear division between these three dimensions, because of the overlapping nature of all three features. Text as an analytical tool focuses on the linguistic features of any discourse and urges to describe and analyze lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors before delving into the other two dimensions. The second dimension focuses on the shared knowledge between the producer of the discourse and the audience receiving it. To take a close look into the discursive practice of the discourse, we look at the shared knowledge, intertextuality, and the production of the discourse in question and how the audience receives and comprehends it. The third dimension is the social practice, which looks into the several social statuses in a society, the social identities, ideologies, hegemony, and the social relationship between the producer of the discourse and the audience (Fairclough 1, 62-100).

**5.2. Political Discourse**
Wilson 9 differentiates between two types of political discourse. The first one focuses on political discourse that has an authentic association to politics, and the second type -which he withdraws from Shapiro 10- that claims all discourse as political regardless of its actual relation to political content or context. Wilson suggests that this confusion stems from the fact that the conditions upon which any discourse is considered political are very common in most of the discourses; these conditions involve power, control, conflict, or dominance. However, this broad definition of political discourse is not practical in the field of linguistics, which is why Wilson resorts to limiting the definition of political discourse into formal and informal political context and political actors, i.e. “politicians, political institutions, governments, political media, and political supporters operating in political environments to achieve political goals” (398).

Moreover, Wilson refers to Orwell’s 11 remarks on political discourse, and to the way politicians formulate language to deliver more peaceful and acceptable messages. For instance, he refers to the use of ‘pacification’ instead of ‘invasion’, which politicians use to mask the horrors and hostilities of invasions. The issue that presents itself here is the manipulation of language that blinds the masses to the negativity that might surround them, which is the case in every political statement or speech, and Abdel Nasser’s speeches are no exception.

Wilson acknowledges the essential ties between linguistics and socio-politics and highlights the efforts in combining both in any political discourse analysis. He insists to focus on the language as the main tool of analysis, and still manages to emphasize the importance of sociopolitical analysis claiming the language-based analysis do not consider answering ‘why’; why does this politician arrange his sentences in this manner, or what formulates his word choices? and so on.

**5.3. Previous Studies**
Bajri and Othman 12 conduct a comparative critical discourse analysis of Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech ‘I have a Dream’ and Malcolm X's speech ‘A Message to the Grassroots’. They use Fairclough's 3D model to deconstruct both discourses into their basic features, and divide the analysis into three major headlines; text, discursive practice, and social practice. Under each headline, a few other sublines talking specifically about certain features that fall under the headlines. For example, headline: text, subline: lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors. Bajri and Othman highlight the importance of the devices in both speeches -especially rhetorical-, and conclude on the importance of style in changing societies and perspectives, and point to the massive change that these discourses have inflected.

Equally as important is the work of Lahlali 13, in which he touches on pan-Arabism in Abdel Nasser’s speeches. According to Lahlali, Abdel Nasser uses words like ‘Arab unity’ and ‘Arab values’ to promote for pan-Arabism in order to gain support for his image as a leader of the Arab nation. Lahlali suggests that with his charisma and mastery of the Arabic language, Abdel Nasser manages to make the audience across Arab countries feel like one family. This mirrors what Diong 4 notices of Abdel Nasser's rhetoric techniques, whereby she asserts the importance of Abdel Nasser's word choices in the broadcasting of his propaganda and ideology. She states that the word choices “[are] made specifically to target the West and to spread anti-colonial sentiments amongst those who heard his speeches” (4). Diong withdraws from Al-Ahmed's 5 study that discusses Abdel Nasser’s use of language, in which Al-Ahmad states that his language has had waves of sympathy and aggression.

### 6. Methodology

**6.1. Theoretical Framework**
This paper utilizes Fairclough’s 1 model of critical discourse analysis to investigate Gamal Abdel Nasser’s 1967 speech.

**6.2. Data Collection**
The paper will analyze Gamal Abdel Nasser's stepping down speech, which has been delivered on June 9 th, 1967 through Sawt Al-Arab radio station from his office in Kubbeh palace in Cairo. The text has been retrieved from an online source dedicated to all of Abdel Nasser’s speeches.

**6.3. Data Analysis**
To analyze the data, application and discussion section will focus on the first dimension of Fairclough’s 1 3D model, which is text. Under text umbrella falls three subcategories; lexical items, rhetorical devices, and metaphors.

### 7. Application and Discussion

**7.1. Text**  
**7.1.1. Lexical Items**
Linguistic etiquette -according to Allan and Burridge 14- is used in implicit and indirect discourse and is found in our everyday speech. It includes “euphemism, swearing, polite talk, slang and political correctness", and it gives an indication of the speaker's attitude and intentions. Furthermore, linguistic etiquette -specifically talking about euphemism here- is a way of leveling the message, and delivering by masking the negativity in it 14.

Euphemism occurs repeatedly in Abdel Nasser’s stepping down speech. He mentions the word ‘al-naksa’ which is translated to ‘the setback’ four times, serving as a substitute for the word ‘defeat’. This word, in particular, is what frees Abdel Nasser from any consequences following his action that lead to the war and to losing the war.

As shown in Table 1, Abdel Nasser's speech is thematic; words reoccur in different synonyms and different stems from the same root. The main themes that appear in the speech are as follows:

1- Brotherhood: This theme is assembled in the word ‘brothers’ reoccurs many times in the speech to spread a feeling of intimacy and closeness among the audience.

2- Nationalism: As previously mentioned in the literature review, Pan-Arabism and the ideology of the Arab nation is heavily pushed in all of Abdel Nasser's speeches. In fact, Abdel Nasser himself mentions this ideology inflection in this very particular speech, wherein he states that the opposing forces of pan-Arabism talk about it as if it is Abdel Nasser's own empire -which he denies.

3- Togetherness and Honesty: Again, this speech is loaded with intimate words that Abdel Nasser tucks in, to draw a friendly, warm, and informal image. He uses his words to paint an image of himself and the public sitting ‘together’ and talking ‘together’, and getting accustomed to being honest ‘together’. He talks about ‘open hearts’ and ‘professing the truth’, which help him create an atmosphere of trust and closeness among his audience.

4- Righteousness: As a person who is responsible for the upsetting defeat, Abdel Nasser insists that his path is the right path, and his choice is the right choice. He mentions ‘victory’ and ‘righteous road’ as if the defeat is a natural catastrophe that happens despite all forces. Which is what Al-Azm 2 builds his argument around. Al-Azm claims that when Abdel Nasser uses the word of ‘al-naksa’ instead of defeat, he means to strip himself of any responsibility and to throw this defeat on the worlds' shoulders (2, forward)

5- Courage and Arab values: Abdel Nasser mentions a few traits that all Arabs value, such as ‘courage’, ‘honor’, ‘pride’, and ‘manliness’. These are a few traits that are deeply rooted in the psychology and history of Arabs. Abdel Nasser emphasizes on these word choices to be connect more with his audience; Arabs all over the world.

8- Revolution: ‘Revolution’ is Abdel Nasser’s background and validation. It is how he has come into power, and it is how he gains authority, so it is not strange that he mentions it for validity in almost all of his speeches. In this discourse, Abdel Nasser mentions ‘revolution’ in the context of achievements. He advertises for himself through the accomplishments of the revolution. He states that the revolution -represented in his own persona- has evacuated colonialism, brought independence to Egypt, defined Egypt’s Arabic character, retrieved the Suez channel, built the High Dam, and used petroleum resources. This is a short version of the long list that Abdel Nasser mentions in his speech as achievements of the revolution. Moreover, he asserts in every other sentence that these achievements have come after a long time of waiting. Abdel Nasser, being a communist, is proud in his speech that he has brought communism into Egypt and established its grounds.

9- Unity: Assertion on unity –‘Arabs unity’ and ‘Egyptians unity’- is another recurrent theme in the speech. In which Abdel Nasser manages to include all Arabs when the context revolves around the nation and manages to include all spectrums of society when the context revolves around Egypt.

  
**7.1.2. Rhetorical Devices**
The first rhetorical device in this discourse is ‘euphemism’ as mentioned in the previous section. On that matter, Abdel Latif 6 comments that the use of the word ‘al-naksa’ as an alternative for defeat comes of important significance. This is because Abdel Nasser and the while Egyptian media devices have promoted victory before and during the war, and the use of any words that indicate loss will harm his image (152). Abdel Latif mentions another rhetoric device in the speech, which is ‘dysphemism’. Examples for that is when Abdul Nasser uses the word ‘aggression’ instead of words like ‘invasion’, ‘occupation’, and ‘war’ to further emphasize the injustice and vices of the enemy (154).

*   
#### Table 2. Examples of Euphemism

[![Image 6](https://pubs.sciepub.com/jll/4/1/5/image/tab2.png)](http://pubs.sciepub.com/jll/4/1/5/Table/2 "Click for larger image")

*   
#### Table 3. Examples of Dysphemism

[![Image 7](https://pubs.sciepub.com/jll/4/1/5/image/tab3.png)](http://pubs.sciepub.com/jll/4/1/5/Table/3 "Click for larger image")

Another rhetorical device is ‘digression’, which is heavily used in the discourse at hand. According to Shahatah 15, ‘digression’ is of important significance in Arabic rhetoric because it is used by highly fluent people, and it is used as a sudden and surprising element. This style stimulates the receiver and charges his senses into paying closer attention to what is being said (3119). The following table contains a few examples of this rhetorical device.

*   
#### Table 4. Examples of Digression

[![Image 8](https://pubs.sciepub.com/jll/4/1/5/image/tab4.png)](http://pubs.sciepub.com/jll/4/1/5/Table/4 "Click for larger image") 
*   Download as [PowerPoint Slide](http://pubs.sciepub.com/portal/exportppt?doi=10.12691/jll-4-1-5&filename=tab4.png&ins=Table%204.%20Examples%20of%20Digression)  [Tables index](http://pubs.sciepub.com/jll/4/1/5/tables)  View option [Full Size](http://pubs.sciepub.com/jll/4/1/5/image/tab4.png)Previous Table  

Rhetorical questions are another style that Abdel Nasser uses in his speech. A rhetorical question, according to Harris 16 is a question that does not need answering, because the answer is self-evident, and it is usually implied in the question itself (171). An example of this is Abdel Nasser’s question: “Does this mean that we have no responsibility for the consequences of this setback?”, in which the answer is implied in the question so he does not need to assert on it.

  
**7.1.3. Metaphors**
Abdel Nasser's speech does not carry a lot of metaphors, perhaps for the urgency of the matter, and the hardships that accompany the topic. However, it is not totally empty of metaphors, and the first metaphor is ‘no matter how dim the light is’, which comes in the context where Abdel Nasser talks about the defeat. The other metaphors serve as eloquent style employed to tackle emotions like the metaphors that talks about the achievements of the revolution. For example, ‘an individual is a tool in the hands of popular will’, and the High Dam was built to spread fertile greenery over the desert’. He also uses metaphors to talk about the fallen soldiers, e.g. ‘glorious tournaments written by officers and soldiers of our armed forces with their blood’, and these tournaments ‘will remain a torch of light intact in our history’, along with: soldiers ‘defended the grains of sand in the desert to the last drop of their blood’.

### 8. Conclusion

The analysis shows the linguistic tools that Abdel Nasser uses in his speech on the text level. The nature of the lexical items he uses can be distributed into themes; brotherhood, nationalism -to assert on Pan-Arabism-, togetherness, and honesty - a tool to gain sympathetic reactions-, righteousness -to endorse his image as a leader-, courage and Arab values -to relate to all the masses in Arab countries using their values and identity-, revolution, and unity. The analysis also focuses on rhetorical devices and finds the main devices Abdel Nasser uses, such as euphemism, dysphemism, digression, and rhetorical questions. Some of these are used to mitigate the intensity of the defeat or magnify the enemy's responsibilities for what has happened, and the other devices are used to strengthen the speech. Regarding metaphors, the speech is not heavily loaded, but it contains some metaphors that serve as a tool to tackle emotions like the metaphors that talks about the achievements of the revolution. Other metaphors are used to describe the sacrifices and heroism of the fallen soldiers on the battlefield. All of these linguistic tools are of essence to Abdel Nasser to turn the tables in his favor. These tools are a part of the reasons why people have flooded into the streets to cheer for him despite his failure and despite the aftermath of this defeat. With that in mind, this analysis although thorough is not complete yet, since it does not cover the other dimensions of Fairclough’s 1 model, which are discursive and social practices. This limitation is due to the lack of time, but further study will be conducted to cover the rest of the dimensions.

## Bir 'Pan-Arap Kahramanın' Sosyal İnşası: Cemal Abdülnasır

## Abstract

 Bu makale, Cemal Abdülnasır'ın pan-Arap kimliğinin inşasını sosyal inşacı kuramsal bir yaklaşımla incelemektedir. Nasır’ın sembolik siyaseti akıllıca manipüle ederek, sosyal ve politik olarak bağlayıcı normlar oluşturup ve nihayetinde o normlar tarafından kısıtlanarak pan-Arap milliyetçiliğinin bir kahramanı olarak nasıl inşa edildiği konusunu ele almaktadır. Pan-Arap normlarının Nasır tarafından inşası ve yeniden inşasını açıklamada teorik bir model olarak sosyal inşacılıktan yararlanan bu çalışma, rasyönelizm ile açıklanamayan Mısır’ın ve Nasır’ın mutlak çıkarlarına aykırı olmasına rağmen Birleşik Arap Cumhuriyeti'nin kurulmasında, Kuzey Yemen İç Savaşı’nda (1962) ve 1967’de gerçekleşen Altı Gün Savaşı’nda yer almasını bu normların bağlayıcılığıyla açıklar.

## The Social Construction of a ‘Pan-Arabist Hero’: Gamal Abdel Nasser

## Abstract

 This article investigates the social construction of Gamal Abdel Nasser’s pan-Arab identity from a social constructivist theoretical approach. In this sense, it scrutinizes how Nasser came to be constructed as a pan-Arab hero by cleverly manipulating the symbolic politics and establishing socially and politically binding pan-Arab norms and eventually made himself constrained by them. This study also examines social constructivism’s explanatory power as a theoretical model in understanding and explaining Nasser’s political motives and moves by comparing it with that of rationalism. It is argued that Nasser’s power did not come from the economic or military capabilities, as rationalism fails to explain, but his power came from his ability to frame the events within a historical narrative in such a rhetorical way to establish new Arab norms. He was the leading figure in the establishment of United Arab Republic, North Yemen Civil War and The Six-Day War of 1967, despite all were against his and Egypt’s absolute material national interests. This article analyzes the path to nationalist ascent and descent of Nasser’s Arabism by chronologically scrutinizing on the discourses and events in order to examine the power of the given theories in explaining each period.

## Bir 'Pan-Arap Kahramanın' Sosyal İnşası: Cemal Abdülnasır

## Abstract

 Bu makale, Cemal Abdülnasır'ın pan-Arap kimliğinin inşasını sosyal inşacı kuramsal bir yaklaşımla incelemektedir. Nasır’ın sembolik siyaseti akıllıca manipüle ederek, sosyal ve politik olarak bağlayıcı normlar oluşturup ve nihayetinde o normlar tarafından kısıtlanarak pan-Arap milliyetçiliğinin bir kahramanı olarak nasıl inşa edildiği konusunu ele almaktadır. Pan-Arap normlarının Nasır tarafından inşası ve yeniden inşasını açıklamada teorik bir model olarak sosyal inşacılıktan yararlanan bu çalışma, rasyönelizm ile açıklanamayan Mısır’ın ve Nasır’ın mutlak çıkarlarına aykırı olmasına rağmen Birleşik Arap Cumhuriyeti'nin kurulmasında, Kuzey Yemen İç Savaşı’nda (1962) ve 1967’de gerçekleşen Altı Gün Savaşı’nda yer almasını bu normların bağlayıcılığıyla açıklar.

## The Social Construction of a ‘Pan-Arabist Hero’: Gamal Abdel Nasser

## Abstract

 This article investigates the social construction of Gamal Abdel Nasser’s pan-Arab identity from a social constructivist theoretical approach. In this sense, it scrutinizes how Nasser came to be constructed as a pan-Arab hero by cleverly manipulating the symbolic politics and establishing socially and politically binding pan-Arab norms and eventually made himself constrained by them. This study also examines social constructivism’s explanatory power as a theoretical model in understanding and explaining Nasser’s political motives and moves by comparing it with that of rationalism. It is argued that Nasser’s power did not come from the economic or military capabilities, as rationalism fails to explain, but his power came from his ability to frame the events within a historical narrative in such a rhetorical way to establish new Arab norms. He was the leading figure in the establishment of United Arab Republic, North Yemen Civil War and The Six-Day War of 1967, despite all were against his and Egypt’s absolute material national interests. This article analyzes the path to nationalist ascent and descent of Nasser’s Arabism by chronologically scrutinizing on the discourses and events in order to examine the power of the given theories in explaining each period.

# Gamal Abdel Nasser, the Suez Crisis, and Arab Nationalism

## Authors

*    Zihao Guo  Shanghai Pinghe School, Shanghai, China  Author 

## DOI:

[https://doi.org/10.71222/x1xxna23](https://doi.org/10.71222/x1xxna23)
## Keywords:

 Arab nationalism, Ottoman Empire, Suez Canal, Free Officers' Movement, Aswan High Dam 
## Abstract

Egypt, long celebrated as the cradle of civilization, flourished along the Nile River but endured centuries of foreign domination that diminished its cultural prominence. Autonomy briefly resurfaced after Napoleon's 1798 expedition, yet Western imperial control soon prevailed, especially following the construction of the strategically vital Suez Canal. By the early twentieth century, Egypt had become an Arab nation striving for independence. Three milestones marked this process: the establishment of a British-protected monarchy in 1922, the Free Officers' Movement of 1952 that founded the republic, and the 1956 Suez Crisis. The latter, provoked by Egypt's nationalization of the Suez Canal, ended with the failure of a joint British, French, and Israeli invasion under pressure from both the United States and the Soviet Union. This moment signified Egypt's true independence and a triumph for Arab nationalism. While most studies emphasize Britain's decline or U.S. opposition to the invasion, this paper adopts an Arab-centered perspective. It investigates Egypt's motives for nationalizing the canal and shows how the Suez Crisis elevated President Gamal Abdel Nasser as the leading figure of the Arab world. The discussion highlights economic, social, and political dimensions of how the crisis advanced Nasser's vision of Arab nationalism.

# Gamal Abdel Nasser, the Suez Crisis, and Arab Nationalism

## Authors

*    Zihao Guo  Shanghai Pinghe School, Shanghai, China  Author 

## DOI:

[https://doi.org/10.71222/x1xxna23](https://doi.org/10.71222/x1xxna23)
## Keywords:

 Arab nationalism, Ottoman Empire, Suez Canal, Free Officers' Movement, Aswan High Dam 
## Abstract

Egypt, long celebrated as the cradle of civilization, flourished along the Nile River but endured centuries of foreign domination that diminished its cultural prominence. Autonomy briefly resurfaced after Napoleon's 1798 expedition, yet Western imperial control soon prevailed, especially following the construction of the strategically vital Suez Canal. By the early twentieth century, Egypt had become an Arab nation striving for independence. Three milestones marked this process: the establishment of a British-protected monarchy in 1922, the Free Officers' Movement of 1952 that founded the republic, and the 1956 Suez Crisis. The latter, provoked by Egypt's nationalization of the Suez Canal, ended with the failure of a joint British, French, and Israeli invasion under pressure from both the United States and the Soviet Union. This moment signified Egypt's true independence and a triumph for Arab nationalism. While most studies emphasize Britain's decline or U.S. opposition to the invasion, this paper adopts an Arab-centered perspective. It investigates Egypt's motives for nationalizing the canal and shows how the Suez Crisis elevated President Gamal Abdel Nasser as the leading figure of the Arab world. The discussion highlights economic, social, and political dimensions of how the crisis advanced Nasser's vision of Arab nationalism.

Propaganda  or  Reality?  Reevaluating  the  Tripartite
Aggression  and  the  Dynamics  of  Post-Colonial  Power

Salma  Abuelatta

Abstract

By  1954,  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser  had  successfully  consolidated  power  and
outmanoeuvred  internal  opposition.  After  Britain,  the  United  States  and  the
International  Bank  withdrew  their  offers  to  fund  the High  Aswan  Dam,  Nasser
resolved  to  nationalise  the British  and  French  owned  Suez  Canal  Company.  In the
ensuing  Suez  War,  despite  Egypt’s  military  defeat  at the  hands  of Britain,  France
and  Israel,  Nasser’s  power  and  popularity  were  amplified,  arguably  to  mythological
levels.  He  remains  a  monumental  figure  of  pride  to many  in contemporary  Egypt,
particularly  due  to the  Suez  Crisis.  Whether  this isdue  to the  success  of  his actions
and  policies,  or  charisma  and  propaganda,  remains  unclear.  Through  the  case  study
of  Nasser,  this paper  aims  to  identify  patterns  of how  dictators  in  quasi-colonised
and  post-colonial  states  construct  narratives  against  and  manipulate  the unpopularity
of  oppressive  colonialist  nations  to fortify their  own  power.  This  essay  argues  that
although  Nasser  did  help  eliminate  the  remnants  of  British  and  French  colonial
presence  in  Egypt,  his  successes  in  aggrandising  certain  aspects  of  the  Crisis
through  propaganda  was  more  significant  to cultivating  his mythological  status  and
power.
Keywords:  Post-colonial  states, Egypt,  Suez  Crisis,  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser,  Middle
Eastern  History,  British  Foreign  Policy,  Collapse  of the British  Empire,  Suez  Canal

Introduction

By  1954,  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser  had  successfully  consolidated  power  and  outmanoeuvred  internal
opposition.1  In July  1956,  Britain,  the  United  States  and  the  International  Bank  withdrew  their offers
to fund  Nasser’s  project,  the  High  Aswan  Dam,  citing  Egypt’s  bankruptcy,  although  the  true reason
was  Nasser’s  flirtations with  the East  during  the  Cold  War.2  In retaliation,  Nasser  set  his sights  on
nationalising  the  Suez  Canal  Company,  which  he  estimated  could  potentially  cover  the  costs  of the
Dam  alone,  and  he  did  so  on July  26,  1956.3  British  and  French  ownership  of Suez  Canal  Company

After  Nasser  nationalised  the  Suez  Canal,  Britain,  France,  and  Israel conspired  an invasion  to

resolved  to  resign  as  a  result, there  were  protests  on  the streets  calling  for  his  return.7 He  remains  a
monumental  figure  of  pride  to many  in contemporary  Egypt,  especially  due  to the  Crisis.8  Whether
this is due  to the  success  of his  actions  and  policies,  or  charisma  and  propaganda  remains  unclear.  It is
worth  re-evaluating  how  dictators  in  quasi-colonised  countries  use  rhetoric  against  colonialist
aggressor  nations  to fortify their  power  to the  extent  of creating  such  loyalty.9
Outside  of  secondary  literature,  this essay  will  draw  upon  primary  research  in  the form  of
interviews  conducted  with  middle-class  Egyptians,  Mariam  who  was  17  years  old at  the time  of the
Suez  Crisis,  and  Ahmed,  who  was  born  in 1959  and  grew  up  in the  ensuing  aftermath.  Their  names
have  been  changed  for  anonymity.  This  is supplemented  by  other  external  accounts,  popular  music,
the British  cabinet’s  meeting  minutes,  and  Nasser’s  speeches  to examine  the impact  of propaganda  on
public  opinion.  This  paper  is split  into themed  sections  oriented  around  different  aspects  of the  Crisis
and  the  nationalisation  of  the  Suez  Canal  that  helped  Nasser  maintain  his  power.  Each  section
examines  whether  it was  presentation,  such  as  propaganda  and  Nasser’s  charisma,  or reality,  as  in
Nasser’s  concrete  actions,  policies,  and  results,  that aided  Nasser’s  maintenance  of power.  I argue  that
although  Nasser  did  help  eliminate  the  remnants  of  colonial  presence  in  Egypt,  his  success  in
aggrandising  certain  aspects  of the  Crisis through  propaganda  was  more  significant  to his  maintenance
of power.

Funds  and  The  High  Aswan  Dam

In his initial announcement  of the nationalisation  of  the Canal  on  July  26 1956,  Nasser  made  repeating
reference  to one  argument  for  nationalising  the  Canal:  itsenormous  financial  potential,  particularly  to
fund  his project,  the  High  Aswan  Dam.  The  Dam  was  meant  to  lessen  the  loss  of  silt, reign  in
detrimental  annual  flooding  from  the  Nile,  thus  increasing  farmland  by  20-30%,10  as  well  as  store
additional  water  in  the Lake  Nasser  reservoir  for irrigation.11  However,  the Dam  was  barely  funded  by
Canal  revenue.12  Instead,  Egypt  primarily  used  Soviet  loans  acquired  in  1958.13  Therefore,  the  Dam

Yet,  the  High  Dam  seems  to  have  been  eternalised  in the collective  Egyptian  mind  as being  a
result of  the  nationalisation  of  the  Canal  in how  itwas  presented.  A  key  example  of this is Abdel
Halim  Hafez’s  song  ‘Hekayet  Sha’b’  (the  story  of a nation).  Hafez  was  one  of the Arab  world’s  most
popular  celebrities,  making  his  music  greatly  influential.15  Therefore,  his  song  is  useful  to
understanding  public  opinion.  The  song  details  how  Egyptians  built  the Dam  “with  our own  money”16
(referencing  Canal  proceeds),  despite  the  fact itwas  released  after the  Soviets  agreed  to aid in funding
the Dam,  thus  linking  the  two  together  more  than  was  reality. 17 Moreover,  there  ismuch  evidence  that
these  messages  effectively  impacted  Egyptian  audiences.  The  song  is laid  out  as a simple  emotive
narrative  and  uses  simpler  language,18  thereby  making  it more  memorable  and  accessible  to allclasses
of Egyptians,  particularly  because  Egypt  had  an  illiteracy  rate of  77.2%  in 1947.  19 Historian  Joel
Gordon  comments  that  all the  “Wataniya”  songs  generally  from  this time  had  a similar  joyous
atmosphere  and  were  made  to  be  accessible  to the  lower  class.20  Ahmed  claims  that everyone  was
listening  to (Hafez’s  song).21  Indeed,  Ahmed  even  directly  parallels  claims  made  in the  song,  with
Hafez’s  song  stating  “nationalisation  irritated the  colonialists,  why  should  we  be able  to  restore  our
glory?”22  and  Ahmed  noting  “we  wanted  to  improve  our  country,  everyone  stood  against  us”.23
Mariam  also  adds  that the  song  ‘perfectly’  embodied  the Crisis.24 This  reveals  how  the song  was  able
to directly impact  Egyptians’  opinions.
This  combination  of  presenting  the Dam  as a symbol  of  the struggle  against  colonialism  and  a
symbol  of  Egypt’s  advancement  helped  popularise  the  belief  that  ‘the  colonialists’  were  not  just
attempting  to maintain  their power,  but  were  purposefully  aiming  to undermine  Egypt’s  progress  and
‘return  to greatness’  by  refusing  to  finance  it, and  indeed,  Ahmed  refers  to the invasion  as an  attempt
to thwart  Egypt’s  progress.25  This  garnered  support  for Nasser,  because  he  was  the  man  known  for
building  the  Dam  and  fighting  colonialist  oppression  by defiantly  nationalizing  the Canal.  This  can  be
seen  in the  popular  nationalist  song  Al Geal  El Saeed,  released  in 1960  by  Mohammed  Abdel  Wahab,
which  concludes  with  references  to how  Egyptians  “Build  with  you  (Nasser)”.26
The  Dam  was  an  important  factor  in bolstering  Nasser’s  maintenance  of power  as it served  as
a symbol  of Egypt’s  progress.  However,  itwasn’t  a consequence  of the  nationalisation  of the  Canal.
The  way  the  Dam  was  presented  in relation  to the  Crisis  in popular  media,  helped  engineer  the
popular  perception  that the  Dam,  this symbol  of progress’,  existence  was  intimately  dependent  on  the
Suez  Crisis,  thus  making  Egypt’s  advancement  in general  seem  dependent  on  the  Crisis. Therefore,
the presentation  of  the Crisis  was  more  significant  to Nasser’s  maintenance  of power  in  the case  of the
High  Aswan  Dam.

Cementing  Nasser’s  Cult  of Personality

Nationalising  the  Canal
Through  the  act of  nationalising  the  Canal,  Nasser  was  able  to validate  his regime’s  anti-colonialist
rhetoric  and  affirm  his  persona  as the only  man  who  sticks to his word  and  is defiant  in the face  of the
colonialists, thus  enhancing  his power.
The  weakness  of the  previous  government  in its handling  of  British control  over  Egypt  was  a
key  factor  to its downfall.  When  King  Farouk  refused  to appoint  a Wafd  government  at the behest  of
the British  in  1942,  tanks  were  positioned  outside  his  palace  in a show  of force,  forcing  Farouk  to
concede.  27Cook  claims  this  incident  significantly  discredited  both  the  parliamentary  system  and  the
monarchy.28  Indeed,  this incident  showcased  the  government’s  subservience  to  the British  as  well  as
highlighting  the inability  of Farouk  and  parliamentary  parties  to be an  effective  united  front  in the face
of British  interference.  Considering  how  important  abolishing  British  presence  was  to Egyptians,  the
government’s  inability to  do  so made  them  seem  inept  and  inadequate.  Therefore,  Nasser  standing  up
to the British  so  openly  and  seemingly  fearlessly  for Egyptian  interests contrasted  with  such  incidents
where  fear  of  the  British  seemed  to  dictate  Egyptian  leaders’  actions.  Mariam  asserts  “they  (the
previous  government)  were  unable  to act…  Nasser  clearly  didn’t  have  that  issue”.29
Due  to  this context,  some  historians,  such  as  Joel  Gordon,  argue  that  no  propaganda  could
save  the  regime  -  only  action.30  Certainly,  Nasser  was  initially  in a  tumultuous  and  contentious
position,  as  highlighted  by  the  March  Crisis  of 1954,  where  Nasser  and  his  Command  Council
Revolutionary  (CCR)  had  battled  a  beloved  military  figure,  Mohammed  Naguib,  for  the position  of
Egypt’s  leader.  There  had  even  been  protests  demanding  Nasser’s  head  and  200  military  officers
protested  in  favor  of Naguib.31  Yet,  by  the point  of  the Suez  Crisis,  Nasser’s  power  and  persona  was
arguably  widely  consolidated.  In the  Manshiya  incident  of October  26, 1954,  Mahmoud  Abdel  Latif, a
member  of  the  Muslim  Brotherhood,32  failed  to assassinate  Nasser  while  he was  giving  a speech  in
Manshiya  Square.  33 Nasser  capitalised  on  the  opportunity,  giving  his iconic  “Each  of  you  is Gamal
Abdel  Nasser”  speech  which  turned  public  opinion  strongly  in his favour,  34 consequentially  enabling
his crackdown  of  the  Muslim  Brotherhood  with  mass  arrests.35 In  fact, civilians  themselves  across
Cairo  set  fire to Muslim  Brotherhood  headquarters.36  Thus,  Nasser  had  already  acquired  a decently
stable level  of power  and  public  support  by  the  time  of the  Suez  Crisis, and  he  managed  to do  so by
using  opportunistic  propaganda,  suggesting  that  it is entirely  within  the  realm  of  possibility  that the
popularity  surrounding  his  decision  to nationalise  the  Canal  was  more  majorly  manufactured  by
propaganda  than  the act in of  itself.
Indeed,  Nasser’s  speech  announcing  the  nationalisation  of  the  Canal  was  extremely
sensational.  He  gave  it in Manshiya  Square,  recalling  to Egyptian’s  his previous  inflammatory  speech
in the Manshiya  Incident  and  hence  evoking  a stronger  sense  of support.  Beyond  this,the  speech  was

Still, whilst  Nasser’s  propaganda  may  have  amplified  the  potency  of  his  actions,  there  is
reason  to believe  that  the desire  to stand  up  to colonialist  oppression  did not  originate  with  Nasser’s
speech.40  A  minister  in Nasser’s  cabinet,  Sami  Sharaf,  claimed  he felt “internally  proud”  when  Nasser
firstsuggested  nationalising  the Suez  Canal  Company  to him  in private,  prior  to  the speech.41  While
Sharaf  may  be  embellishing,  Mariam  adds  further  credence  by  stating  that  the reason  the  Egyptian
public  was  overjoyed  by  the  nationalisation  of  the  Canal  was  because  itwas  an  ancient,  pre-existing
dream  Nasser  had  managed  to  fulfil,not  one  he  pioneered.42  While  the ‘120,000’  figure  iscontentious,
there  are  numerous  other  examples  of  colonialist  oppression  that  would  make  Egyptians  desire  a
general  complete  removal  of  British  presence.  A  notable  example  is the  Denshawai  Incident  of  1906,
where  a  confrontation  between  British  soldiers  and  Egyptian  villagers  led  to mass  unjust  executions
and  sentences  of  hard  labour.43  The  incident  lived  on  in the  Egyptian  memory,  as  evidenced  by
Mariams  joy  that  Egyptians  could  fight  back  during  the  war  “unlike  Denshawai”44  and  casual
references  to it by  famous  journalists  such  as Muhammed  Heikal.45
Nasser’s  speech  was  effective  in  amplifying  public  support,  and  iteven  exaggerated  certain
details  to ensure  enough  outrage  at  the  Suez  Canal’s  colonial  past.  Yet,  Nasser’s  actual  action  was
capitalising  on,  and  not  pioneering,  pre-existing  strongly  established  Egyptian  desires  to remove  the
British  entirely.  Thus,  Nasser’s  actions  in nationalising  the Canal,  more  significantly  than  propaganda,
solidified  his  strength  of  character  and  cemented  him  as  an  improvement  upon  ‘the  old  order’  of
government  and  politicians.

powerful  militaries.

Numerous  historians,  such  as  Steven  Cook,  assert that  itwas  the  United  States’  stance  against

documents  from  official  British  cabinet  meetings,  such  as  the meeting  where  they  discussed  their
declining  economic  position,  where  a  highlighted  reality  was  their  need  for  US  economic  assistance
and  their  inability  to obtain  it due  to  their actions  in the  Crisis.53  In  fact, the final  straw  was  when
Eisenhower  didn’t  support  Eden’s  pursuit  of a $1  billion loan  from  the International  Monetary  Fund.54
The  fact  that  the US  played  such  a  big  role in  the  crisis shows  that there  is a dissonance  between
propaganda  and  reality, where  propaganda  consistently  perpetuated  an  inaccurate  image  of Nasser  just
as the  man  who  nationalised  the  Suez  Canal,  but  also  as  the  man  who  successfully  ravaged  the
enemies’  armies  even  under  impossible  conditions.
The  concept  of victory  against  the  powerful  oppressors  after so  many  years  of struggle  was
overwhelming  to Egyptians.  Ahmed  describes  how  “despite  his shortcomings”,  the most  prominent
part  of Nasser’s  “legacy”  in his  memory  is how  he  led  Egypt  against  Britain,  “a  hugely  powerful
country”  and  “overcame”  them.”55  This  again  displays  an underlying  belief  that Nasser  was  the  cause
of  Egyptian  victory  over  the  British  and  French.  Furthermore,  Ahmed’s  words  reveal  how,  in
believing  Nasser  was  the  cause  of  victory,  Egyptians  finally  believed  their capabilities  could  be
expanded,  particularly  after decades  of  failure  to eliminate  repressive  colonialist  presence  in Egypt
with  previous  governments,  because  an  Egyptian  had  led  them  to victory  and  lived up  to  his words.
Mariam  also  comments  that in  winning  the war,  Nasser  had  achieved  “the  impossible”  56 and  how
“overjoyed”57  she  was  at that fact. To  Egyptians,  Nasser  did  not merely  win  the war,  he  revived  Egypt,
belief in Egypt’s  potential  and  pride  in Egyptian  national  identity.
Of  course,  Egyptians  weren’t  completely  ignorant  of the role  of American  opposition.  Mariam
acknowledges  that  the  American  helped  end  the  war.58  Yet,  the specific  diction  highlighted  above
perpetually  reveals  an  underlying  subconscious  belief  in an  exaggerated  view  of  Nasser’s  role.  For
example,  Mariam  discusses  how  through  achieving  victory  under  unfavourable  conditions,  Nasser
restored  “that sense  of hope”  that Egyptians  “could  be  more”.59

Propaganda or Reality?

The  victory  in the  war  being  deemed  as Nasser’s  victory  was  more  significant  in legitimising
Nasser  than  even  the  nationalisation  of  the  Canal  was.  The  nationalisation  highlighted  Nasser’s
courage  and  lack  of hesitance  to act towards  progress,  unlike  his predecessors.  Yet, as revealed  by the
above  comments,  his  ‘victory’  over  the  aggressors  solidifies  him  as  not  merely  courageous  but
substantively  capable  of  leading  Egypt  beyond  its colonial  past.  This  would  consequently  instil great,
potentially  blind,  trust in Nasser  as a  leader  and  his Arab  Nationalist  ideology  beyond  the Suez  Crisis
to mythological  levels, thereby  intensely.
Thus,  Nasser’s  effort  to  nationalise  the  Canal  was  a  bold  move  that  helped  propagate  his
persona  as  Egyptians  were  overjoyed  simply  to  observe  concrete  action  being  taken.  However,
Egypt’s  victory  in the  war  was  more  significant  as it provided  Nasser’s  words  with  tangible  results
previously  thought  unobtainable  and  promulgated  a new  sense  of  hope  throughout  Egypt  in the
country’s  potential,  cementing  Nasser’s  cult  of  personality  as the  much  stronger  and  more  effective
leader  in  the process.  Yet,  Egypt’s  victory  was  not  a result  of Nasser’s  actions.  Instead,  he  solidified
the idea  that they  were  through  propaganda.  Therefore,  propaganda  painting  Nasser  as the  cause  of
Egypt’s  victory  is what  cemented  his  cult  of personality  and  allowed  him  to become,  as  Anwar  El
Sadat  claimed,  an  “Egyptian  mythological  hero”.60

Costs  of War  and  Battling  the  Colonialists

As  is conventional  for  war-time  propaganda,  Nasser’s  propaganda  glorified  the  costs  of war  as
necessary  losses  to Egypt’s  liberation,  implying  that  propaganda  allowed  Nasser  to palliate  the  costs
of war.  An  example  of this  isin  ‘Sawt  Al  Arab’  (Voice  of  the Arabs),  a nationalistic  radio  program  run
by  the Egyptian  government  which  was  also  widely  popular  over  the  whole  Arab  world.61  Numerous
enthusiastic  speeches  calling  to  Egyptians  “to strike  out  against  the  aggressors”62  aired  frequently,
alongside  Nasser  himself  claiming  it to be  a duty  of the  people  “to  struggle  to get  the  enemy  out  of
their country”63  and  playing  nationalistic  songs.64  Mariam  claims  that in the  aftermath  of the  Crisis,
Egyptians  were  “overwhelmed  with  joy”.65  She  passionately  asserts  the  necessity  of  martyrs  and
glorifies  their deaths  because  “they  died  fighting  for  the freedom  of  their country”.66  Suffering  in war
is intertwined  with  a sense  of the  honour  and  vindication  of obtaining  freedom,  thereby  transforming
that suffering  into  a  source  of pride  in  of itself. Egypt  experienced  the  heaviest  losses  in  the war  on
every  front,  as  it took  place  entirely  on  Egyptian  soil  and  in  Egyptians  towns  that  were  destroyed,67
and  having  the  highest  number  of  casualties.68  Infrastructure  was  badly  damaged  during  the  war,
particularly  when  itcame  to transportation  like  railways,  roads  and  airports,69  a particularly  difficult
setback  for  a  nation  pushing  industrialisation.70  Egypt  opted  to  blockade  the  Canal,  causing  an

However,  this  feature  of  Nasser’s  propaganda  is merely  a  reflection  of  the  context  Egypt
faced.  Nasser  had  committed  a provocative  but  legal  action  in nationalising  the Suez  Canal.72  The  fact
that Eden  had  seen  this action  as a threat  and  was  determined  to destroy  Nasser  and  reassert  British
military  presence  in  the Canal  for it is evidence  that  he  was  an  aggressor  and  a real threat  to Egypt’s
sovereignty.73  Eden  made  many  attempts  to add  a façade  of legality  to his actions  and  present  Egypt  as
the true  aggressor,  with  the British-French  request  for a  ceasefire  between  Egypt  and  Israel  being
intentionally  done  in  a  manner  that  would  weaken  Egypt’s  position  comparatively,  making  it
impossible  for Nasser  to  accept.74  Thus,  it was  Britain’s  own  actions  which  reinforced  the  popular
public  conception  that  it was  stilloperating  under  the apparatus  of an  oppressive  colonialist  state in
Egypt.  Ahmed  observes  how  “Britain  was  being  ridiculous”  in beginning  the  war  “just  because  we
nationalised  something  in  our  own  land”.75  Mariam  also  acknowledges  that “no  one  was  happy  their
country  was  being  invaded,  but  the people  were  ready  to fight”.76 This  notion  was  omnipresent  across
Egypt  and  instigated  a great  deal  of unified  action  amongst  civilians.  Civilians  were  given  guns  and
encouraged  to  fight  themselves,  resulting  in numerous  civilian  makeshift  troops.77  Samir  Ghanem,  a
member  of the  Egyptian  military  intelligence  at the  time,  claimed  “every  Egyptian  was  willing  to
sacrifice  himself  to  defend  his  country”.78  This  may  be  exaggeratory,  given  Ghanem’s  position,
however  these  claims  are  somewhat  supported  by  Mariam,  who  details  how  her brother  attempted  to
get personally  involved  in the  struggle  and  claims  “the  regular  people  were  fighting”,79  “when  faced
with  an  external  threat,  we  unified”.80  Common  cause  was  established  between  Nasser  and  his  people
through  the creation  of a  common  enemy.  The  destruction  of war  was  not  whitewashed,  but rather  the
responsibility  of that  destruction  was  rightly  allocated  to  the real aggressors  rather  than  Nasser,  which
in turn allowed  for that  destruction  to be a symbol  of the resilience  of Egyptian  nationalism.
Nasser’s  power  was  aided  by  the destruction  of  war  as  itallowed  him  to capitalise  on Britain
proving  themselves  to be  the  oppressive  colonialists  Egyptians  saw  them  as. As  with  the  case  of the
nationalisation  of the  Suez  Canal,  Egyptian  state-owned  media  did not  manufacture  the impact  of the
aggressors’  oppression.  Rather,  it constantly  perpetuated  narratives  of it and  capitalised  on  it to
amplify  the  nationwide  sense  of unified  resistance.  Nasser’s  actions  in  creating  civilian  troops  also
had  a  similar  effect.  Hence,  both  Nasser’s  actions  and  propaganda  capitalised  on  anti-colonialist
sentiment,  but  itwas  the actions  of Britain,  France  and  Israel,  both  in the Suez  Crisis  and  previously,
which  created  the foundation  of that sense  in the Egyptian  public  mind.

Conclusion

The  Suez  Crisis  greatly  elevated  Nasser’s  power.  Many  of  Nasser’s  actions  helped  him  maintain  his
power,  such  as the  shocking  defiance  and  strength  he  demonstrated  in nationalising  the Canal  and  his
strategic  decision-making  during  the war.  Often,  Egyptian  unity  with  Nasser  was  effectively  promoted
by  propaganda  surrounding  the  destruction  of  the  war,  but  it was  not  founded  on  itas  anti-Western

the nationalisation  of the  Canal  and  the  myth  of Nasser  as  the man  who  achieved  victory.  The  latter
most  majorly  contributed  to Nasser’s  power  as Egypt  had  failed  for  decades  to do  so,  making  such  a
victory  seem  ‘impossible’.  Thus,  Nasser  ‘achieving  victory’  mythologised  him  and  created  an
overwhelming  sense  of trust  not just  in his courage  but  also in  his infallibility.It also  restored  hope  in
the potential  for Egyptian  greatness  in the  future,  validating  and  popularising  Nasser’s  ideology  of
Arab  Nationalism.  Therefore,  the  presentation  of the  Suez  Crisis  was  more  significant  to Nasser’s
maintenance  of  power  than  Nasser’s  actions.
This  case  study  of Nasser  reveals  much  about  the machinations  of power  for authoritarians  in
post-colonial  states.  Even  after decolonisation,  the  lasting  influence  of Britain  maintained  a sense  of
oppression  in the  Egyptian  public  mind,  and  this  continued  to be  one  of the  most  salient  areas  of
political discontent.  What  was  most  pertinent,  however,  was  not  Nasser’s  real  demonstration  of his
capabilities  through  his  actions,  but  rather  the  perception  of  Nasser’s  ability  to  ‘beat  back’  the
colonisers.  Nasser’s  competency  was  not  a  prerequisite  to  his  popularity  but  was  sufficiently
compensated  by  the  perception  his propaganda  was  able  to promulgate.  On  Nasser,  Fouad  Ajami
comments  that  “the  calculus  of  achievements  and  errors  doesn’t  seem  to  apply  to  charismatic
leaders”.81  Whilst  not untrue,  itis essential  to understand  the context  under  which  this charisma  arose.
It was  not  merely  Nasser’s  charisma,  but  rather  his  strongman  appearance  before  what  Egyptians
believed  to be  an  impossible  enemy,  with  much  desperation  to  find  someone  willing  to fight  back
rather than  rely on  Britain’s  endorsement  to maintain  their  power.

Aggression  and  the  Dynamics  of  Post-Colonial  Power

Salma  Abuelatta

Abstract

By  1954,  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser  had  successfully  consolidated  power  and
outmanoeuvred  internal  opposition.  After  Britain,  the  United  States  and  the
International  Bank  withdrew  their  offers  to  fund  the High  Aswan  Dam,  Nasser
resolved  to  nationalise  the British  and  French  owned  Suez  Canal  Company.  In the
ensuing  Suez  War,  despite  Egypt’s  military  defeat  at the  hands  of Britain,  France
and  Israel,  Nasser’s  power  and  popularity  were  amplified,  arguably  to  mythological
levels.  He  remains  a  monumental  figure  of  pride  to many  in contemporary  Egypt,
particularly  due  to the  Suez  Crisis.  Whether  this isdue  to the  success  of  his actions
and  policies,  or  charisma  and  propaganda,  remains  unclear.  Through  the  case  study
of  Nasser,  this paper  aims  to  identify  patterns  of how  dictators  in  quasi-colonised
and  post-colonial  states  construct  narratives  against  and  manipulate  the unpopularity
of  oppressive  colonialist  nations  to fortify their  own  power.  This  essay  argues  that
although  Nasser  did  help  eliminate  the  remnants  of  British  and  French  colonial
presence  in  Egypt,  his  successes  in  aggrandising  certain  aspects  of  the  Crisis
through  propaganda  was  more  significant  to cultivating  his mythological  status  and
power.
Keywords:  Post-colonial  states, Egypt,  Suez  Crisis,  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser,  Middle
Eastern  History,  British  Foreign  Policy,  Collapse  of the British  Empire,  Suez  Canal

Introduction

By  1954,  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser  had  successfully  consolidated  power  and  outmanoeuvred  internal
opposition.1  In July  1956,  Britain,  the  United  States  and  the  International  Bank  withdrew  their offers
to fund  Nasser’s  project,  the  High  Aswan  Dam,  citing  Egypt’s  bankruptcy,  although  the  true reason
was  Nasser’s  flirtations with  the East  during  the  Cold  War.2  In retaliation,  Nasser  set  his sights  on
nationalising  the  Suez  Canal  Company,  which  he  estimated  could  potentially  cover  the  costs  of the
Dam  alone,  and  he  did  so  on July  26,  1956.3  British  and  French  ownership  of Suez  Canal  Company
